name: Daily Montanan
title: Immigration authorities are detaining a Montana child illegally, attorneys allege
description: A 9-year-old child with special medical needs from Billings is being held at the Havre Border Patrol Station after U.S. Customs and Border Patrol made an unlawful arrest earlier this month, according to a petition filed in the U.S. District Court of Montana. Federal agents detained parent Adrián Espinoza De La Cruz and the child […]
text:
Photo illustration by Getty Images.A 9-year-old child with special medical needs from Billings is being held at the Havre Border Patrol Station after U.S. Customs and Border Patrol made an unlawful arrest earlier this month, according to a petition filed in the U.S. District Court of Montana.
Federal agents detained parent Adrián Espinoza De La Cruz and the child on Aug. 11, and they are being held at a facility that lacks basic amenities, including proper bedding, the court filing states.
The petition filed Tuesday alleges Custom and Border Patrol agents detained the child and parent without a judicial warrant and are holding them without considering their ties to Billings. Attorneys with Upper Seven Law are calling for their immediate release.
The petition names acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche; Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials, including Utah Field Office Director Michael Bernacke; and Havre Chief Patrol Agent Zachary Crosson with CBP.
Espinoza De La Cruz has lived in Billings for four years, according to the petition, and his child has lived there for three years and attends elementary school there.
The child has medical issues and upcoming appointments that took months to schedule, the court filing says. “(The child’s) parents made the appointment at the beginning of May. (The child) needs to complete bloodwork and an ultrasound one week before,” the petition states.
The lawyers also note the detention center in Havre is not designed to be a “long-term detention facility,” and an incarcerated minor is entitled to specific protections, including “suitable living conditions, appropriate and routine medical care, (and) screening for infectious diseases.” Standards for minors also include proper food, clothing, grooming items, contact with family members, and a “reasonable right” to privacy.
In a response filed Wednesday on behalf of the U.S. government, the U.S. Attorney’s Office acknowledged that officers arrested the parent and child without a warrant and without evidence they were an escape risk.
Assistant U.S. Attorneys Timothy Tatarka and Randy Tanner said the government issued warrants after the parent and child arrived at the station in Havre, and they said Espinoza De La Cruz and the child are from Mexico and present in the United States without legal permission.
The lawyers admitted the court rejected similar arguments in other cases but said nevertheless, the government maintains releasing the parent and child would not be appropriate.
The lawyers did not address in their court filing how the U.S. government is meeting the more stringent standards for holding a minor, and in a brief phone call Wednesday, Tatarka said he could not comment on the question.
Tatarka directed the Daily Montanan to the communications office, whose spokesperson declined to comment and directed questions to Customs and Border Patrol. The Daily Montanan reached out to CBP, ICE and U.S. Department of Homeland Security media contacts, as well as Crosson with the Havre sector, and did not hear answers as of press time.
The child and parent are part of a potential class action case, also filed by Upper Seven, alleging the federal government is detaining 17 people in the Cascade County Detention Center on illegal immigration holds.
“We are appalled to witness the federal government using its immense power not only to unlawfully take and detain adult Montanans, but to grab children from our streets,” said Upper Seven’s senior staff attorney Andres Haladay in an email. “There is nothing righteous in this utter failure of law enforcement. Nine-year-olds belong in school, not in border patrol stations for days on end without proper bedding.”
A hearing in the potential class action case is set for Sept. 4, but the lawyers argue the detention of the minor requires immediate attention from the court.
“The exceptional circumstances of a nine-year-old child being incarcerated in a temporary CBP detention facility in Havre … necessitates immediate relief,” the petition says. “Petitioners attempted to negotiate relief from respondents, prior to filing, but respondents refused any potential relief.”
A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office said the office typically does not comment on active litigation.
In court filings, attorneys for the plaintiffs argue the court should release the father and child because their detention violates the Immigration and Nationality Act and the Due Process Clause of the U.S. Constitution. But if they are not released, the court should hold a bond hearing as is standard, they wrote.
“Immigration detention must reasonably relate to the government’s goals of preventing flight and protecting the community from harm and be accompanied by adequate procedural protections to ensure those goals are being served,” the petition states.
Attorneys also note DHS is required to “release a minor from its custody without unnecessary delay.”
They ask the court to assume jurisdiction, ensure the respondents don’t transfer the parent and child outside the district, and order their immediate release or a bond hearing.
They also ask the court to award attorneys’ fees and costs.

text:
The Ohio burgee. (Getty images file photo.)Every morning in the Ohio Capital Journal’s free newsletter, The Eye-Opener, we round up the news and commentary from across Ohio and around the country and world that is catching our attention. We call this feature Catching Our Eye, republished here.
Please subscribe to our free daily newsletter to get all the Ohio news you need to know right to your inbox every weekday morning.
If you already subscribe, please share with your family and friends so they know about the Ohio Capital Journal too: https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/subscribe/
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Catching Our Eye

• Springfield. The Dayton Daily News’ Rich Gillette and Jessica Orozco report, “Springfield mayor urges community to ‘treat one another with dignity’ following ICE operations.”
Mayor Rob Rue confirmed Wednesday, Aug. 19, that federal immigration enforcement activity is taking place in Springfield, including arrests by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
“ICE has advised city staff that its enforcement and removal operations is conducting field enforcement activity throughout the nation as part of its daily duties, including in Springfield and surrounding areas. ICE has also indicated that targeted enforcement activity will continue throughout Ohio. These are federal immigration enforcement operations. The city does not direct or control ICE enforcement activity,” Rue said.
• Not concerned. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Sarah Donaldson reports, “Husted, Moreno not worried about Springfield’s economy with TPS gone for Haitian immigrants.”
Thousands of Haitians living in Ohio, including Springfield, lost their legal status in late July. With it, went their ability to work.
Neither of Ohio’s U.S. senators are concerned about the local workforce there, even as the state touts new investments in Springfield, like Electra’s recently announced headquarters and manufacturing facilities. Electra has said it will add about 2,000 jobs.
• Following the money. WCMH’s Katie Millard reports, “Ohio governor’s race: Where donations are coming from.”
Not including his own donations or Musk’s, Ramaswamy’s records reflect he has raised $14.36 million so far in 2026. Records show 54% of those funds came from Ohio, with $7.75 million from Ohio donors. After Ohio, Ramaswamy received the most support from Florida ($1 million), Texas ($742,299.19) and California ($674,203.67)…
Since the start of 2026, Acton has raised $16.47 million. Records show 72% of the funding has come from Ohio, with Acton raising $11.8 million in-state. After Ohio, she received the most money from California ($796,260.17), New York ($534,135.61) and Washington, D.C. ($306,532.03).
• Six tornados. WYSO’s Mike Frazier reports, “National Weather Service confirms 6 tornadoes touched down in western and central Ohio.”
The National Weather Service’s analysis of the Aug. 11 storms continues, with six confirmed tornado touchdowns in western and central Ohio.
• One case resolved. Jessie Balmert reports in the Columbus Dispatch, “Ohio Supreme Court dismisses legal challenge to abortion rights amendment.”
The Ohio Supreme Court unanimously dismissed a Trumbull County judge’s lawsuit challenging the state’s abortion rights amendment.
Trumbull County Domestic Relations and Juvenile Division Court Judge David Engler, a Republican, asked the Ohio Supreme Court to block a portion or all of the reproductive rights language that voters approved 57%-43% in 2023.
Engler contended that the amendment blocked him from weighing in on whether minors can obtain abortions if their parents object to them, a concept called judicial bypass.
• Making life even more difficult for trans people, part infinity. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Karen Kasler reports, “Form used for 17 years to change gender marker on state-issued IDs no longer accepted in Ohio.”
Transgender Ohioans who want to update the gender indicated on their driver’s licenses or state IDs can no longer do that with a form that’s been used for years. And the state’s leading LGBTQ+ advocacy group says that’s a sudden and cumbersome change.
Equality Ohio said it found out Tuesday that the declaration of gender change form signed by a medical or mental health provider that’s been in use since 2009 will no longer be accepted by the Bureau of Motor Vehicles to change a gender marker.
• The latest in the Afroman saga. The Ohio Newsroom’s Kendall Crawford reports, “Ohio rapper Afroman strikes back at officer who raided his home and sued him.”
Earlier this year, Adams County resident Joseph Foreman – better known to rap fans as Afroman – prevailed in a defamation lawsuit that local law enforcement filed against him. Now, the rapper is turning the tables.
Afroman is suing one of the law enforcement officers who previously sued him, accusing him of malicious prosecution, abuse of process, intentional infliction of emotional distress and tortious interference with contract.

title: Rosen to DHS: Disclose info-sharing agreement between ICE, TSA
description: U.S. Sen. Jacky Rosen on Tuesday led a group of senators in condemning recent immigration enforcement activity at airports nationwide and calling on Trump administration officials to disclose how ICE and TSA are collaborating. Recent incidents at airports, including two at Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas, “create fear in our communities and cau[...]
text:
Recent incidents at airports, including two at Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas, “create fear in our communities and cause disruption and distress to the traveling public,” the senators wrote. (Photo: Hugh Jackson/Nevada Current)U.S. Sen. Jacky Rosen on Tuesday led a group of senators in condemning recent immigration enforcement activity at airports nationwide and calling on Trump administration officials to disclose how ICE and TSA are collaborating.
Recent incidents at airports, including two at Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas, “create fear in our communities and cause disruption and distress to the traveling public,” the senators wrote in a letter to U.S. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Transportation Security Administration Administrator David Cummins, and Immigration and Customs Enforcement Acting Director David Venturella.
The senators are asking the agencies to publicly disclose existing information sharing agreements between ICE and TSA.
American Oversight late last month reported the two agencies have a formal agreement to coordinate “the sharing, storage and management of passengers’ sensitive information.” The agreement, revealed through documents obtained through a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request and lawsuit, appears to contradict congressional testimony TSA Acting Director Ha Nguyen McNeill gave in January.
Rosen and the senators also want assurances that immigration enforcement agents are operating solely on active judicial warrants, wearing and utilizing body cameras, wearing and displaying clear identifying information, and refraining from wearing masks.
The letter references documented ICE activity last month at Reid Airport in Las Vegas. The first, which was recorded on video and widely shared, involved masked and plain-clothed ICE officers attempting to arrest a 57-year-old man but being thwarted when bystanders intervened. A second incident involved a pregnant woman being arrested as she attempted to fly to Connecticut after a vacation.
Both people were accused of overstaying visas, according to media reports.
The senators expressed concern about the apparent targeting of people with expired visas, noting that the U.S. has a backlog of nearly 12 million visa applications and that “a person can have an expired visa with a legitimate pending application yet still be detained by ICE at an airport due to visa processing delays that are out of their control.”
The letter notes that immigration enforcement activity has been reported at Reno-Tahoe, Denver, and San Francisco international airports.
“Such actions have only served to disrupt local communities, create fear among immigrant families, and undermine the travel and tourism sector by actively discouraging travelers from visiting the United States,” reads the letter. “They hurt our nation’s travel and tourism industry at a time when it is trying to rebound from a 5.5% decline in international tourism in 2025 that occurred due to President Trump’s misguided tariff, immigration, and foreign policies.”
U.S. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto signed the letter, as did U.S. Sens. John Hickenlooper and Michael Bennet of Colorado, Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, Tammy Duckworth of Illinois, and Ron Wyden of Oregon.
The full letter, which includes specific questions the senators want answered, is available here.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Supreme Court reverses convictions for failure to pay $20 administrative fee
description: Kansas Supreme Court reverses felony and misdemeanor convictions for man claiming he was unable to pay $20 fee when filling out offender registry form.
text:
Kansas Supreme Court Chief Justice Eric Rosen supports the court's reversal of a Wyandotte County man's conviction for failure to pay a $20 fee when filling out an offender registry form but prefers constitutional questions about the process to be considered at a later time. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The Kansas Supreme Court reversed convictions of a Wyandotte County man who filled out an offender registry form as required by state law but was convicted of misdemeanor and felony offenses because he repeatedly failed to pay the mandatory $20 fee.
The latest intervention by the Supreme Court followed previous rulings by a district court judge, the Kansas Court of Appeals and the Supreme Court regarding Terrance Sims’ conviction on two felonies and one misdemeanor for not paying the administrative fee.
Sims’ case began more than a dozen years ago when he claimed he was indigent and unable to pay the $20 fee each of three times he filled out the offender registration document in Wyandotte County.
The Supreme Court, which chose not to conduct oral arguments earlier this year on this case, agreed last week that all three convictions must be reversed. The five justices who took part were split in their reasoning.
Justice Caleb Stegall’s concurrence, which was joined by Justices K.J. Wall and Larkin Walsh, argued the Kansas Legislature likely surpassed the limit of its police power under the Kansas Constitution by imposing strict criminal liability for those unable to pay the fee.
This three-justice plurality viewed the statute as arbitrary and expressed doubt it served a legitimate state interest in terms of public safety. In other words, these justices suggested the mandate violated constitutional due process rights.
“Sims was convicted of three crimes — two of them felonies — over a matter of $60 after showing up to the sheriff’s office to register pursuant to KORA,” Stegall wrote. “Indigency aside, I cannot image what evils the government must protect the public from by tossing into prison a registered offender who actually registers but who owes $20 in KORA fees.”
Chief Justice Eric Rosen’s separate concurrence, endorsed by Justice Dan Biles, said Sims’ convictions had to be dismissed because prosecutors didn’t timely appeal.
Justice Melissa Taylor Standridge was not a participant in Supreme Court deliberations because of her involvement with the case at the Court of Appeals level. The seventh position on the Supreme Court was vacant because of the retirement of Chief Justice Marla Luckert.
Sims was convicted of aggravated sodomy and two counts of rape. He was sentenced to prison in 2005 and paroled before his sentence expired in 2016. Under the Kansas Offender Registration Act, he must register every three months for the rest of his life. Kansas considers the first registry infraction a misdemeanor, but subsequent violations were felonies.
Sims completed the registration forms in October 2013, January 2014 and April 2014, but didn’t pay the fee within 15 days as mandated by state law. He claimed he was indigent and argued it would be unconstitutional to impose criminal penalties for nonpayment of fees based on “substantive” due process guarantees.
Because no judge declared him indigent before the 2013 and 2014 incidents, Wyandotte County District Judge Bill Klapper convicted him of all three offenses. He included in the record a statement about a “problem with the statute.” The Kansas Court of Appeals upheld Sims’ convictions in 2017.
Before the Supreme Court considered Sims’ appeal, the Court of Appeals decided in a separate 2018 case that nonpayment of offender registration fees violated “procedural” due process rights. Sims’ appellate counsel asked the Supreme Court to take that outcome into account.
In a rare order, the Supreme Court in 2019 retained jurisdiction of Sims’ appeal but asked the district court to consider whether his trial attorney performed deficiently by not raising procedural due process arguments. The district court said in 2020 that Sims had been prejudiced at trial. The Supreme Court asked that a copy of the district court finding be filed with the Supreme Court within 30 days. Neither party met that deadline.
In 2024, the Supreme Court received a copy of the district court’s decision. Rosen’s opinion said the delay meant the state no longer had an opportunity to appeal. Questions of the law’s constitutionality should be left for another day, he said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: For early grade reading gains, states look to Mississippi and consider holding students back
description: Western Line School District Superintendent Lawrence Hudson, wishes second grader Dalary Salazar, center, a happy birthday, during a visit at Riverside Elementary School, Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026, in Avon.
text:
When Mississippi overhauled its literacy education in 2013, one of the most controversial pieces was a policy to retain third graders if they couldn’t pass the reading portion of the state’s English language arts assessment.
Years later, as education officials across the country have taken notice of Mississippi’s literacy gains, more states have adopted their own retention policies. 
More than two dozen states now have laws requiring or allowing schools to retain third grade students who are not reading at grade level, according to an analysis from the Education Commission of the States, a nonprofit that tracks state legislation in the United States. 
But the research on retention is mixed. 
Historically, most studies indicated that students who had to repeat a grade often benefited very little and had long-term negative consequences. Research from the past decade complicates that picture: Younger students may see some positive effects from retention if schools are also combining it with high-intensity tutoring and support, some studies have shown.
Federal data also shows retention rates vary widely by state. 
For most of the U.S., high school students made up a large share of those who repeated a grade level from 2011 to 2021, the most recent years in which national data was available. (The U.S. Department of Education Office for Civil Rights, the only source for consistent data across all states, is now eight months behind in releasing new data.) 
Western Line School District Superintendent Lawrence Hudson chats with fourth graders during a visit at Riverside Elementary School on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026, in Avon. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Mississippi stands out. The state has one of the highest third grade retention rates in the country. 
“If the retention happens in earlier grades and is combined with help — not just a threat, but some kind of positive intervention — the results, at least in the short-run, tend to be good,” said Dan Goldhaber, director of the Center for Education Data and Research at the University of Washington.
‘We have to do something’
Rachel Canter, an education policy expert who helped craft the Literacy-Based Promotion Act, said that in 2013, the Legislature was desperate to improve reading in Mississippi. 
“The rationale was that we have to do something about the fact that we have kids graduating high school that are barely literate,” she said. “We had been living in that reality for a long time.”
Mississippi lawmakers started looking to Florida, she said, where former Gov. Jeb Bush made ending “social promotion” — the practice of passing students because of their age — one of his signature policies.
“The argument that won was, ‘We have to do something, and we know how harmful it is when kids pass with no skills,’” Canter said. 
Tenette Smith, who at the time helped lead the Mississippi Department of Education’s literacy initiatives, said the Legislature wanted the retention policy to hold administrators and leaders accountable to the state’s children. 
The policy was met with criticism. Opponents were worried that it was punitive and would set children up for failure. Across the country, retention policies have become a partisan issue, Canter said, with Democrats largely viewing them as harmful to children. 
Read more: A national divide over holding back students: Some states do it young, others wait until high school
School administrators in Mississippi said many children would be retained if the policy was passed. But Canter took issue with that mindset and the assumption underneath it: That it’s impossible to get kids ready to read.
“We were sort of taking a leap of faith,” she said. “The goal wasn’t to retain them, but that was what was going to happen if we couldn’t get them ready.”
Despite arguments from people who doubt Mississippi’s reading success and claim the fourth grade reading scores are boosted by holding students back, Canter said Mississippi’s retention rate didn’t significantly spike after the 2013 act. 
Jason Griffin, 11, reads Katherine Applegate’s “The One and Only Ivan” during Operation Shoestring’s Summer reading program at Galloway Elementary School in Jackson on Monday, June 15, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Federal data shows that about 4% of students were held back during the 2011-12 school year. By the 2015-16 school year, after the reading gate was implemented, that percentage increased by a point.
Retention became a hallmark of the state’s literacy overhaul, but the literacy act established other components that were essential to students’ success, she said. 
The act funneled money into literacy education across the state, sending literacy coaches to schools and mandating high-quality curriculum. Teachers received literacy instruction.
“If retention is the only thing we would have done, I don’t think it would have worked,” she said.
Raising the bar for early grades
The state’s third grade retention policy has had a trickle-down effect: Retentions in Mississippi are concentrated in kindergarten through second grade, too. 
Researchers including Canter say that’s because the literacy legislation established more monitoring and higher standards in those grades as well.
That holds true at Western Line School District, with schools located on the banks of the Mississippi River. Western Line held back 68 students in kindergarten through third grade during the 2021-22 school year, compared to 56 students in all other grades combined. 
Not all of those retentions are tied to reading, Superintendent Lawrence Hudson said, but the policy raised the bar for students in early grades.
About 4 in 5 Western Line third graders passed the reading component of the state test on their first try last year, higher than the state average of 75.6%. Passing the test wasn’t the school’s focus, Hudson said. 
“We want to make sure kids are successful for the rest of their life,” he said. “We know if children have deficits at younger grades, they’ll get to third grade with those deficits. 
“The longer you wait, the harder it is to clear those deficiencies.”
Rep. John Hines, a Democrat from Greenville, fears the retention policy is making it harder for students to graduate in his Delta district, which is one of the poorest regions in one of the poorest states in the country. He said he doesn’t want students in his district to be disproportionately retained. 
But Hines can’t deny how beneficial retention was for his younger brother decades ago.
“He was extremely shy and nervous, so he wouldn’t talk, and once he became nervous, he shut down,” Hines said. “The teacher talked my mom into letting him stay back in the first grade.”
That marked the beginning of a transformation, Hines said. His brother was coaxed out of his shell and became an honors student. 
Students don’t automatically improve when they’re retained, Canter said. To help students, schools have to get them the academic support they need in that year they repeat. The decision to retain a student is difficult, she said, but combined with intervention, it can pay dividends. 
Western Line School District Assistant Superintendent James Johnson, chats with second graders about books the class is reading at Riverside Elementary School on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026, in Avon. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
“Any time a child is retained, it is a signal that we have not done what we needed to do as adults,” Canter said. But the retention policy paired with additional support has “done great things for kids,” she said. 
Extending the gains
Despite Mississippi’s gains among fourth graders on a national reading assessment, those gains haven’t continued into higher grades. 
With hopes of extending those gains to fourth through eighth grades, Mississippi lawmakers passed another literacy policy this year, modeled on the 2013 literacy act. 
The state education agency will deploy coaches to schools across the state, provide training for teachers, require screeners throughout the year to assess students’ proficiency and mandate that schools use agency-approved curriculum. 
There’s one glaring difference: The Adolescent Literacy Initiative omits the retention policy.
Research shows holding older students back can negatively affect their chances of graduating, so lawmakers intentionally left a retention policy out, said Rep. Kent McCarty, a Republican from Hattiesburg who is vice chairman of the House Education Committee. 
Without a firm accountability component, Canter is skeptical the Adolescent Literacy Initiative will have the same impact as the 2013 literacy act. 
“Is it going to be enough?” she asked.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Hundreds mourn Nolan Wells at South Mississippi vigil on teen’s 19th birthday
description: Elmore Wonsley, right, reacts as the crowd sings happy birthday during a vigil for Nolan Wells at Greater St. John AME Church in Biloxi on Wednesday, August. 19, 2026.
text:
Wednesday was supposed to be Nolan Wells’ 19th birthday.
Instead, hundreds of people gathered for a prayer vigil mourning the beloved Ocean Springs teen’s death and celebrating his life at Greater St. John AME Church in Biloxi.
“As we celebrate what would have been his 19th birthday, I am reminded as a father of a 24-year-old son and the uncle of four nephews between the age of 20 and 24, how dangerous, precarious life can be for a young Black man in America,” CEO of the National Urban League Marc Morial said.
People begin to pray as a choir sings during a vigil for Nolan Wells at Greater St. John AME Church in Biloxi on Wednesday, August. 19, 2026.Doris Jones waves her arms in the air as she prays during a vigil for Nolan Wells at Greater St. John AME Church in Biloxi on Wednesday, August. 19, 2026.Attorney Ben Crump escorts the Wonsleys through a crowd of people as he and event attendees raise their fists during a vigil for Nolan Wells at Greater St. John AME Church in Biloxi on Wednesday, August. 19, 2026.The Rev. Dr. Jamal Harrison Bryant gives a speech during a vigil for Nolan Wells at Greater St. John AME Church in Biloxi on Wednesday, August. 19, 2026.Christine Wonsley gives a speech in remembrance of her son during a vigil for Nolan Wells at Greater St. John AME Church in Biloxi on Wednesday, August. 19, 2026.Christine Wonsley smiles as she is presented with a birthday cake for her son during a vigil for Nolan Wells at Greater St. John AME Church in Biloxi on Wednesday, August. 19, 2026.Event attendees stand outside holding signs in support of Nolan Wells’ family during a vigil for Wells at Greater St. John AME Church in Biloxi on Wednesday, August. 19, 2026.
As people packed into the pews of the church, various speakers stepped up to the podium to celebrate the life of Wells and continue to call for transparency and justice as the investigation into his death conducted by the Jackson County Sheriff’s Department continues.
“This family has lost a whole lot,” the Rev. Cory Watts said. “It’s up to us to ensure justice is served for this family’s young man.”
Throughout the vigil, speakers called for everyone to join in prayer as they stand in solidarity with the Wonsley family, following an anonymous complaint filed against Wells’ mother, Christine Wonsley, to the Mississippi Board of Nursing.
“It’s so unfair, it is so unfair to lose your child and to be attacked just for asking for answers,” attorney Ben Crump said. “How is it wrong for them to want answers for what happened to their son?”
The crowd erupted as the Rev. Jamal Harrison Bryant took the stage demanding an end to the cycle of violence against Black people in America. “Mississippi does not have 31 years,” Bryant said in reference to other investigations that took years to be solved.
“We have a moment to disrupt a cycle,” Bryant said. “Because the same blood that absorbed in Genesis 4 is now the same blood that is staying in Mississippi.”
As Bryant called for the Wonsleys to come up to the stage for their own remarks, the crowd began to chant “we love Nolan Wells,” out of support for the family.
On stage, Christine Wonsley talked about memories of her son and how she wished she could have called him on his 19th birthday. “This morning I had to fight the urge to Facetime you and sing my off-tune Happy Birthday song,” Wonsley said. “I miss the warmth of your hugs, I miss hearing you say ‘I love you mom,’ I miss everything about you.”
As the Wonsleys concluded their eulogy for their son, Crump led a final chant, demanding that everyone “say his name” as the crowd shouted back “Nolan Wells.”
As the vigil concluded, a birthday cake and balloons were presented to the Wonsleys. Ending the night was a singing of “Happy Birthday” from the crowd as Christine and Elmore Wonsley blew out the candles for what would have been their son’s 19th birthday.
This story and photos were produced by Jackson Ranger of The Sun Herald.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Odd bedfellows: Progressive critics join Democratic, Republican party bosses to oppose election reform ballot question
description: “It’s not that our current system is good. It’s that this alternate one is worse,” says Jonathan Cohn, policy director for Progressive Mass.
text:
IT’S NOT OFTEN you find the state Democratic Party, whose members control Beacon Hill, the state Republican Party, which often agitates against the majority, progressives who love to criticize the status quo, and influential labor unions all in agreement about a specific policy.
But that unusual confluence is exactly what’s happened as voters prepare to decide whether Massachusetts should reshape its system for electing candidates.
Both major parties, labor groups with significant political muscle, and groups that want to push state government to the left have all signaled opposition to a ballot question that would scrap the existing Democratic and Republican primary elections, replacing them with a single contest featuring candidates from all parties.
Proponents of the measure on the November ballot argue that an “all-party primary,” after which the top two vote-getters would face off in the general election, can counter some of the most corrosive dynamics in state politics, especially a widespread lack of competition.
Yet opponents suggest the impact would be the opposite, making it harder for first-time candidates to get a foothold and elevating the influence of moneyed interests. And different members of the “vote no” coalition all think the idea would disadvantage their own slice of the political spectrum.
“Hating jungle primaries,” as all-party primary structures are sometimes dubbed, “is maybe the most bipartisan issue in America,” said Jordan Berg Powers, the chair of the campaign committee urging voters to say “No on 3.”
Political insiders have been skeptical about the proposal since it emerged last year, and the opposition campaign formally launched earlier this month.
Early members include the Massachusetts Democratic Party, whose governing body voted in April to oppose the question, groups that lean further to the left like Progressive Mass and Act on Mass, and half a dozen unions, such as the American Federation of Teachers Massachusetts chapter and 32BJ SEIU. The Massachusetts Republican Party is not officially a member of the coalition, but it “firmly opposes” the ballot question.
“This misguided initiative would undermine core democratic principles by eroding the ability of political parties to select their own nominees, marginalizing smaller parties, stifling ideological diversity, suppressing general-election turnout, and amplifying the role of big money while disadvantaging grassroots efforts,” MassGOP chair Amy Carnevale said in a statement.
Many of the skeptics agree with proponents’ assessment of Massachusetts politics: too much power is concentrated at the top and too many races go uncontested, they say, allowing lawmakers to grow complacent.
“It’s not that our current system is good. It’s that this alternate one is worse,” said Jonathan Cohn, policy director for Progressive Mass.
For supporters of changing the system, the train of logic is simple: In Massachusetts, where Democrats control more than 80 percent of state legislative seats, most elections are essentially decided in the lower-turnoutprimary election. So why not ensure that the general election almost always gives voters an option, even if the choice is between two people from the same party?
“The general election electorate is younger, more diverse, less wealthy, and better represents the demographics of the state,” said Jesse Littlewood, campaign manager for Yes on 3. “That’s where the decision ends up resting, which creates more competition in the sense that the largest share of voters now have a decisive vote in the election.”
Opponents, however, don’t think that funneling all candidates through a single primary ballot will actually do much to solve worst-in-the-nation competitiveness issues in a state where three in five legislative races this cycle feature a single candidate.
They argue that needing to land in the top two of a crowded primary field and then win again in November is a heavy lift that will dissuade many contenders, plus disadvantage independents and small parties who have fewer resources to command voter attention in low-turnout primaries.
Skeptics also contend a single primary election would put even more power in the hands of well-financed candidates and big donors because those with the most money could spend their to the top of a more crowded field.
“In order to have more competition, more people need to run for office, and this is giving people a longer ramp to get there,” said Scotia Hille, executive director of Act on Mass, a progressive group pushing Beacon Hill to embrace transparency and good-government reforms. With a single primary election featuring all candidates, Hille said, “you need to raise more money because you need to reach more voters.”
Steve Kerrigan, the chair of the state Democratic Party, said the proposed new system “would give more power to wealthy donors and corporate PACs, letting candidates with deep pockets or personal fortunes outpace grassroots campaigns before a single door is knocked.”
That’s another point on which proponents contend the facts show the opposite. The Yes on 3 campaign said candidates with significant fundraising advantages won races in California and Washington more frequently under prior systems with partisan primaries than they have since those states embraced all-party primaries.
Like the opposition, the constellation in support of the question cuts across partisan divides. Prominent backers include former Democratic governor Deval Patrick, former Mass. GOP chair Jennifer Nassour, and the NAACP New England Area Conference. Perhaps the most visible supporter is Danielle Allen, a Harvard University professor who briefly ran in the 2022 Democratic primary for governor.
Littlewood said he’s not surprised sitting political party leaders on both sides oppose the idea because it could reduce their power as “gatekeepers.” As for the skepticism from progressives, he finds that more “frustrating.”
“There actually often is agreement that we need more competition, and yet, for some reason, this change — they want to defend the status quo in the face of a pro-democracy change,” he said. “The question for them is: What’s so good about the status quo that they are trying to defend?”
Early polling suggests Massachusetts voters are leaning toward approving the question, but not with the cushion of overwhelming majority support that ballot campaigns often look for. A new UMass Amherst/WCVB survey of 800 registered voters found 51 percent would definitely or probably vote yes, compared to 32 percent who would definitely or probably vote no and 17 percent who are still undecided.
A handful of other states have similar systems in place for all candidates to appear on a single primary ballot. In California and Washington, the top two finishers in the primary move on to the general election. In Alaska, the top four advance.
Voters in Colorado, Arizona, Montana, and South Dakota each rejected ballot measures in 2024 that sought to adopt all-party primary systems. In at least one case, Massachusetts played a minor role: US Sen. Elizabeth Warren lent her voice to the opposition campaign in Colorado, calling that ballot question “a wolf in sheep’s clothing, completely funded by billionaires to tilt the political landscape toward their own special interests.” (Warren’s office did not respond to a CommonWealth Beacon inquiry about whether she also opposes the Massachusetts ballot question.)
For months, Democrats feared the high number of candidates from their party running for California governor, including billionaire Tom Steyer, would divide their base into small enough fractions that the two Republican candidates could snag the top two positions in the primary there. That did not happen, and Democratic candidate Xavier Becerra and Republican candidate Steve Hilton advanced to the November general election.
Critics nonetheless point to such close calls, or rare instances of one party missing the general election ballot, as cautionary tales.
“Despite its framing as a pro-democracy initiative, Question 3 limits voter choice at the ballot box and stifles competition in our elections,” said Kevin Brosseau, secretary-general of the Massachusetts AFL-CIO. “We only need to look to California’s recent primaries to see how this experiment forces voters to abandon their preferred candidates for the most well-funded campaigns, with a billionaire able to almost buy his way into the general election.”
California got its primary system the same way Massachusetts might: a statewide ballot question. Voters there approved a measure in 2010 that had the backing of Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger and influential business groups.
In the cycles since then, the all-party primary system has led to general-election contests between two Democrats or two Republicans with some regularity. Between 11 percent and 18 percent of California’s congressional and state legislative general elections since 2012 have featured a pair of candidates from the same party, according to an analysis by CalMatters.
But “lockouts” — or instances in which two candidates from one party advance while sharing less than 50 percent of the vote because too many candidates from the other party split their base — are far more rare. Littlewood said that’s only happened three times in more than 2,000 elections in California and Washington.
Fears of the “spoiler effect” cut both ways. Republicans are also worried that, in deep-blue Massachusetts, two Democrats will advance in many races, ending the GOP’s guaranteed path to contesting any general elections where it fields a candidate.
“You can have Republicans who fear that this system will lead to Republicans being shut out of the general election, Democrats who fear that it’s going to lead to Democrats being shut out of the general election, and they can both be right in different races,” Cohn said.

title: Missouri prepares for final marijuana microbusiness lottery under tougher rules
description: Missouri received nearly 900 applications for its final round of marijuana microbusiness licenses, with the Missouri Lottery scheduled to draw applicants on Sept. 9 for 77 available licenses. But unlike the entrepreneurs selected in the program’s first two rounds, this year’s applicants will enter a system reshaped by two years of growing pains and dozens […[...]
text:
Greg Ferenbach, facility manager of Ozark Mountain Gyspsy wholesale microbusiness, works in the greenhouse (photo submitted).Missouri received nearly 900 applications for its final round of marijuana microbusiness licenses, with the Missouri Lottery scheduled to draw applicants on Sept. 9 for 77 available licenses.
But unlike the entrepreneurs selected in the program’s first two rounds, this year’s applicants will enter a system reshaped by two years of growing pains and dozens of license revocations.
Jimi Poe, owner of 816 Dispensary in Platte City, was among the first microbusiness licensees selected in 2023. Two years later, he opened Missouri’s first operating microbusiness dispensary.
“It was definitely a long journey,” Poe said during the Missouri Division of Cannabis Regulation’s latest podcast episode. “It was a journey that round three people are not going to have to go.”
The microbusiness program was established through the 2022 constitutional amendment voters approved to legalize recreational marijuana. It was “designed to expand opportunities for marginalized or under-represented individuals to participate in the state’s regulated marijuana industry,” according to the state’s website.
As part of the DCR Out Loud episode, Poe spoke with Lesley Turek, the division’s chief equity officer, about the evolution of the program since its inception in 2023.
New rules take aim at ‘predatory’ contracts in Missouri cannabis microbusiness program

This is the third and final lottery for microbusinesses, where the state will issue at least 29 wholesale and at least 34 dispensary licenses to meet the constitutional requirement of 144 total micro licenses. 
Poe was one of the “pioneers” of the microbusiness industry, Turek said, and as of Aug. 18, there are 21 operational microbusiness licenses —five dispensaries and 16 wholesale.
These companies heavily relied on each other to learn and grow their businesses, Poe said, so it’s important for new owners to build relationships right away. 
“That’s one of the great benefits of the microbusiness program,” Turek said, “is that it really is a community.”
Turek, who oversees the microbusiness program, also stressed that the winners should also develop a relationship with their compliance officers so they understand the new rules put in place in May. They’re rules cannabis regulators proposed in 2024 after they revoked numerous licenses due to unconstitutional ownership deals. 
“I think it’s really important too for licensees,” she said, “both current and future applicants, to understand — any sort of arrangement or agreements that you are trying to get into, include DCR with those so that we can make sure that you’re remaining compliant.”
The new rules governing the microbusiness program provide a deeper explanation of what it means to “majority own and operate” a license, which was a requirement in the 2022 constitutional amendment. 
They allow regulators to complete an extensive review of potential ownership arrangements before the licenses are issued, rather than afterwards. And they mandate that regulators communicate directly with majority owners, not consultants, and that applicants take a course on compliance before applying and after receiving the license. 
 Poe’s journey

When Poe was 20, he said he got slapped with a nonviolent marijuana charge. 
“I had a so-called friend get in trouble,” Poe told Turek, “and he wanted to get out of that trouble, so he hooked me up with an undercover cop and told me it was his uncle.”
He ended up selling 12 pounds to the undercover cop and did 14 months in prison. 
“I was dating my wife at the time, and I remember telling her that, ‘Hey, do this bit with me, and I promise I’ll never sell marijuana again,’” Poe said. “And I never did until here we are, selling marijuana together in the dispensary under a state license.”
Aug. 4 was the 20th anniversary of the day he got busted.
Now his charge is an important part of his business’ story, and it also made him eligible to apply for a microbusiness.
Jimi Poe, owner of 816 Dispensary, and his wife, Summer, who is assistant manager at the dispensary in Platte City (photo submitted).
“I remember when I first won the license, I was like, ‘I’m gonna be the first to open,’” he said. “That was my goal from the time I won the license, and I also wanted to make my mark within the industry. So I felt like I achieved those goals.” 
While it took two years instead of the six months he anticipated to open, Poe stressed that it won’t be as hard for these new winners.
“There’s a lot more people that are coming online,” he said, “and there’s a lot more stuff out there than when I first started. There were a lot of gray areas, and people were still trying to figure it out.”
When he opened his doors, “people thought I was crazy,” he said.
He only had nine different strands of what the industry calls “flower,” or dry weed in containers. 
Now he has 32 different strains of flower, disposable distillate carts, multiple different dabs and 12 different pre-rolled joints. His menu started as one page and now it’s eight pages long, so “things have grown tremendously,” in a year, he said. 
“We’re still lacking on the manufacturer side,” Poe said of the microbusiness community. “The manufacturing and equipment and the know-how, people are still trying to figure that out.”
Turek said before the Missouri Lottery draws the winners, cannabis regulators will vet the applications for basic things, like making sure no one has applied twice and application fees have been paid.
“It does take a little bit of time,” she said, “because if, for example, an application fee doesn’t come through, we give that person a chance to make that payment so that they can go to the lottery.”
Then after the draw, Turek said they’ll be in “full processing mode.” 
They will be conducting a full review of the top-drawn applications, making sure that all the business arrangements are compliant with state law and background checks show no disqualifying felonies. 
“We’ll start by making a phone call to reach out to the owners and say, ‘Hey, it’s us, DCR. Here’s your specialist with this team,’” Turek said. “Give you specific names to contact and tell you what’s going to happen in the process.”
If that application doesn’t meet state requirements, then the next top-drawn applicant will be processed. This is part of the new rules to prevent numerous license revocations.
Lisa Cox, spokeswoman for the Missouri Department for Health and Senior Services that oversees the cannabis division, said the division plans to award microbusiness licenses from Round 3 before the end of 2026.
Currently, there are 46 microbusiness licenses from the Round 1 and 2 that are active but not yet approved to operate.
Poe said that’s partly because owners were nervous to open and unsure if the microbusiness program was going to thrive.
“I’ve been operational for over a year,” he said, “and I’ve proven that we’re going to make it.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Nye County totally bans data centers in over-appropriated water basin
description: Following a county-wide moratorium on any new data center applications, the Nye County Board of Commissioners voted Tuesday to completely ban data centers in one of the most over-appropriated water basins in Nevada. After hours of public comment, the Nye County Board of Commissioners voted unanimously to ban the construction and operation of data centers […]
text:
The Nye County Board of Commissioners on Tuesday voted 5-0 to ban data centers in the Pahrump Valley. (County Commission stream screengrab)Following a county-wide moratorium on any new data center applications, the Nye County Board of Commissioners voted Tuesday to completely ban data centers in one of the most over-appropriated water basins in Nevada.
After hours of public comment, the Nye County Board of Commissioners voted unanimously to ban the construction and operation of data centers in Nevada’s Hydrographic Basin 162, becoming the first municipality in Nevada to outright ban data centers. 
“I am not willing to sacrifice your or my welfare in regards to a data center here in Pahrump Basin 162,” said Nye County Commissioner Bruce Jabbour to a room of about 100 residents, who mostly spoke in support of a ban.
The vote comes after county commissioners approved a temporary county-wide moratorium in June on any new data center applications, which will remain in effect until the county adopts local data center regulations. The temporary moratorium followed an emergency order in May from the Nye County Water District Governing Board recommending a pause on data centers in the Pahrump Valley.
The ban is also a blow to Gigawatt Development Partners LLC’s controversial Manse Technology Campus, a proposed 900-acre data center facility in the Pahrump Valley. 
Gigawatt had already secured the water rights needed to operate the data center, according to the company, but the ban would effectively prevent the development of any data centers in and around the town of Pahrump. 
Nevada Hydrographic Basin 162 covers a total area of more than 500,000 acres, covering the vast majority of southern Nye County including Pahrump, and extending east toward the Clark County border. 
Gigawatt Development Partners LLC did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the future of the data center following the data center ban in Pahrump’s Basin 162.
Nye County Commission Chair Ron Boskovich, who proposed the original temporary moratorium, expressed concern about the amount of water data centers required before his vote to ban their development in Nye County. 
“Lake Mead has plunged to a new record low,” Boskovich said, pointing to the growth of data centers in Las Vegas. “I don’t know if they’re correlated. Maybe not, but they’re running out of water out there, so we don’t really know.”
At full buildout, the Manse Technology Campus was expected to use about 300 acre-feet of water annually, according to the developer. 
County commissioners also agreed to hold a special meeting Sept. 14 to establish land use regulations for developers who attempt to build a data center outside of the banned area. 
Nye County Commissioner Debra Strickland said the county should take the tax benefits data centers could provide into consideration as they develop local regulations. 
“I want to remind you that you only have 2% of the taxable land in Nye County, everything else is federally owned,” Strickland said. “Somewhere we got to make money, guys. So let’s put data centers somewhere, come up with a place that’ll work.” 
Boskovich echoed the need for new tax revenue in Nye County and noted that data centers are being pushed statewide and nationally. 
“I know that our president wants more of these, and I know that our governor wants more of these,” Boskovich said. 
Gigawatt officials said they were in the process of applying for the Nevada Data Center Tax Abatements program, which offers a 75% tax break on personal  property — vehicles, equipment, and other property used in conjunction with the business — for 10 years through the Nevada Governor’s Office of Economic Development for capital investment projects that commit at least $25 million in expenditures.
After the tax breaks, the developer estimated the project would generate about $22.4 million in personal property tax revenue. Without the 75% tax break, the personal property tax would equal $90 million.  
Real property tax, which is not available for abatement in Nevada, would bring in about $91.8 million in tax revenue every year once the data center is developed, according to the developer’s estimates.
Before voting for a total ban, some county commissioners hoped to approve a special election that would allow the public to decide on a data center ban themselves. However, they missed the deadline to place the question on the November ballot, and would need to hold a special election in January at the county’s expense. 
“I still feel the people need to make that determination,” Strickland said.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Data center fight moves to NJ courts, with developers blaming local bans on ‘public hysteria’
description: At least three New Jersey towns are now being sued by data center developers challenging local bans on the facilities.
text:
At least three New Jersey towns are now being sued by data center developers challenging local bans on the facilities. Data center critics want a statewide moratorium on new construction. (Photo by Getty Images)As residents across the state protest plans for new data centers, developers are increasingly going to court to challenge municipal ordinances banning the facilities.
Montgomery, Andover, and Monroe have each been sued in recent weeks by developers seeking to overturn municipal prohibitions on data centers. The suits argue that local officials acted arbitrarily and without proper planning in mind when enacting the bans.
“The action of the Township Committee was clearly based upon public hysteria and political attention rather than sound land use planning,” says the lawsuit targeting Montgomery’s ordinance.
Nearly three dozen New Jersey municipalities have passed bans or restrictions on data centers, including Asbury Park, Neptune, Red Bank, Logan, and Millville, as residents statewide have griped that when data centers come to town, they bring noise, increased water use, and rising electricity demands.
Ben Dziobek, executive director of the Climate Revolution Action Network, said he isn’t surprised developers are turning to the courts in their bids to construct data centers. Dziobek said it’s a trend happening nationwide.
“Throughout the process of building a data center, these companies have just been so antidemocratic from the start,” he said. “To try to subvert the will of residents who demanded their elected officials pass these ordinances to ban data centers in the municipality is no surprise to me at all.”
He said he expects the tactic to keep spreading as opposition to data centers grows across the Garden State, and he noted that sentiment against data centers can be found in towns governed by Democrats and those run by Republicans.
“It’s becoming clearer and clearer that hundreds of people are going to show up in opposition to these projects no matter where they are,” Dziobek said. “This is the result of data centers and data center developers losing the support of public opinion.”
The legal fights are unfolding against a broader debate in Trenton and town halls across the state over whether New Jersey should rein in the nascent data center industry. In May, Gov. Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat, said she backs legislation that would regulate data centers and seeks to implement new policies aimed at limiting the industry.
Assemblyman Mike Inganamort, left, said many residents have raised legitimate questions about data centers, but he does not think the facilities are all bad. (Photo by Hal Brown/New Jersey Monitor)
Assemblyman Mike Inganamort (R-Sussex) said artificial intelligence technology is still new enough that residents’ concerns should be taken seriously, but he cautioned against blanket judgments. He said some data center developers have addressed concerns about noise and water usage.
“The bottom line is we’re all using technology, we’re all using artificial intelligence, that’s just the reality. Those things don’t exist in the atmosphere, they exist in a data center,” he said, adding, “They’re not all good or all bad.”
Two of the three lawsuits filed in recent weeks allege that local officials who moved to ban data centers were motivated by public pressure, not the principles of law or planning.
Monroe in Gloucester County is facing a $300 million suit from Hexa Builders, a Princeton-based developer that seeks to build a 1-million-square-foot data center and warehouse. The 20-count complaint filed in June accuses the town of violating the state’s Municipal Land Use Law and its own application procedures after local officials reversed a 2025 ordinance that had allowed data centers. The lawsuit also argues the data center ban violates the First Amendment.
“Data centers are a medium of expression and banning data centers would impose a significant burden on the free speech rights of all citizens in the United States,” the complaint says.
That case is now pending in federal court.
Montgomery also faces a legal challenge after E. Khan Development filed suit in state Superior Court in Somerset County in July over the town’s ordinance banning both data centers and detention centers. E. Khan, a Pennsylvania-based company that owns the 257-acre Kenvue campus in Skillman, argues the town targeted its property.
The company’s site plan application for an industrial project on the site was declared complete on June 9, days before Montgomery’s township committee adopted the ban.
Khan is asking a judge to declare the ordinance invalid and block the town from enforcing it, as well as seeking $300 million in damages.
Andover Township faces a similar suit, filed July 10 in Superior Court in Sussex County. National Land Developers LLC wants to build a data center on a roughly 100-acre former airport site, land the company says has sat vacant for over a decade. The township had amended its zoning laws to allow data centers there in 2025.
In May, the township committee voted 4-1 to introduce a separate ordinance adding new standards for data centers rather than an outright ban, but reversed course five days later following a rowdy township meeting that went viral on social media. A resident was removed from the meeting by police after cursing at the mayor and committee.
The committee held a special meeting where members unanimously introduced a townshipwide ban on data centers instead, repealing earlier ordinances that had allowed them. The lawsuit says the committee gave no explanation for the about-face.
Officials with the three towns did not respond to requests for comment.
Dziobek predicted that more lawsuits will come without a statewide moratorium in place. This week, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro signed an executive order that Shapiro said provides “the strictest guardrails in the nation” on data center construction, though it falls short of a ban. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul last month signed a one-year moratorium on large data centers.
Dziobek called on Sherrill to follow Hochul’s lead.
“We’re waiting, we’re waiting, we’re waiting. Everyone around us is already doing something,” Dziobek said.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah lawmakers get a primer on data centers after a summer of protests and political fallout
description: Data centers took center stage at the Utah Capitol Wednesday as lawmakers met to figure out where to focus their attention come 2027.
text:
The sun rises over a part of Hansel Valley, in Box Elder County, near the proposed Stratos Project, a massive data center planned for 40,000 acres of land, on Thursday, May 28, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Data centers took center stage at the Utah Capitol Wednesday as lawmakers met to figure out where to focus their attention when they convene for their 2027 session in January. 
They didn’t take any action, but focused on listening to experts, administrators and everyday Utahns for insights on the industry and its impacts on the environment and economy during their interim meetings.
They also acknowledged loud and bipartisan public outcry. Fierce opposition to new data center development, erupting across the country, has ignited in Utah in response to a massive proposed project near the northern tip of the Great Salt Lake in Box Elder County. 
“We know this is a hot-button issue. Each of us has received, probably, hundreds of emails on this issue, so we know it’s a big concern,” said Rep. Jon Hawkins, R-Pleasant Grove, chair of the Economic Development and Workforce Services Interim Committee.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
State leaders are also keenly aware of how that concern has translated into political consequence. Wednesday’s meetings followed the stunning defeat of a top lawmaker, Senate President Stuart Adams, in June’s Republican primary. 
Adams, a Republican from Layton, had earlier voted to advance the Stratos data center project as chair of Utah’s Military Installation Development Authority, a move seen as a key factor in his primary loss. Two Box Elder County commissioners who cast votes in favor of the project also lost their seats. 
The presentations at the Capitol left some lawmakers with questions that have also vexed constituents in recent months. 
Tim Davis, commissioner of Utah’s Department of Environmental Quality, noted no single state agency can fully approve a data center on its own. He showed lawmakers a chart displaying the many layers of approvals that developers must generally obtain, including from land authorities, along with divisions overseeing air quality, water use and wastewater permitting. 
It left Rep. Doug Fiefia wondering who exactly Utahns could hold to account if something important falls through the cracks in an approval process. 
“That’s just the concern from a constituent’s perspective, of who do we hold accountable for this data center coming in? And if there’s a million people I have to contact, then I never really get to the right person that I have a question or concern to,” Fiefia, R-Herriman, said. 
Rep. Doug Fiefia, R-Herriman, is pictured on the House floor at the Capitol in Salt Lake City on Thursday, Feb. 19, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
Davis said state agencies have been discussing how to coordinate better. He also pointed out that his agency’s work overseeing air quality permitting hasn’t begun for the large-scale Box Elder County project backed by celebrity investor Kevin O’Leary. Once it does, it’ll take a year just to obtain data on existing air quality before developers can apply — a process that involves opportunity for public comment, he said. 
“We haven’t even started our process with them,” Davis told the economic development committee. 
The Military Installation Development Authority has said it’s hitting pause on the Stratos project as a group of citizens pushes to allow Box Elder County voters to pursue a referendum vote on the county commission’s decision to green light the data center, which would give them a chance to effectively reject the development. But Stratos backers are “full steam ahead on the project,” O’Leary told The Salt Lake Tribune in July. 
Rep. Jim Dunnigan, R-Taylorsville, was focused Wednesday on the money Utah gives up by offering “significant” tax incentives to data centers. 
“I know we need the jobs, and yet we’re giving away significant tax breaks to attract them,” Dunnigan said. 
Jessica Wiarda, of Salt Lake City, told a natural resources panel Wednesday her biggest concerns surrounding data centers revolves around effects on wildlife, especially deer.
But it was also upsetting that the public didn’t have more information on the Stratos project before public officials voted on it, she said. Wiarda told the committee she was grateful to learn more since then and gave them a piece of advice. 
“The transparency will reduce the public pressure,” she said.
