name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Restaurant inspection update: Dead mice, expired food, kitchen closures
description: State, city and county inspectors have cited Iowa restaurants and stores for hundreds of food-safety violations during the past several weeks, including unsanitary kitchens, rodent droppings, long-expired food and buffets with food served at unsafe temperatures. At least two restaurants temporarily closed due to the issues reported by inspectors. The finding[...]
text:
The Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing oversees restaurant inspections in Iowa. (Photo via Getty Images; DIAL logo courtesy of Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing)State, city and county inspectors have cited Iowa restaurants and stores for hundreds of food-safety violations during the past several weeks, including unsanitary kitchens, rodent droppings, long-expired food and buffets with food served at unsafe temperatures.
At least two restaurants temporarily closed due to the issues reported by inspectors.
The findings are reported by the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing, which handles food-establishment inspections at the state level.
Listed below are some of the more serious findings that stem from inspections at Iowa restaurants, stores, care facilities and other businesses between June 17, 2026, and Aug. 10, 2026. (DIAL withholds from public disclosure all food-safety inspection reports for eight days past the date of inspection.)
The inspections department reminds the public that its reports are a “snapshot” in time, and violations are often corrected on the spot before the inspector leaves the establishment. For a more complete list of all inspections, along with additional details on each of the inspections listed below, visit the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing’s website.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Black Sheep Social Club, 600 1st St., Cedar Rapids — During an Aug. 5 visit, a Linn County inspector cited this restaurant for 10 risk-factor violations, an unusually large number. Inspectors alleged a “pattern of non-compliance regarding handwashing” and noted that “multiple items” in the walk-in cooler were holding at 48 to 72 degrees, significantly warmer than the maximum of 41 degrees. All of the items in the cooler that were out of acceptable temperature ranges were discarded and the cooler was repaired.
Inspectors also noted that access to the handwashing sink on the cook line was blocked and there were no paper towels or hand soap available there. In addition, there was no hand soap at any of the handwashing sinks in the bar area. The inspector noted the visit was in response to one illness complaint and one non-illness complaint. “No pests were found on site during the inspection,” the inspector wrote in her report. “Complaint investigation is ongoing.”
Hy-Vee Food Store, 320 W St., Grinnell — During an Aug. 4 visit, a state inspector noted that rotisserie chickens were being held in a cooler at 47 degrees and fried chicken, sushi rolls and egg rolls were being held at 44 degrees. In a separate cooler, pulled pork and cooked ribs were being held at 45 and 46 degrees. All of the out-of-temperature food items were discarded.
Also, the sink in the sushi department that was designated for handwashing was littered with food debris, and a jug of chemical sanitizer was stored with milk inside the walk-in cooler in the dairy department. The inspector also reported that a display-case cooler had been ranging in temperature from 52 to 59 degrees, and there was no complete log of thermometer calibrations for sushi preparation. “Sushi records are incomplete, corrective action is not documented, and not reviewed by managers on multiple dates,” the inspector reported.
The visit was in response to a non-illness complaint that pertained to improper holding temperatures. The inspector deemed the complaint verified.
Hacienda Vieja, 1101 E. 1st St., Grimes — During an Aug. 3 visit, a state inspector noted that the rice on the steamtable was holding at 68 degrees. The staff pulled the rice from the steamtable and placed it on the stove for reheating to 185 degrees. The inspector also observed that items in the walk-in cooler — including pico, diced tomatoes and salsa — were holding 45 to 47 degrees and had to be discarded. In addition, the cooler that was part of the kitchen’s main food-preparation table was holding items at 62 degrees and had not been switched on. Food in that cooler was then discarded.
The inspector also reported that the dishwashing machine had no detectable amount of sanitizing solution, and the kitchen’s handwashing sink was leaking and had no hot-water supply due to the valve being turned off.
Also, vacuum-sealed fish was not removed from the packaging prior to thawing, increasing the risk that any spoilage would go undetected, and the most recently filed inspection report had not been posted. The inspector also reported the restaurant opted to shut down while waiting for repairs to the coolers and sinks.



Quotation







Two pails of rice with water sitting on the floor, with one of the buckets having an insect floating in it ... Raw chicken stored on the floor in walk-in cooler.


– Inspector's report on Indian Garden Bar & Grill in Bettendorf 


Indian Garden Bar & Grill, 2503 E. 53rd Ave., Bettendorf — During a July 22 visit, a Scott County inspector cited this establishment for 11 risk-factor violations, an unusually high number. The inspector observed that “several food items” in the food-preparation coolers and in the walk-in cooler were not date-marked to ensure freshness and safety. Other items in the coolers were dated but also expired, with expirations dating back to mid-May and mid-June.
In addition, the shelving in the food-prep cooler and walk-in coolers was marred with excess food debris, and shelving throughout the kitchen had excess food debris and grease on them. The inspector also reported that several pieces of kitchen equipment – including a can opener, microwaves, all of the prep coolers, the handwashing sink, and a large mixer — had “excess dirt and debris” on them.
The inspector also reported the presence of “fly insect spray” in the kitchen that was presumably not intended for commercial kitchen use. “Two pails of rice with water sitting on the floor, with one of the buckets having an insect floating in it,” the inspector wrote in her report. “Raw chicken stored on the floor in walk-in cooler.”
Also, the inspector reported, water was pooling on the bottom of the food-prep cooler near the grill, all of the kitchen equipment was marred by excess food debris and grease, kitchen fans had excess dust and debris on them, and the floors, walls and ceiling were marred by excess grease and food debris.
Trinity Medical Center, 4500 Utica Ridge Road, Bettendorf — During an Aug. 3 visit to this hospital’s food-service area, a Scott County inspector noted the hospital did not have on hand any of the required forms for employees to report illnesses. Also, cottage cheese in one cooler was measured at 50 degrees, as were sliced tomatoes in a food-preparation cooler, and sliced cheese next to a hot-holding unit. The tomatoes and cheese were then placed in ice to cool them to 41 degrees, while the cottage cheese was discarded.
In addition, several food items — such as sliced lunchmeat and tuna salad — were not properly date-marked to ensure freshness and safety. Also, several food items were past the date of expiration, such as sliced roast beef dated Aug. 2, sliced celery dated Aug. 2, and batter dated July 29. In addition, the interior of the microwave oven had an excess of food debris in it, and the surface of all kitchen carts, both plastic and stainless steel, was marred by food debris.
The inspector also made note of three packages of frozen soup that were being thawed by being placed in a sink without running water over the top of them, and reported that salmon fillets were being thawed while still in vacuum-sealed packaging, increasing the risk that any spoilage would go undetected.
The inspector also found that the shelving in the grill station was marred by food debris and the dishwasher was leaking, leaving water pooling on the floor.
Anchor Inn Supper Club, 906 Front St., Garber — During a July 31 visit, a state inspector reported there were no currently certified food protection managers on staff. In addition, an “unknown dough-like mixture” was found inside a beverage cooler and “had a mold-like substance on it.”  Also, raw hamburger was improperly stored inside a cooler and a box of potatoes was stored on the floor.
The inspector also found that pork loin that was prepared more than 24 hours prior to the inspection had no date-markings to ensure freshness and safety and had to be discarded. Several items throughout out the facility were reported to be well past their seven-day expiration limit, including pizza sauce dated May 19, salsa dated July 17 and noodles dated July 20.
In addition, the bottoms of various coolers and freezers were marred by a “moderate” amount of debris, the hot-water faucet in one sink sprayed water when turned on, and the dishwasher was spilling water onto the floor each time it was used. State records indicate the “most recent” inspection at the Anchor Inn prior to the July visit was in November 2019.
The Fountains Independent and Assisted Living Center, 3752 Thunder Ridge Road, Bettendorf — During a July 29 visit, a Scott County inspector found that raw-egg French toast mix was improperly stored on top of jalapenos, risking cross-contamination. Also, raw sausage links were improperly stored over garlic bread and several foods items in multiple coolers within both the independent- and assisted-living facilities were not date-marked to ensure freshness and safety.
The inspector also reported finding cooked bacon bits date-marked July 6, and stated that some items — such as an opened bag of hot dogs and lunchmeat – had to be discarded due to their uncertain expiration dates. Food debris and buildup marred a can opener, the interior of an ice chest, the pop dispensers, food racks, a microwave oven and a juice machine.
In addition, salmon fillets were improperly thawed, creating an increased risk that any spoilage would go undetected, and food was being stored on the floor of a walk-in freezer. Also, water was pooling on the bottom of one food-preparation cooler, an oven and grill were marred by excess food debris and grease, all of the kitchen shelving in the assisted living area was marred by food debris, and the floor under all of the kitchen equipment in both facilities was soiled by excess food debris.
La Herradura Mexican Grill, 6854 Championship Drive, Bettendorf — During a July 27 visit, a Scott County inspector cited this establishment for 14 risk-factor violations, an exceptionally high number.
The inspector noted that one ready-to-serve chicken dish was measured at 145 degrees and had to be reheated to 165 degrees. Other food items, such as queso and various sauces, were measured at 114 degrees in a hot-holding unit and had to be reheated to 165 degrees.
Also, several pans of refried beans, queso and cooked chicken made the previous day had yet to cool to 41 degrees and were measured at 49 to 59 degrees, resulting in them being discarded. In addition, the inspector found dessert cups that had no date-markings, resulting in them being discarded.
The inspector also reported that the handwashing sink in the bar area was being used to store kitchen equipment. Inside one of the walk-in coolers, water was leaking from the cooling fan onto food products and into a bucket placed on the floor.
Southern Hills Mall Dairy Queen, 4400 Sergeant Road, Sioux City — During a July 23 visit, a Siouxland District Health Department inspector noted that the hamburgers in the hot-holding unit were measured at 65 to 73 degrees and had to be discarded. Also, the soda nozzles, syrup nozzles, ice machine, and several dishes throughout the facility were visibly soiled. Most of the equipment was visibly soiled, as were the floors, walls and ceilings, the inspector reported.
Sippi’s American Grill, 406 W. 2nd St., Davenport — During a  July 23 visit, a Scott County inspector noted mouse-like droppings on the top of a can in the dry-storage area and in a janitor’s closet, below the dishwashing machine, below the racks with canned goods, and other areas. The inspector also observed an “excessive amount of fruit-fly activity.”
Also, the cold unit of a food-preparation table was holding pasta salad, potato salad and dressings at temperatures of 51 to 56 degrees, rather than 41 degrees or colder. In addition, pre-portioned pork and prime rib had been pulled from the freezer and was dated July 16 – beyond the seven-day limit for holding such food.
Also, two cans of Eliminate insecticide, not approved for restaurant use, were found in the establishment, and ribs prepared earlier in the day were being improperly cooled in a deep pan that was tightly wrapped, inhibiting the cooling process. In addition, the air conditioning unit’s condenser above the walk-in freezer was leaking, causing standing water and sludge to pool in front of the freezer door.
The inspection was prompted by an illness complaint the inspector deemed unverified.
Siouxland Senior Center Coffee Shop, 313 Cook St., Sioux City — During a July 22 visit, a Siouxland District Health Department inspector noted that the establishment’s certified food protection manager’s food-safety certificate had expired more than two years earlier, in February 2024.
Also, there were prepared yogurt parfaits containing sliced strawberries and blueberries dated July 20 and which measured  52 degrees. Also, a deli sandwich was measured at 58 degrees. The inspector found that the ambient air temperature of the refrigerator was 66 degrees. The yogurt parfaits and the sandwich were discarded and the malfunctioning refrigerator was removed from the coffee shop.
The inspector also made note of a meat slicer and an ice machine that were visibly soiled.



Quotation







Mouse droppings were observed in several areas throughout the facility, including around the perimeter of the doughnut preparation area … One sticky trap with a dead baby mouse was observed underneath a shelving unit.


– Inspector's report on Tommy's Café in Davenport


Tommy’s Café, 916 W. 3rd St., Davenport — During a July 22 visit, a Scott County inspector cited this establishment for 13 risk-factor violations, an exceptionally  high number. The inspector observed a stack of sliced cheese left uncovered inside a cooler, and uncovered containers of apples and applesauce, risking contamination. In addition, two containers of cut lettuce and one container of sliced cheese were holding at temperatures of 51 to 54 degrees, and several containers of prepared or opened food products — such as diced ham, mushrooms and peppers — were not date-marked to ensure freshness and safety.
Also, a container of expired, shaved ham, dated July 13, was located in the reach-in cooler that was being used on the cook line. In addition, the interior of the ice machine, a container of knives, the magnetic knife racks, and the interior of a reach-in cooler all had a buildup of “dried food debris or soil” and required additional cleaning and sanitizing.
The inspector also reported the handwashing sink located on the cook line was being used to store dirty dishes, and “mouse droppings were observed in several areas throughout the facility, including around the perimeter of the doughnut preparation area … One sticky trap with a dead baby mouse was observed underneath a shelving unit … Several sticky fly traps were observed being hung from the ceiling throughout the kitchen and food-prep areas.”
The visit was prompted by an illness complaint the inspector deemed unverified.
Gog Dynasty Buffet, 5388 Elmore Ave., Davenport — During a July 17 visit, a Scott inspector noted that several cooked items — including macaroni and cheese, noodle dishes, cooked vegetables and meat dishes — that had been prepared during the previous two days had yet to cool to 41 degrees inside the walk-in cooler. All of the items were discarded.
“Several refrigeration units throughout the facility” were holding food items at above the maximum of 41 degrees, the inspector reported, including both of the walk-in coolers, the sushi-prep cooler, two cola coolers near the sushi station, and a food-prep cooler in front of the main cook line.
The inspector also found that several cold items on the buffet line were not properly nested in ice and were above 41 degrees — such as the watermelon, cut lettuce, salads with cut tomatoes and raw seed sprouts. The inspector also reported the staff was “pre-populating” times in the book used to record the time of day at which sushi rice was prepared. “Inspector cannot verify that times are accurate,” the inspector noted, adding that this was one of several repeat violations.
The inspector also reported that the dishwashing machine was dispensing no detectable levels of sanitizing solution, food was not being properly cooled, the walk-in coolers were being “set at higher temperatures,” and the handwashing sinks couldn’t dispense hot water that topped 90 degrees.
The inspection was performed in conjunction with a visit by the City of Davenport’s building and fire departments, the inspector noted, adding that repairs were being made to the restaurant’s fire suppression system and the building department was assisting with structural issues, electrical issues and “grease cleanup.”
In April 2026, the county’s food inspectors cited Gog Dynasty Buffet for 16 risk-factor violations, an exceptionally large number.
Mason Dixon, 163 Main St., Dubuque — During a July 16 visit, a City of Dubuque inspector observed that the cooler used to store cut fruit was holding items at 60 degrees. The food in the cooler was discarded. Also, dead insects were found inside the soda-gun holsters in the establishment’s basement bar, and access to the handwashing sinks was blocked.
Soi 4 Thai,  5023 Competition Drive, Bettendorf — During a July 16 visit, a Scott County inspector reported the person in charge “did not know the basic knowledge of food storage, food temperatures or food safety handling procedures” and cited the business for 11 risk-factor violations, an unusually high number.
Cooked rice heated in a microwave oven was measured at 123 degrees and had to be reheated to 165 degrees. Also, containers of curry that had been prepared the day before had yet to cool to 41 degrees and had to be discarded.
“Several food items in the prep cooler not dated-marked,” the inspector reported. “Curry containers that were pulled from the freezer not date- marked properly. Date was 3/6 written on containers.”



Quotation







Facility has no date-marking system in place. Food-contact surfaces -- including prep tables, pans, containers, and cutting boards -- were heavily soiled throughout the establishment … Establishment was found unclean throughout.


– Inspector's report on Sam's Fine Foods and Egg Rolls, Des Moines


Sam’s Fine Foods and Egg Rolls, 3300 SW 9th St., Des Moines — During a July 14 visit, a state inspector found that raw poultry, fried chicken, cooked pork and cooked rice were being stored in the reach-in cooler at “elevated temperatures” of up to 62 degrees. All of the raw meats and other food items that were out of acceptable temperature ranges were discarded.
“Facility has no date-marking system in place,” the inspector reported. “Food-contact surfaces — including prep tables, pans, containers, and cutting boards — were heavily soiled throughout the establishment … The establishment was found to require additional refrigeration units … Establishment was found unclean throughout.”
The inspector also reported finding an “overflowing bin of water” that was dripping onto various food items stored inside the reach-in cooler.”
The visit was prompted by an illness complaint that was deemed unverified. The inspector reported the owner “voluntarily closed the establishment for the remainder of the evening to clean and relocate food items” into whatever functioning refrigerators remained after one cooler was removed from service. “The owner may resume operations at their discretion,” the inspector reported.
Hy-Vee Foods, 1107 S.E. Army Post Road, Des Moines — During a July 7 visit, a state inspector found egg drop soup that was being held at 124 degrees, and sweet-and-sour soup that was held at 118 degrees. Both soups were discarded. In the Chinese food area, the inspector also found beef held at 56 degrees, chicken at 55 degrees, and raw pork at 45 degrees. All of the items were discarded.
In addition, a large mixer bowl in the bakery department was soiled, as were the display case shelves, walls and dividers in the meat department.
The visit was prompted by two non-illness complaints that pertained to food that was either procured from unsafe sources or was adulterated in some way, and general sanitation. Citing the findings related to the maintenance and cleanliness of the establishment, the inspector deemed the complaints verified.
Uchu, 1704 E. Grand Ave., Des Moines — During a June 25 visit, a state inspector cited this restaurant for 13 risk-factor violations, an exceptionally large number. According to the inspector, the person in charge was unable to demonstrate knowledge of the federal food-safety regulations, specifically with regard to the required temperatures and times for holding hot and cold food, proper methods of safely cooling foods, date-marking items to ensure freshness and safety, and cleaning and sanitizing utensils and food-contact surfaces.
Cooked chicken was being held in the kitchen at 108 degrees and had to be discarded. Cooked beans inside the walk-in cooler had yet to cool to 41 degrees after being prepared the previous day or earlier and had to be discarded. In addition, various unspecified food items prepared in “prior days” were found throughout kitchen without any date-markings. Also, the owner indicated dishes were being washed with soap, but no sanitizer was being used.
Tony’s Chicago Pizza and Breakfast, 2297 Falcon Drive, Bettendorf — During a June 23 visit, a Scott County inspector cited this business for 11 risk-factor violations, an unusually high number. The inspector observed that a salad-preparation cooler was holding food items at 45 to 50 degrees. The cooler was then placed out of service.
In addition, the kitchen’s main food-prep cooler was holding items at 44 to 45 degrees. Several food items in the coolers were not date-marked to ensure freshness and safety. Separately, the inspector found linguine noodles that were date-marked June 11 and salsa that was dated April 7. Both items were discarded. In addition, the water had been shut off to one of the handwashing sinks.
Thai Basil Altoona, 550 36th Ave., Altoona — During a June 18 visit, a state inspector cited this establishment for 12 risk-factor violations, an unusually high number. Multiple frozen foods had been placed on sheet pans inside the walk-in freezer where they were left uncovered, risking contamination, the inspector reported. Also, cooked chicken and beef prepared earlier in the day was measured at 68 and 64 degrees, having yet to cool to 41 degrees.
In addition, a large bowl of soup prepared the previous day was still holding at 66 degrees inside one of the coolers. The chicken and beef were transferred to the freezer, while the soup was discarded. The inspector also found multiple containers of house-made curry sauce holding at 70 degrees. The sauces were discarded. Separately, several house-made sauces in the reach-in cooler were past their discard dates and had to be thrown away.
Also, raw fish was being improperly thawed, increasing the risk of any spoilage going undetected, and several of the stored knives were soiled. The inspector also made note of frozen chicken that was left to thaw on a counter while immersed in a bucket of standing water.

name: WyoFile
title: ‘True’ conservatives, public lands, data centers top issues for Wyoming primary election voters
description:
Many will be happy when the deluge of election-related mailers and text messages is over, they told WyoFile on Tuesday.
The post ‘True’ conservatives, public lands, data centers top issues for Wyoming primary election voters appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
RIVERTON—There wasn’t a single issue or race that spurred Harold Johnson to cast his ballot at the Fremont County Fairgrounds, but rather a set of values that he said shaped his decisions. 
These include small government, authentic conservatives and budget cutting — the same core values he always votes on. As for how he determines which GOP candidates in crowded primary-election races are genuine articles, he said, one thing’s for sure. 
“I don’t believe what the mailers say,” he said. 
Johnson, like many Wyoming voters, has been fishing stacks of political fliers and attack ads out of his mailbox all summer. Some voters told WyoFile they don’t give much credence to those mailers and door hangers — or the incessant text messages that have become part of the primary campaign cycle. 
Instead, he said, he did his own homework to assess which candidates most align with his vision of ideal government. 
The definition of a true conservative was top of mind for many in this red state during Tuesday’s primary election, which underscores growing tensions in the Republican party between the hard-line Freedom Caucus and more moderate colleagues considered the “old guard” of the GOP.
A child waits while his mother votes in the Aug. 18, 2026 primary election at the Fremont County Fairgrounds in Riverton. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
The caucus aims to build on its victorious 2024 election season, when it won control of the Wyoming House. Several caucus members and allies are pursuing Senate seats. The Senate thwarted some of the caucus’ priorities during the most recent legislative session such as cuts to the University of Wyoming and the Wyoming Business Council. 
And with statewide and congressional campaigns also crowded with Republican candidates — including nine vying for the state’s lone U.S. representative seat — sussing out conservative bona fides was no small feat. Because Wyoming is so dominantly Republican, primary election winners often go on to sweep the general election.
Around Wyoming, voters who cast ballots on everything from mayoral contests to governor and congressional seats also cited public lands, data centers and taxes as motivating factors. Here’s a rundown of what they had to say.
From local to national
Many Wyoming voters were spurred to the polls by issues that will impact their local communities. They spoke of implications to road construction, EMS funding and public safety. 
In Laramie County, voter Carrie Pritchard listed data center water usage as a top concern. 
“Our water table is getting low,” Pritchard said. “We don’t have enough water for the people, for our reservoirs and everything, and [data centers] use a lot of the water.”
In Lander, Danny Kness was most concerned with a local sales and use tax measure that would raise revenue for ambulance systems, commercial air service and public ground transit. 
“The main thing that brought me out was the three-quarter percent tax,” said Kness, who opposes the measure. Taxpayer dollars should not fund private business, he said. 
The tax measure was also significant to Kirsten Brown of Lander, but in a different way; it was one of the main things she wanted to vote yes on. Brown sees the measure as a way to “support and help out our neighbors,” she said.  
For other voters, national issues were dominant. That was the case for Laurie Jenkins, one of the first at her polling station in Teton County, who said public lands were chief among her issues.  
“They’re foundational to everything I have worked for and believe in,” the former National Park Service employee said. She had 40 years of experience with the agency before she left her post.

Casper resident Kenny Mayer said access to public lands was among his top priorities for choosing 2026 primary election candidates. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)

In Casper, 63-year-old Kenny Mayer also paid close attention to candidates’ stances on public lands. The avid bowhunter and fisherman favored those who will “protect our public lands and not sell them out to big corporations,” he said. 
Fealty to the Trump administration guided the decisions of a Riverton voter who declined to give her name. Her main hope was to see the national status quo maintained, she said. 
“I definitely want the country to go forward with the Trump agenda,” she said. “I want the Trump agenda to succeed.” 
Other voters were hopeful their votes could help defeat candidates they didn’t like. 
“I won’t vote for Gray,” said Louise Kranz, 89, outside of the polls in Riverton, referring to Republican U.S. House candidate and current Wyoming Secretary of State Chuck Gray. After all, she noted, he is from California. 
“And I won’t vote for Friess,” said Sandy Wilder, who was accompanying Kranz. She was referring to one of Gray’s competitors in the U.S. House race, Republican Steve Friess. Friess, Wilder noted, is from Jackson, which is “the California of Wyoming.”
Some old, some new
Issues that have long mattered to Wyoming voters, like energy, education and the Second Amendment, still carry weight. 
For Casper voter Michael Broyles, education was top of mind. As a band teacher at Kelly Walsh High School and a father of four young children, Broyles is concerned not only about funding cuts to education, but what he sees as politicians who don’t value public schools or the teaching profession in general.
A poll watcher sits on the sidelines during the Wyoming primary election on Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026, at Laramie County Community College in Cheyenne. (Dan Cepeda for Oil City News and WyoFile)
“Lately, the Wyoming state government has made a lot of cuts to education and funding for various things through the Freedom Caucus,” Broyles said. “So one of my biggest priorities as a voter today was to try to eliminate as many of those Freedom Caucus members as possible and try to get people in office that support educators and schools.”
Barbara Cardenas of Riverton, meanwhile, said she wants to see little to no government interference.
“I just sit home and mind my own business,” she said. Ideally, she said, elected officials would let her be.
This story was produced with reporting from WyoFile staff in Casper, Cheyenne, Lander, Jackson and Laramie.

name: VTDigger
title: Alleging illegal retaliation, union wins temporary halt to closure of St. Albans dairy plant
description:
A federal judge granted an order to stop Dairy Farmers of America from closing the plant, which had been set to shut down on Monday. The dispute goes to court Thursday.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Alleging illegal retaliation, union wins temporary halt to closure of St. Albans dairy plant.
text:
Members of the Teamsters local 597 union picket outside the Dairy Farmers of America plant in St. Albans in September 2025. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Workers at the Dairy Farmers of America processing plant in St. Albans can hold onto their jobs this week after a federal judge issued a restraining order to temporarily halt a planned closure.
In a complaint filed Friday, the Teamsters Local No. 597 requested the order, claiming that multiple supervisors told some employees that the decision to close the plant was related to last year’s strike. 
The union said the DFA’s decision to idle the plant was an illegal act of retaliation.
The complaint also describes what the union says is an internal memo found by a janitor last week that labels “union decertification” as the “#1 reason” for the closure. A legal representative for DFA called the memo “fake” in an email to the union, which was attached to the court filings.
At the time of the complaint’s filing, the union said DFA had started to shut down operations, including largely ceasing milk processing and drastically reducing labor hours.
The temporary restraining order, issued Monday by U.S. District Judge William K. Sessions III, will last for five days. The district court will hold a hearing Thursday afternoon, where the union will argue for a longer stay until its grievances have been resolved in keeping with the collective bargaining agreements made with DFA.
DFA rejected any attempt to link the closure to union activities. “First and foremost, neither the union nor the 2025 strike was the reason for the closure of the St. Albans plant,” DFA’s lawyer said in the email to the union. The company also said in a Facebook post that the reasons for the closure had to do with broader operational and network changes.
In July, Jesse Case, director of the Teamsters Food Processing Division, which includes Local No. 597, alleged the shutdown was payback for union activity.
“Dairy Farmers of America is shutting down its St. Albans facility and eliminating good union jobs in what appears to be retaliation against members of Teamsters Local 597, who were forced to strike last year after the company refused to negotiate a fair contract,” he said in a statement. “This closure is not an isolated business decision. It is the result of a broader strategy by DFA to consolidate market share and power across the dairy industry.”
Vermont’s U.S. Sens. Bernie Sanders and Peter Welch wrote a letter Tuesday to DFA President and CEO Dennis Rodenbaugh urging the co-op to keep the plant open and reach a fair agreement with the union.
“At a time when Vermont’s family dairy farms are already facing enormous economic pressures, losing an important piece of the processing infrastructure that connects those farms to markets creates another serious challenge,” they said in the letter. “We are very concerned that Vermont dairy farmers were not consulted before this decision and will face even steeper costs as a result of this idling.”
The St. Albans plant and the adjoining St. Albans Creamery & Supply have operated in the county for decades, with the factory producing dairy for Vermont vendors, including Ben & Jerry’s and Cabot Creamery. The June closure announcement came after St. Albans Creamery & Supply announced it would close its co-op grocery store last summer, transitioning solely into a retail business. It also followed the plant’s unionized workers’ reaching a contract with Dairy Farmers of America in October 2025, after alleging “brutal” working conditions, including mandatory overtime that extended their shifts into 12-hour workdays.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Alleging illegal retaliation, union wins temporary halt to closure of St. Albans dairy plant.

name: Daily Montanan
title: District Court judge says he’ll rule quickly on term limit lawsuit
description: Montana District Court Judge Chris Abbott said on Tuesday afternoon he will decide quickly on a lawsuit filed by two longtime Republican state legislators over Attorney General Austin Knudsen’s reinterpretation of  the state’s term limit statue. Knudsen published his opinion just days before the secretary of state must certify who will be on the November […]
text:
Lewis and Clark Courthouse is pictured on Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026, in Helena, MT. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)Montana District Court Judge Chris Abbott said on Tuesday afternoon he will decide quickly on a lawsuit filed by two longtime Republican state legislators over Attorney General Austin Knudsen’s reinterpretation of  the state’s term limit statue.
Knudsen published his opinion just days before the secretary of state must certify who will be on the November ballot.
Montana lawmakers are limited to serving eight years in each the House and Senate within a 16-year period. Some lawmakers have stayed in office longer than 16 years by switching between chambers. 
But Knudsen’s decision overturned a 2012 decision by then-Attorney General and Democrat Steve Bullock, which interpreted the term limits statute as allowing candidates to run for election in the House or Senate immediately after completing eight years in the opposite chamber. They then could return to their original chamber 16 years after they began their term, with no break between those.
Knudsen’s opinion differs, saying the clock starts when a candidate is voted into office in November — not when they take office in January. Legislators would have to have a break between returning to office, and two legislators would be disqualified from being certified this week for office.
District Court Judge Christopher Abbott presides in the Montana First Judicial District Court on Friday, July 17, 2026. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)
And on Tuesday, lawyers for the Attorney General’s Office argued that eight years means eight years, full stop.
“As soon as you hit that eight years, the constitution doesn’t contain any other provisions,” Deputy Solicitor General Brent Mead told the court Tuesday. “It is eight years that triggers the prohibition, and that’s it.”
House Majority Leader Steve Fitzpatrick and House Rep. Llew Jones, along with Ted Kronebusch — a longtime ally of Jones and leader of the Pondera County Republican Party — are plaintiffs in the case, and all briefly took the witness stand. 
Jones, chairman of the powerful House Appropriations Committee and an architect of the state budget, beat Rep. Zach Wirth in a tight Republican primary for Senate District 9 earlier this year. Fitzpatrick is running for reelection in House District 24.
They will be barred from being on the ballot if Knudsen’s decision stands. Jones and Fitzpatrick both won their Republican primaries in districts that have historically gone to conservatives in the state. 
Senate President Matt Regier, a Flathead Republican, requested Knudsen look at Jones’ eligibility on July 9, just six weeks before the ballot certification deadline, which is Aug. 20.
Fitzpatrick said after the hearing that he felt it went well and that Judge Abbott was asking questions he felt favored the plaintiffs. Both sides agree that court is the proper venue for settling the issue, said Jesse Laslovich, who gave arguments for the legislators on Tuesday.
But the timing is an issue, Laslovich said, even pointing out that more legal documents had been filed in the time leading up to the 2:30 p.m. hearing that no one — not the court, not the defense, not the plaintiffs — all fully had time to read.
“If we were sincere about this 800-pound gorilla in the room needing to be addressed, we would do it the right way,” Laslovich said. “It would not be 90 days before the secretary of state is to certify the ballots for the general election.”
Austin James, representing the Secretary of State’s Office, said they are under a massive time crunch. They also don’t know what to do with the replacement candidates that the state Republican Party has asked for.
On Monday night, members of the state’s Republican Party nominated Kronebusch as a replacement candidate for Jones — the state GOP previously instructed county parties in the districts Jones and Fitzpatrick would represent to find replacement candidates for them.
“We’re not sure what to do with that once we get it, and we would ask the court to declare whether a vacancy hazard has not occurred depending on its ruling, and simultaneously what that replacement process looks like depending on its ruling,” James said. “But at the end of the day, we also want to make sure that our voters have a candidate on the ballot, and that that candidate is eligible.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah leaders meet to drill down on more changes for homelessness, mental health and jails
description: Inspired by the “Miami model” in Florida — where Miami-Dade County has been diverting nonviolent people with mental illness away from jails and into mental health facilities — Utah state, city and county leaders are taking the next steps to put a plan into action.  The mastermind behind the “Miami model,” former Judge Steven Leifman, sat […]
text:
From left, Utah's homeless coordinator Tyler Clancy, Salt Lake City Mayor Erin Mendenhall, Salt Lake County Mayor Jenny Wilson, and former Judge Steven Leifman hold a news conference at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Aug. 18, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)Inspired by the “Miami model” in Florida — where Miami-Dade County has been diverting nonviolent people with mental illness away from jails and into mental health facilities — Utah state, city and county leaders are taking the next steps to put a plan into action. 
The mastermind behind the “Miami model,” former Judge Steven Leifman, sat next to Salt Lake County Mayor Jenny Wilson, Salt Lake City Mayor Erin Mendenhall, and the state’s homelessness coordinator, Tyler Clancy, at the Utah Capitol on Tuesday to brief reporters on what they’ve been working on, based on earlier recommendations by Leifman. 
For three days this week — starting with a closed-door meeting earlier Tuesday also attended by Gov. Spencer Cox, who threw his support behind the effort — state, city and county officials said in a news release they’ll be launching new workgroups and holding “executive team and stakeholder meetings” to implement the plan while drawing on expertise from law enforcement, the courts, behavioral health providers and other community organizations. 
Former Judge Steven Leifman listens during a news conference at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Aug. 18, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
Leifman said his group’s recommendations aren’t just focused on diverting people from homelessness and incarceration — but rather “modernizing” behavioral health services to help people experiencing mental health crises. He said while the U.S. shuttered state mental hospitals, focused on “crime and drugs” and “massively cut housing,” people experiencing mental illness “got thrown into communities … that just were not built for them.”
“So instead of designing a system for them that worked, we blame them and incarcerate,” he said, adding that “70% of people in jail in the U.S. today either have a serious mental illness, a substance abuse disorder, or both.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Leifman said his recommendations are not focused on “coddling a criminal” but rather “getting smart, wrapping our arms around the person that needs it and getting them the right care that they need.”
After partnering with Salt Lake County leaders in late 2025, the Leifman Group developed 25 recommendations to improve how state, city and county systems help people with mental health and substance use needs — meant to pull them away from cycling in and out of the courts and jails and into services that can actually help them. 
“Today’s meeting was to launch the work around those 25 recommendations,” Wilson told reporters. “What’s really reassuring to me is the commitment across party lines to solutions and the interest of people who get up every day, care about this work … to come in and recognize that collaboration will not only be a path to a better outcome for an individual who is facing challenges, but also will be ultimately benefiting the taxpayer by the reduction of cost.” 
Salt Lake County Mayor Jenny Wilson speaks during a news conference at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Aug. 18, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
Leifman Group recommendations
In a report outlining those recommendations, the Leifman Group applauded state and local leaders for having an “amazing amount of coordination and political will” compared to other states to tackle the issue, but also found Salt Lake County faces “significant challenges,” including:

Still fragmented coordination across systems and agencies.
Limited data sharing and no unified data hub.
Insufficient housing — especially deeply affordable and supportive housing.
Gaps in diversion, supervision, and care coordination.
A proliferation of committees and bodies with overlapping mandates but no single, unified implementation structure.

The Leifman Group’s recommendations’ key themes, according to that report, included:

Invest in early prevention — like child trauma screenings — of substance use and mental health concerns to prevent people entering homelessness and criminal justice systems in the future.
Strengthen crisis response, including changing 911 scripts, expanding mobile crisis outreach teams specifically trained to respond to people experiencing a mental health crisis, and building more crisis receiving centers in the south end of the county.
Implement universal jail screening and full service and better coordinated multi-agency case management. 
Expand assisted outpatient treatment and civil commitment options while addressing bed capacity constraints.
Increase housing systemwide and carefully implement “potential large congregate ‘campus’ models to avoid “risk-mixing,” which the Leifman Group described as co-locating “criminogenically low- and high-risk individuals” that would likely lead to more “recidivism, victimization, and crime.”
Create a “cross-system data hub and data-sharing protocols” for better coordinated care, accountability, and data-driven decision-making.
Establish an implementation structure with shared leadership, clear priorities, and subcommittees.

Salt Lake County Mayor Jenny Wilson and former Judge Steven Leifman hold a news conference at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Aug. 18, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
How are state, local leaders already acting?
Last year, state leaders eyed building a massive, 1,300-bed homeless campus in northwest Salt Lake City, but that plan faced intense pushback. Earlier this year the Legislature didn’t put any money toward the campus but rather funded Cox’s administration’s plans to expand shelter, supportive housing, and bolster mental and behavioral health services while also looking to break cycles of “high utilizers” of jails and homeless shelters. 
If successful, state officials have said those strategies could later inform a campus’ operations — or maybe divert enough people that a campus is no longer needed. 
Once a hostel, a new mental health group home for women opens in Salt Lake City

Some of the Leifman Group’s recommendations may take up to 10 years to implement, while others could be adopted in a matter of months, Wilson said. 
Some changes will require more money than others, the county mayor added. 
“There are things that we can do that don’t cost a penny that are just changing policy or investment,” she said, but other changes may require state funding that would need approval from the Utah Legislature. “We are not prepared today to have a legislative ask, but in the weeks to come we will. And I think many of the things (implemented) this year will be systemic change, not big-cost items.”
But Wilson and Clancy noted work has already started — including the recent opening of mental health group homes that are expected to eventually total 90 beds. And state leaders are expanding Salt Lake City’s Project CONNECT, which is a program focused on the city’s 50 most-arrested people that the city has described as a “cross-agency initiative to divert high utilizers of the justice system into treatment to relieve strain on resources.” 
Utah homeless leaders look to focus funding on ‘high utilizers’ while not ‘backing away’ from campus

Wilson also said there’s a group already working to evaluate the existing 911 script to include responses tailored specifically for people experiencing a mental health crisis.  
“We know often if somebody’s calling 911, it can be due to a family member or friend’s mental health crisis,” she said. “Yet the dispatch person taking the information doesn’t have the option on their list to (ask), ‘is this indeed a mental health emergency?’ (But) what we need to do before we throw that on the script and get all these dispatch people trained is to make sure that we have an adequate and fully implemented path (to help).”
One recommendation that Leifman pointed out was risk assessments for children as early as possible to prevent spirals later in life. He said oftentimes people who are in jail with mental illness “have horrific histories of trauma.” 
“We need to be screening kids at early ages for trauma as quickly and best we can, getting them help as early as we can, so they don’t end up in the criminal justice system,” he said.
Utah’s homeless coordinator Tyler Clancy, Salt Lake City Mayor Erin Mendenhall, Salt Lake County Mayor Jenny Wilson, and former Judge Steven Leifman hold a news conference at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Aug. 18, 2026. (Courtesy of Ashley Detrick/Salt Lake City Mayor’s Office)
Mendenhall, Salt Lake City’s mayor, applauded the Leifman Group’s recommendations. 
“It’s not just picking up the cookie cutter of Miami-Dade and punching it through Salt Lake County,” she said, but rather it’s tailoring a plan to the state and county’s needs “and helping us arrange it into a much more effective, humane and taxpayer friendly situation so that we can stop spinning the wheels of waste and lack of services for people who need it most.”
Wilson and Mendenhall said in coming months as more details of their plan take shape, they expect to put together funding or legislative proposals for the Utah Legislature’s upcoming session, slated to start in January. 
Clancy also said they’ll be looking at the system’s “capacity needs” and whether that needs to be expanded, “as well as our laws” and if anything needs to change to help implement the plan. 
“Whether it’s looking at things with civil commitment or plea and abeyances … those are all things we’re going to dive into pretty deep here,” Clancy said.
Salt Lake City Mayor Erin Mendenhall speaks during a news conference at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Aug. 18, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)

title: Idaho has spent $31 million on firefighting while nearly 700K acres have burned statewide
description: Nearly 700,000 acres have burned across Idaho so far this year, and state officials are predicting fire risk will remain high through September.  As the costs to fight fires increase, state agency staff said they plan to increase Idaho’s dedicated funding to boost firefighting resources amid tight budget conditions as staff prepare the budget request […]
text:
A smoke column billows over rangeland near South Mountain in Idaho. (Photo courtesy of InciWeb) Nearly 700,000 acres have burned across Idaho so far this year, and state officials are predicting fire risk will remain high through September. 
As the costs to fight fires increase, state agency staff said they plan to increase Idaho’s dedicated funding to boost firefighting resources amid tight budget conditions as staff prepare the budget request for next fiscal year. 
Dustin Miller is the director of the Idaho Department of Lands. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Department of Lands)
The Idaho Department of Lands has about $25 million in its fire suppression fund, but it’s unclear where that will stand by the end of fire season, IDL Director Dustin Miller told statewide officers who sit on the Idaho Board of Land Commissioners Tuesday. 
“We’re entering a more challenging period of the 2026 fire season as conditions continue to dry across the state. The significant wildland fire potential outlook indicates above average fire potential statewide through August and September,” Miller said at the meeting. 
Many of the blazes state firefighters have been working on include assisting other agencies, such as federal agencies, and it will take time to determine the state share of the costs and reimbursement totals. 
So far, the state agency has spent an estimated $31 million on fighting fires, and it is expected to be reimbursed around $10.9 million, Miller said.

 Busy fire season in the Pacific Northwest leads to strain on firefighting resources

There’s a lot of fire activity in the Pacific Northwest, which can put a strain on resources, Miller said. Across the U.S., more than 7.2 million acres have burned, Miller said, which is above the 10-year average for this point in the year. 
When rangeland fires were burning in southern Idaho, Miller said, the U.S. Department of Interior Wildland Fire Service had a hard time allocating resources to them, because there was a focus on areas such as Spokane, where people and communities were in danger. 
Miller said Gov. Brad Little’s activation of the Idaho National Guard to assist with fighting was helpful because of a lack of federal resources. 
“The Guard helped a lot out on the Big Grass Fire in particular, by allocating their helicopters and their crews,” Miller said. “Because we were in such a dire situation, resource orders were unable to fill, having that additional support from the Guard made a big difference I think down in Owyhee County.” 
The Big Grass Fire is 82% contained as of Tuesday and burned nearly 580,000 acres, according to federal fire reporting website InciWeb. 
 After this year’s legislative budget cuts, Idaho agency will seek boost in fire funding 

In its budget proposal to the governor’s office, the Idaho Department of Lands will seek the restoration of some fire funding and increases in other areas to mostly support firefighting at the agency. 
“The majority of our budget enhancements are for fire that align with our fire strategic plan and will be supported entirely with dedicated funds,” said Rachelle Vance, IDL financial executive officer. 
During the 2026 legislative session, state budget writers approved cuts across nearly every state agency to avoid a projected budget shortfall. Some firefighting costs were funded at lower levels than requested or on a one-time basis. 
In June, the state’s fire suppression fund hit $0, the Idaho Capital Sun reported. However, the Legislature had approved a one-time transfer of interest earnings into the account of $32.8 million, which occurred at the start of the new fiscal year on July 1. 
The agency in its fiscal year 2028 request will ask for $131,800 paid annually out of the state general fund toward fire costs to restore the 1% budget cuts the Legislature approved for fiscal year 2027, according to the budget proposal presented Tuesday. The agency will also request four new full-time, fire-related employees and one new financial employee position. 
The request also includes one-time equipment purchases and replacements, such as fire radios, tactical service vehicles, and fire detection cameras. 
The total request is for about $10 million. 
 Land board members approve surcharge increase to boost fire preparedness fund 

Land board members on Tuesday also voted to approve an increase in the surcharge paid on property tax assessments for forested land with residential structures on them. The board first heard of the proposal at its meeting last month, the Sun reported. 
Private and state land owners on forested parcels in Idaho pay Forest Fire Protection Assessment fees on their property tax bills to cover costs associated with protecting their properties from wildfire. The money goes into the state’s “fire preparedness fund,” which is one of the dedicated sources the agency would tap to fund its budget requests. 
The assessment is set at 60 cents per acre, charged at a minimum of 25 acres, with a $40 surcharge if a residential structure is on the parcel. The surcharge was last increased in 2009. 
Board members approved increasing the surcharge to $90, with members wanting to look into implementing a tiered rate that would differ depending on the value of the residence on the land. 
There are around 68,000 parcels that will be affected by the new surcharge, said State Forest Julia Lauch.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont, CT officials fear nuclear merger could raise electricity costs
description: The proposed merger between NextEra and Dominion would create the world's largest regulated electric utility. CT has concerns.
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont announced on Tuesday that his administration is seeking intervene in federal regulators’ review of a proposed merger between two utility giants that would consolidate control over New England’s two nuclear power plants.
While neither of the companies involved in the merger — Virginia’s Dominion Energy and Florida’s NextEra Energy — sell power directly to residential customers in Connecticut, together they control more than a quarter of all the electricity produced in the region through their ownership of nuclear, solar and natural gas power plants. Much of the power those plants produce is sold to the utility companies that serve Connecticut customers. 
The deal requires approval from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, or FERC. 
Two Connecticut state agencies, the Department of Energy and Environmental Protection and the Office of Consumer Counsel, have filed formal motions to intervene in the case before FERC, as has Attorney General William Tong, who joined Lamont in issuing a press release Tuesday warning the deal could reduce competition and raise prices for consumers.
“We’ve seen what happens when utility companies establish near-monopolies: Connecticut families pay the price while shareholders reap the rewards,” Lamont said in a statement. “We’re intervening to protect the best interests of Connecticut families and businesses and to ensure the regulatory review process considers the potential risks this merger poses for Connecticut ratepayers, who already pay some of the highest utility prices in the country.”
Cathryn Vaulman, a spokesperson for the governor, later clarified that Lamont was not yet calling for regulators to reject the merger between the two companies.
Instead, she said, Lamont was “raising concerns and seeking very strict scrutiny” over the deal’s potential impact on ratepayers. 
Tong, however, went further with a statement opposing the deal, which he said comes at a time when customers are already “getting crushed by surging energy costs.”
“The last thing we need is consolidated corporate control over the core of Connecticut’s energy supply,” Tong said. “I cannot support this merger. The Office of the Attorney General has intervened in this proceeding and is weighing all legal options to protect Connecticut’s access to affordable, clean, reliable energy.”
In a statement Tuesday, Dominion spokesman Ryan Frazier did not address the proposed merger but said the company shares Lamont’s and Tong’s concerns about energy affordability.
“Nuclear power is the region’s most reliable, efficient, and cost-effective form of electricity,” he said in the statement. “We will continue working with lawmakers and policymakers throughout Connecticut and New England to ensure that nuclear power remains a viable option in the region.”
A spokesperson for NextEra did not respond to requests for comment on Tuesday. 
NextEra, the larger of the two companies, announced its plans to acquire Dominion in May for $67 billion. If approved, the deal would create the world’s largest regulated utility company, with more than 10 million customers and 110 gigawatts of electric generation.
Dominion owns the Millstone Nuclear Power Plant in Waterford, which is the largest power plant in all of New England. NextEra owns Seabrook Nuclear Power Station, a slightly smaller facility in New Hampshire.
NextEra also owns gas power plants, solar and battery facilities and high-voltage transmission lines throughout the region.
Lamont’s statement on Tuesday coincided with a release from the New England States Committee on Electricity voicing similar concerns, which the committee said where shared by five New England states (New Hampshire being the exception). NESCOE pointed to NextEra’s previous efforts to block the construction of a major transmission line through Maine as evidence the merger deserves close scrutiny.
“The proposed acquisition would concentrate an unprecedented amount of leverage in NextEra,” the group’s statement said. “NextEra is an entity with a history of using its already considerable resources to obstruct new transmission infrastructure projects that New England needs.”
NESCOE also accused Dominion of having a “problematic history” in the region, specifically referring to the company’s threats to close Millstone in 2018 amid negotiations with the state over long-term power purchase agreements.
That outcome was avoided the following year when Lamont announced a deal to purchase half the plant’s output — roughly 9 million megawatt-hours a year — through 2029. Connecticut has a similar contract to purchase power from Seabrook.
In January, DEEP began seeking bids for new grid-scale clean energy procurements, including successors to its current contracts with Millstone and Seabrook. Both NextEra and Dominion submitted bids on behalf of their respective plants, spokespeople for the companies previously told the Connecticut Mirror.
That procurement process is expected to be completed before the merger between NextEra and Dominion is final. Neither company has announced plans to close or significantly expand either facility.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: State audit finds $3.73 million in misspent Tulsa Public Schools bond funds
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — A former bond director at Tulsa Public Schools wrongly profited from millions of dollars meant for student facilities, a state audit alleged Tuesday. State Auditor and Inspector Cindy Byrd released the final installment of her office’s multi-part audit of Tulsa schools, this time focusing on the district’s former executive director of bonds [[...]
text:
State Auditor and Inspector Cindy Byrd presents the findings of her office's second audit of Tulsa Public Schools on Tuesday at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — A former bond director at Tulsa Public Schools wrongly profited from millions of dollars meant for student facilities, a state audit alleged Tuesday.
State Auditor and Inspector Cindy Byrd released the final installment of her office’s multi-part audit of Tulsa schools, this time focusing on the district’s former executive director of bonds and energy management, Charles Christopher Hudgins.
Hudgins and construction contractors Thomas McKenna and Gayle Gwinup were charged in Tulsa County District Court on June 4 with defrauding Tulsa schools of $779,317 in bond funds. State auditors now allege Hudgins and various vendors were at the nexus of $3.73 million in improper spending.
Hudgins’ attorney, Rick Cella, said his client “is presumed innocent and maintains his innocence.”
“Press conferences and one-sided audit reports are not evidence,” Cella said. “Chris looks forward to his day in court.”
Gwinup’s attorney, Thomas Reese, declined to comment Tuesday. McKenna’s attorney, Allen Smallwood, did not immediately return a request for comment Tuesday afternoon. 
All three defendants have pleaded not guilty to charges of conspiracy to defraud a school district, embezzlement, and making or receiving a kickback, online court records show.
Attorney General Gentner Drummond said additional charges are possible in light of the audit findings. Drummond filed the original charges with the Tulsa County District Attorney’s Office.
Attorney General Gentner Drummond speaks at a press conference at his office in Oklahoma City on Feb. 25, 2025. (Photo by Janelle Stecklein/Oklahoma Voice)
“This audit confirms what our June charges already made clear – bond dollars meant to repair and improve Tulsa schools were instead treated as someone’s personal piggy bank,” Drummond said in a statement Tuesday. “I thank Auditor Byrd and her staff for their diligence in building out this record. My office is reviewing the full audit now, and we are not finished. Additional charges are on the table.”
Byrd said the misspent funds are a result of the Tulsa Board of Education “putting too much trust in an individual, allowing them years of unilateral control.” The school board “rubber stamped” Hudgins’ recommendations without reviewing project contracts and amendments, she said.
“There’s a lot of money that’s been misappropriated,” she said. “So, either taxpayers paid too much, or else the children and the students didn’t get what they should have gotten as a result of this bond money.”
Tulsa administrators and school board members were “very cooperative” with state auditors, Byrd said, and “they wanted to take steps to make sure that something like this doesn’t happen again.”
She said her office is organizing training sessions for school boards across the state to help them give proper financial oversight.
Tulsa Public Schools Superintendent Ebony Johnson attends a news conference at Eisenhower International School in Tulsa on Oct. 2. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Tulsa Superintendent Ebony Johnson said the district has added safeguards to ensure it has more transparency in its financial reporting protocols. In a statement Tuesday, she said the district intends to seek full restitution.
“Our students and our school communities deserve every dollar meant for them,” Johnson said. “We intend to fight to ensure the district is made whole and remain fully committed to supporting all relevant agencies pursuing justice in this matter.”
At Hudgins’ direction, the district awarded McKenna and Gwinup’s company, Allied Engineering Group, millions of dollars for roofing, interior renovation and HVAC work not performed, according to the state audit’s findings. Allied Engineering kept a portion of the funds but paid most of it, more than $2.6 million, to Hudgins’ personal business between the 2015 and 2025 fiscal years, auditors stated.
The state audit also reported Allied Engineering overbilled the school district by at least $499,573 for engineering work.
Hudgins authorized another business founded by Gwinup and two Allied Engineering employees to process the district’s $2.2 million in rebates from the Public Service Company of Oklahoma’s Energy Program, according to the audit. He did so without board approval, and his partners’ business kept 30% of the rebates, amounting to $547,782, auditors found.
The former bond director of Tulsa Public Schools and multiple vendors hired for school bond projects are accused of misspending district funds. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Byrd said Hudgins gave “favorable treatment” to other vendors when recommending which companies should be awarded bids for bond projects.
Hudgins left the district in February 2025 when Byrd and her office initially identified him as a concern in their first state audit of Tulsa schools. The first audit noted that Hudgins was listed as a subcontractor for Allied Engineering while he was overseeing the district’s bond projects.
The initial audit also reported a widespread lack of transparency, failure to comply with purchasing rules and attempts to circumvent school board oversight by former Tulsa Superintendent Deborah Gist’s administration. 
Gist and most of her leadership team have since left the district. One of her former top administrators, Devin Fletcher, is serving 30 months in federal prison after pleading guilty to a charge of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, stemming from actions in his district role.

name: Source New Mexico
title: U.S. Energy Secretary Wright says New Mexico has ‘room to grow’ amid oil, gas boom
description: During a visit to Hobbs on Tuesday, United States Energy Secretary Chris Wright said that New Mexico, already the nation’s second highest oil-producing state, still has even more to offer as President Donald Trump seeks to boost domestic energy production.
text:
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright speaks with Mewbourne Oil Company CEO Ken Waits on Aug. 18, 2026, during a visit to a Mewbourne oil production facility in Hobbs, New Mexico, as part of his “Great American Energy Comeback Tour.” (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)During a visit to Hobbs on Tuesday, United States Energy Secretary Chris Wright said that New Mexico, already the nation’s second highest oil-producing state, still has even more to offer as President Donald Trump seeks to boost domestic energy production. 
Wright made those comments following a tour of a Permian Basin oil production facility as part of a series of stops his department has dubbed the “Great American Energy Comeback Tour.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The secretary’s tour touts record-breaking domestic oil and gas production during Trump’s second term, thanks largely to production in the Permian Basin, which covers southwestern New Mexico and west Texas. 
In 2025, the Permian Basin produced 6.6 million barrels per day of crude oil, comprising 48% of total U.S. oil production. Lea County, where Wright visited Tuesday, produces the most crude oil of any county in the Permian Basin.
Wright’s visit comes amid high oil prices resulting from the Iran war that have sent oil prices to nearly $100 per barrel. The price increase has resulted in a windfall in revenues to state coffers, recently projected to be roughly $850 million. 
Wright said the state should wear its oil-producing status as a “badge of pride,” and that the state’s remaining oil reserves present opportunity for “a lot of room to grow,” especially if the state joins the federal government in quickly approving permits for oil and gas drilling operations. 
Since Trump’s second term began, the U.S. Bureau of Land Management has typically taken less than 90 days to issue permits for various oil and gas extraction efforts, Wright said Tuesday. That’s down from more than a year during President Joe Biden’s term, he said. 
Wright visited a facility that Mewbourne Oil Company owns near Hobbs. Republican Greg Cunningham, who is currently running against incumbent U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) for the 2nd Congressional District seat, also attended. He told Source NM he was there to “listen and learn” about how oil companies operate and how better to support them if elected to Congress. 
It’s unclear who invited Cunningham to the tour. Mewbourne CEO Kenneth Waits said the DOE invited Cunningham; DOE spokesperson Ben Dietderich told Source NM that the company invited the congressional candidate. 
Gov touts New Mexico’s lower methane numbers, but state still falling short on 2030 climate goal

Cunningham did not immediately respond to Source NM’s request for comment. 
In a response to a query from Source NM, Vasquez’s campaign spokesperson Patricia Socarras Santiago said Vasquez was not invited to the event. “While Greg was cozying up with the MAGA Administration, Gabe spent the last few days in Carlsbad, Alamogordo, and Silver City talking to New Mexicans about the uphill battle they’re facing in Trump’s tanking economy,” she said in a statement.
During the tour, Wright heard from company leaders about their operations, including how they’ve adapted to recent state laws aimed at reducing methane emissions. The privately held company is among the largest Permian Basin oil producers and extracts roughly 300,000 barrels of crude a day, CEO Kenneth Waits said Tuesday. 
Company leaders showed Wright a series of separating tanks and technology they said they use to separate gas, water and oil and divert them into separate pipelines. Waits said the company has reduced its methane emissions 81% over the past four years and currently captures 99.8% of all the methane produced in its oil-drilling operations. 
The 0.2% of “excess” is flared into the atmosphere, which happened periodically during the roughly two-hour tour Friday. 
Mewbourne in 2023 faced a $5.5 million fine from the United States Department of Justice under the federal Clean Air Act and New Mexico state law, along with a settlement agreement that government officials said would result in 1,300 fewer tons of methane released annually into the atmosphere.
The company did not admit to wrongdoing in agreeing to the settlement. 
In addition to drastically increasing its rate of methane capture in recent years, Waits also touted the use of a LiDAR emissions tracking system called LONGPATH, which continuously monitors sites for leaks and alerts company officials when one occurs. 
Wright’s visit to Mewbourne followed a tour of the Urenco uranium enrichment facility in Eunice, as well as a visit Monday to another oil facility in Midland, Texas. 


4:47 pmThis story was updated following publication to include a response from the Vasquez' campaign.

name: VTDigger
title: Scott administration installs bird noise devices at downtown Montpelier building
description:
State officials say the noise deterrent devices are meant to reduce human waste and debris associated with people sleeping at the property.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Scott administration installs bird noise devices at downtown Montpelier building.
text:
State officials installed bird noise devices at the Pavilion Building in Montpelier this summer. David Littlefield/Vermont Public

Carly Berlin covers housing and infrastructure for Vermont Public, in partnership with VTDigger. 
The issue of unsheltered homelessness has landed on the doorstep of Gov. Phil Scott.
The Vermont Department of Buildings and General Services has tallied numerous incidents of individuals sleeping on the porches of the Pavilion Building in downtown Montpelier, the white-columned complex that houses Scott’s offices along with those of the treasurer, attorney general and the Vermont Supreme Court.
Earlier this year, the department installed a port-a-let near the Pavilion after its grounds crew repeatedly encountered human waste and debris at the property, according to Deputy Commissioner Emily Kisicki. Yet the problem persisted. 
The department then took an additional step. Earlier this summer, officials installed a set of noise deterrent devices that make loud bird calls, according to public records reviewed by Vermont Public.
“We are hoping this could reduce the nighttime occupancy of these spaces,” Kisicki wrote in a late-June email as the state ordered the devices. 
Responding to encampments has become a perennial issue for municipal leaders across the state as the number of unhoused people living outdoors grows. Over the last several summers, Capital City officials have ordered unhoused people to remove their tents from public areas. 
Last month, outreach workers counted 61 people living outdoors in Montpelier, according to Zach Hughes, chair of the city’s homelessness committee. The city’s sole year-round shelter has space for 18 people and is currently about three-quarters full.
To Hughes, the state’s use of the noise deterrent devices amounts to pushing people along who have few alternative places to stay.
“As a homelessness advocate, this is just disturbing to me,” Hughes said. “Part of the problem is, there’s nowhere for people to go.”
Safety and security officers for the Department of Buildings and General Services have reported encounters with individuals sleeping outside of the Pavilion complex four times between June of 2025 and late July of 2026, according to incident reports reviewed by Vermont Public. 
In an interview, Kisicki said the noise deterrent devices were not meant to address people sleeping at the property, but to mitigate “associated activity.” The buildings department grounds crew was cleaning up human waste at the site on a daily basis earlier this summer, Kisicki said, and had also encountered debris from a fire on the porch as well as discarded needles. Law enforcement had been called to respond to broken windows and a possible assault at the site in April, she said.
Given that the location is heavily utilized by the public — the building’s ground floor houses the Vermont History Museum, and the Statehouse is next door — the department became concerned about risks to public health and safety, Kisicki said.
“The noise machine was viewed as a way to sort of reduce some of the activity that was going on in that location without heavier-handed approaches like law enforcement or fencing,” she said.
Soon after the devices were installed, they caused a twitter on the local Front Porch Forum, as residents shared concerns that a real, distressed bird was nesting at the building. 
Kisicki said the noise deterrent system has reduced the waste issues at the building. It does not, however, appear to have prevented people from sleeping at the site. On July 30, after the devices were installed, a safety and security officer noted encountering several individuals sleeping on a Pavilion Building porch. On Aug. 12, staff responded to an individual experiencing an overdose next to the building, according to Kisicki.
Kisicki said buildings department staff offer resource guides to unhoused people they encounter.
The noise devices had been operating off of a light sensor, but are now on a timer to run from 11 p.m. to 4 a.m., Kisicki said.
In a statement, Jason Maulucci, Scott’s director of policy development and legislative affairs, said the governor is aware of the actions taken by the buildings department “after their persistent efforts to help accommodate the situation.”
“The Governor believes it is important to maintain safe, clean and healthy public spaces,” Maulucci said. 
Unsheltered homelessness has increased in Vermont after state leaders cut back the motel voucher program that provided shelter for the majority of people experiencing homelessness during the pandemic years. Scott has been the motel program’s loudest critic, arguing that it is too costly and ineffective.
Julie Bond, director of Good Samaritan Haven, a network of shelters in Washington County, said interventions like the noise devices do little to solve the underlying problems of unsheltered homelessness.
“My hope is that this is a time for all of us, whether it’s state, community, local partners to really come together and find solutions rather than deterrents,” Bond said.
