name: West Virginia Watch
title: Charleston residents continue cleanup after Sunday’s flash flooding
description: After 30 years of living in the same house on Garrison Avenue, Rhonda and Jerry Walker are planning to leave their Charleston home following Sunday’s flash flooding.
text:
Rhonda Walker (left) and a friend go through Walker’s household items to determine what they can salvage and what to throw away after Sunday’s flood on Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)After 30 years of living in the same house on Garrison Avenue, Rhonda and Jerry Walker are planning to leave their Charleston home following Sunday’s flash flooding.
The couple suffered two previous flooding events, including losing everything to storms and flooding in April 2024. After that, they replaced the home’s floors and everything underneath them, she said.  
“(Flooding) did $35,000 worth of damage last time,” Rhonda Walker said. 
More than 4 inches of rain fell in Charleston, West Virginia, on Sunday, again flooding the Walkers’ home and those of several of their neighbors. This time, the Walkers plan to put what they can salvage into storage while they figure out next steps. 
“It may be a blessing in disguise — that’s what my friend said,” Rhonda Walker said. “It might be. Because before we just kept fixing up and picking up, and we can’t do it this time.”
On Tuesday, Walker and four of her friends were going through household items determining what could be saved and what to throw away. 
The Red Cross will put the couple up in a hotel for two nights. After that, though, they’re not sure where they’ll end up.
Tears filled the woman’s eyes as she talked about the uncertainty of their future.
“I think I would be better if I just knew what the next step (is),” she said. “If I had a secure place, and I knew, you know, where we were going.”
Sunday’s flooding also hit the Cross Lanes and Cabin Creek areas in Kanawha County, and Fayette County, where a woman died after being swept away in the floodwaters.
Gabe Wawrin, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service’s Charleston office, said the severe weekend storms in the area were part of a “convective complex.” Essentially, several thunderstorms joined together on a larger scale, persisting for hours or more and hitting harder than individual thunderstorms would, per the NWS. 
That storm system, Wawrin said, had been moving in a ridge across the central part of the country. As disturbances moved along it, they hit the Charleston area hard. Fueling the storms, he said, was the hot, humid weather that can make downpours generally hit harder, with more precipitation.
“So we had the severe storm potential. Topped with the warm and humid air, you get heavy rain potential, and we’ve been locked into that pattern for the last week to two weeks,” Wawrin said. “That’s led to these, at times frequent, convective complexes.”
Wawrin said the most recent storms were the latest in what has been an already especially wet August in the region. To date this month, he said, the area surrounding Charleston has received about 10.31 inches of rain. The record for monthly rainfall in August for the area stands at 10.54 inches.
“June and July, they were relatively normal, but yes this has been an extremely wet August for the Charleston area,” Wawrin said. “It stands to be fairly likely we could break that record, we’re already very close to breaking it and have 13 days to go in the month.”
Angie and Herbie Means stand inside her house on Garrison Avenue in Charleston, West Virginia, on Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026. The couple was fixing up the house to sell it before it flooded during Sunday’s storms. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)
Flooding also damaged Angie Means’ Charleston home on Sunday. Means, who also lives on Garrison Avenue, was midway through renovating the house with hopes of selling it.
“I was two rooms away from getting it on the market,” she said. “I had walls to wash in two rooms and it (was) done. Done.”
Flash floods rose about 3 inches in the home, taking out the gas line, pushing through the heating vents and into the floor. 
On Tuesday, she and her husband mopped and cleaned up what mud they could reach.
Means has owned the house for more than 20 years. In that time, she said, she’s not seen the flooding as severe as it was Sunday.  
“It’s flooded, but never like this,” she said. “The worst was … probably late ’80s or early ’90s.”
As of Tuesday afternoon, more than a thousand Appalachian Power customers in the Kanawha Valley were still without power, according to the company’s outage map. Several of those outages — near Davis Creek, off Rutledge Road and throughout eastern Kanawha County — were due to downed trees. Power was anticipated to return for most customers by Tuesday evening, per the company. 
Kanawha County Metro 911 said more than 2,100 emergency calls were made to its dispatch center between 8 a.m. on Sunday and midnight that night. Emergency medical services were dispatched for more than 290 calls, while fire departments were sent out for at least 175 and police responded to more than 390.
Kanawha County emergency responders performed more than 60 water rescues throughout Sunday as high water rushed in and stranded motorists along with others. More than 40 collisions were reported on roadways throughout the day, and dispatchers saw over 150 calls for reports of high water, downed trees, gas leaks, compromised utility lines and more.
And while the Kanawha Valley was hit especially hard with weekend floods, northern parts of the state were as well.
In Harrison County, officials told news outlets that “everywhere got hammered.” Harrison County Schools were supposed to start Tuesday, but due to the widespread flooding, the district deferred a day to Wednesday. County officials told WV News on Monday that Clarksburg, Anmoore, Salem and Reynoldsville sustained damage from the flooding. 
No injuries were reported, they said, but there were numerous rescues performed for stranded motorists. Several crews were also responding to homes where the power needed to be cut due to encroaching water in basements and the surrounding area.
Gov. Patrick Morrisey on Tuesday issued a statewide state of emergency in response to the storms and flooding from Sunday through Tuesday. 
“West Virginians have been hit by another round of severe weather at a time when many communities are still recovering from last month’s storms,” Morrisey said in a news release. “This declaration gives our emergency responders, state agencies and local officials the flexibility they need to move quickly, get resources where they are needed and help communities recover from the damage.”
The Women’s Health Center in Charleston was flooded during Sunday’s storms. (Photo courtesy Danielle Maness)
Cleanup was still going on Tuesday at the Women’s Health Center on Washington Street in Charleston, where Clinic Director Danielle Maness said flash floods rose 2 feet on the building’s external wall, breaching the flood prevention gates it had installed. 
Flooding happens “consistently” where the clinic sits at the corner of Greendale and Washington Street West, including in April 2024 and last week during heavy rains, she said. 
“This just happens to be an area that does not drain well,” Maness said. “And when there’s a lot of water coming down the Greendale hill, the drains on Greendale and Washington get clogged and the water just stays still. So I know it’s not just a problem for us; it’s a problem for a lot of other low-lying places on the West Side. 
“And I just want to be very mindful — we’re a business, but this impacted individuals in the community,” she said. “And this impacted people’s homes, and so we were actually, comparable to other people throughout the state, we were relatively lucky.”

title: North Dakota governor declares drought emergency, activates livestock water assistance program
description: North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong declared a drought emergency Tuesday for counties and tribal nations experiencing extreme and long-term drought conditions. Nearly all of North Dakota, except part of Dickey County, is listed as abnormally dry or suffering moderate, severe or extreme drought conditions, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor. “I’m worried,” A[...]
text:
Gov. Kelly Armstrong, center-right, speaks next to Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring, left, Lt. Gov. Michelle Strinden, center-left, and Reice Haase, right, director of the Department of Water Resources, during a meeting of the North Dakota Water Commission on Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong declared a drought emergency Tuesday for counties and tribal nations experiencing extreme and long-term drought conditions.
Nearly all of North Dakota, except part of Dickey County, is listed as abnormally dry or suffering moderate, severe or extreme drought conditions, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor.
“I’m worried,” Armstrong said in an interview Tuesday. His executive order highlighted that the lack of precipitation and higher than average seasonal temperatures are expected to continue through fall.
Armstrong, North Dakota Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring and members of the North Dakota Water Commission voted unanimously to activate the state’s Drought Disaster Livestock Water Supply Project Assistance Program and make up to $2 million available for those producers to begin new water projects.
“Basically, from Bismarck to the South Dakota and Montana border is as bad as we’ve seen in a very long time,” Armstrong said. 
U.S. Drought Monitor map for Aug. 13, 2026. (Screenshot/US Drought Monitor website)
Livestock producers can qualify for up to $10,000 in cost-share assistance per project through the program for new water wells, rural water system connections, pipeline extensions, pasture taps, and contracted labor, materials and equipment rentals to complete those projects. Producers are eligible for three projects at one time, according to the program website.
This will be the first time the program has been activated since 2021, Armstrong said.
“The best part about this program is it helps now, but the reason we’ll spend less money on this program than we did in 2021 is because we drilled those wells in 2021,” he said. “It’s immediate relief now, but it also helps future generations.”
July heat produces ‘flash drought’ with more than half of North Dakota affected

The program is funded through oil and gas extraction tax revenue, said Reice Haase, director of the Department of Water Resources.
Larry Novak, a farmer and rancher in McKenzie County, said some ag producers in his area are having trouble selling their spring wheat and durum to local elevators because drought conditions have had such a negative impact on crop quality. 
“So it’s basically feed grain for cattle,” Novak said. 
He said any state program to help producers access to water is beneficial. But Novak said it can be situation specific and is unlikely to help in his case.  
“Just because you give me money to drill a well for water doesn’t mean that there’s going to be water underneath where I drill it,” Novak said. “There’s just no quality water veins in there.”
The North Dakota Department of Agriculture activated the state’s hay hotline last week to connect hay producers with livestock operations that may need hay to feed animals.
Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring speaks during a meeting of the North Dakota Water Commission on Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
“The drought has dried up livestock dams that producers usually depend on for grazing, and water quality has been a serious concern,” Goehring said in a statement.
Last month was was the sixth warmest July and the 12th driest July in the state’s history, according to the North Dakota State Climate Office, an office that has logged weather data in the state since 1895. The average temperature last month was 86.9 degrees and total average precipitation was 1.25 inches.
For more information on the Drought Disaster Livestock Water Supply Project Assistance Program call 701-328-4959, or email dwrlivestock@nd.gov. 
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska Democrats will vote to fill vacancy for US Senate race after its candidate dropped out
description: Democratic Party chair's affidavit reaffirms strategy of clearing the field for nonpartisan candidate Dan Osborn.
text:
Framed pitctures at the Omaha Nebraska Democratic Party office on April 3, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/ Nebraska Examiner) LINCOLN — The Nebraska Democratic Party will decide at a state central committee meeting this week whether to fill a vacancy caused by its U.S. Senate candidate dropping out. 
In a Lancaster County District Court affidavit, state party Chair Jane Kleeb said a vote to fill the vacancy that arose after U.S. Senate nominee Cindy Burbank dropped out of the race will be held during the committee’s “regularly scheduled meeting beginning on August 21, 2026.”  
“Formally deciding not to fill the vacancy would align with NDP’s organizational strategy and political desires to oust Republican Senator Ricketts and ensure that Nebraskans enjoy more diversified political representation in Congress,” part of Kleeb’s affidavit reads.
Nebraska Democratic Party Chair Jane Kleeb speaks during a press conference in Lincoln on July 29, 2026. (Photo by Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
The affidavit, which was filed late Monday afternoon, is part of a lawsuit brought by William Forbes, the loser of the Senate Democratic primary, seeking to force the party to replace its former Senate candidate. 
Kleeb’s affidavit reaffirmed the state Democratic strategy of clearing the field for nonpartisan U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn. The party’s strategy to oust Ricketts wasn’t a secret. State and national media reported the Democrats’ plan not to actively recruit a Senate candidate throughout the cycle. 
Kleeb also publicly endorsed Osborn in the Senate race last year. Her affidavit said she had supported Burbank because “she publicly committed to this strategy by announcing that she would not remain in the race if she determined she were unable to defeat Senator Ricketts.”
Burbank comfortably won her primary against Forbes. She told multiple news outlets she would drop out of the race only if she didn’t have a clear path to victory in the general election. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Burbank filed her paperwork to withdraw one day after the secretary of state verified Osborn’s petition signatures to be on the fall ballot. Forbes’ lawsuit was filed shortly after the petition verification. 
Forbes and his attorneys argue that wording in state law requires a political party to replace a candidate. Nebraska Democrats said Forbes is misreading state law because the statute he cited addresses the process that must be followed if a party chooses to replace a nominee — an interpretation that Lancaster County District Court Judge Susan Strong so far seems to agree with. 
“I am currently being deprived of my right to associate and the right and opportunity to consider and support a Democratic Party nominee for United States Senate on the November 2026 general election ballot,” Forbes said in an affidavit filed Monday.
Strong, in her ruling declining a temporary injunction, said Forbes’ arguments would raise “serious constitutional concerns” and that he was unlikely to succeed in forcing the party to replace Burbank. Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers has given notice to be heard on the lawsuit. 
Forbes, in his affidavit, said he is willing to be considered as the Democratic Party’s replacement nominee for U.S. Senate. Kleeb’s affidavit said forcing the party to nominate a replacement candidate would sabotage the party’s “strategy, and contradict the overwhelming majority of Democratic primary voters who supported Ms. Burbank and her pledge to exit the race if necessary to ensure unified opposition to Senator Ricketts.”
“If forced to fill the general-election ballot vacancy, I would not consider nominating Mr. Forbes under any circumstance,” Kleeb wrote.

title: Staffing costs drive fee increase for program meant to deter livestock theft
description: PIERRE — South Dakota’s Brand Board will raise its livestock ownership inspection fee for the first time since 2013, after a legislative committee approved the rule change Tuesday. text:
Cattle in a pasture near Saint Onge, South Dakota. (Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)PIERRE — South Dakota’s Brand Board will raise its livestock ownership inspection fee for the first time since 2013, after a legislative committee approved the rule change Tuesday.
The committee, made up of three state senators and three state representatives, voted 5-1 in favor of the change. Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City, voted no.
The Brand Board is responsible for tracking livestock ownership in South Dakota counties west of the Missouri River, where cattle are more likely to roam across wide open spaces. Inspectors check to make sure that horses, cattle and mules sold or moved from those counties belong to the people who sell or move them.
Livestock sold at markets in western South Dakota are inspected for ownership when they arrive. Livestock sold privately also need inspections. At markets, the per-animal fees are withheld from the sale price and remitted to the Brand Board.
The new fee will be $1.45 per head starting Oct. 1.  Brand Board Executive Director Debbie Trapp told lawmakers they need the additional funding to pay for the ownership inspection program.
“This change is needed due to increasing personnel and operating expenses, and the brand board operates entirely on funds generated by the programs it administers,” Trapp told lawmakers.
Over the past two years, the board had to rely on $900,000 from its other programs to maintain the ownership inspection program, according to Brand Board Vice President Cory Bierle, “and we’re still behind.”
With a projected number of livestock inspected at 1.5 million, the fee is expected to generate an additional $601,000 through the remainder of the current fiscal year and $675,000 per fiscal year going forward. The state fiscal year runs from July 1 through June 30.

Though the number of animals is decreasing, “the numbers that we still have are there, and they all still need to be inspected,” Bierle said. “And we have to have the staff on hand inspect the ones that are present.”
Livestock inspection fees largely pay for staffing and staff-related expenses. The state Bureau of Finance and Management increased its per-mile reimbursement for state employees from 67 cents to 70 cents a mile last year.
There are 12 full-time inspectors, four of whom are regional supervisors, as well as office staff and livestock investigators. All are considered state employees, who typically receive annual lawmaker-approved salary increases. The most recent increased state employee pay by 1.3%. The board also employs 129 part-time local brand inspectors.
The board gets most of its funding through brand renewal registrations, which are $90 fees that livestock owners pay every five years to maintain the brands they use to identify animals as theirs. In recent years, the board’s needed to dip into those funds to pay for the inspection program.
Opponent says ranchers can’t afford fee hike
Rick Fox, a rancher from Hermosa, spoke in opposition to the change. He said it could be delayed a year to provide some financial relief for producers affected by the drought. The change would cost him about $400, he said.
“Most ranchers don’t have any kind of reserves. If their hay fund is low, then you’ve got to get it from a different fund or borrow the money,” Fox said. “The Brand Board has a pool of money sitting there that they can borrow from.”
Sen. Howard said that “now is not the time for a 45% increase,” citing financial struggles of West River ranchers.
Brand Board leaders said the increase represents an amount the Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources, South Dakota Stockgrowers Association and South Dakota Cattlemen’s Association could agree on.
The Brand Board still hasn’t reached the legal cap on how much it can charge per head for the inspection fee. Earlier this year, lawmakers and the governor set the cap at $1.65 per head.
“And based on projections,” for ongoing costs to the program, Trapp said, “chances are, we will be back in a few years, probably to increase it again towards the cap.”
Fox, the rancher who opposed the fee increase, told lawmakers that the ownership inspection program is “the best theft deterrent we have.”
“If I was not to brand my cattle, I’d be a little nervous about if one gets gone somewhere,” Fox said. “That’s our return address.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Gov. Shapiro signs data center executive order. Critics say it falls short.
description: Gov. Josh Shapiro's new requirements for data centers don't hit the mark for those critical of industry development.
text:
Muncy Township, Lycoming County, is the site of a proposed data center. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Using fiery language and describing the companies “recklessly” pushing data centers as “greedy” and “predatory,” Gov. Josh Shapiro distanced himself from project developers after months of mounting pressure to take action. 
“Starting today, (artificial intelligence) data center developers who want to do business in our commonwealth must respect our communities and abide by these stringent requirements,” Shapiro said. “And if they can’t agree to do that, well, they should stop considering Pennsylvania a home for their project.”
The first-term governor is up for reelection this year. Both his opponent — Republican state Treasurer Stacey Garrity — and grassroots campaigns have criticized him for not limiting data centers, which provide the computing power behind e-commerce websites, streaming service and more.
Gov. Josh Shapiro said that developers who couldn’t comply with new requirements shouldn’t bring their data center projects to Pennsylvania on Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Shapiro’s executive order signed Tuesday would be “legally binding” under his authority as governor, he told reporters, and requires developers to comply with previously proposed standards that were introduced as voluntary. 
Among the conditions: providing their own power sources, with an increasing portion coming from renewable energy sources like solar, advanced nuclear or battery storage; local hiring processes with a “robust” community benefits agreement; public transparency; and compliance with clean air and pure water standards.
“I’m here to say today that we will not be bullied by these developers. We will not be bulldozed by the lawyers for these big tech companies,” he said. “We have a long history in Pennsylvania of industry running roughshod over our communities to make a buck. That stops with me.” 
He repeatedly called Tuesday’s action “the strictest guardrails in the nation,” though it fell short of a moratorium, such as the one advanced last month in New York and didn’t reverse state tax incentives.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a statement, Garrity’s campaign likened his action to “gaslighting,” saying Shapiro “was the biggest data center cheerleader in the nation” and had received campaign donations from the industry.
“Now that public opinion has turned against him and his donors, Josh Shapiro is playing CYA, and Pennsylvania voters aren’t buying it,” she continued. “Josh Shapiro lit the fuse on the chaos we are seeing in community-after-community across the commonwealth because he was more concerned with his political ambitions than fighting for Pennsylvania communities.”
 How we got here

The two parties have accused the other of flip-flopping on data centers after both Shapiro and Garrity welcomed the state’s largest single investment from Amazon to develop a pair of data centers in Luzerne County one year ago.
Shapiro said the landscape had changed since that announcement. 
“Last summer, I announced two projects that will bring thousands of new jobs and over $20 billion of investment to Pennsylvania,” said Shapiro. “Since then, we have seen an unacceptable number of speculative projects for data center development that is swamping our commonwealth — many of them led by developers who have no regard for local communities.” 
He asserted that “no AI data centers (are) up and running right now” in Pennsylvania, adding that just five projects have the necessary permits to begin operations. According to the executive order, the state Department of Environmental Protection has received 20 permit applications related to projects and just 14 sites statewide obtained a tax exemption.

As part of the executive order, the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection now has its own data center permit tracker displaying in-progress proposals across the state.

Earlier this year, Shapiro pushed his Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development (GRID) Standards, a set of voluntary standards for developers tied to tax benefits and expedited permitting. House members advanced his proposal through the chamber on a bipartisan vote but the Republican-led Senate opted not to move forward with the plan.
Senate Majority Leader Joe Pittman (R-Indiana) pointed to Senate efforts to eliminate a sales tax exemption used by projects, which he said was amended “into something unrecognizable” in the House. He said additional work was underway for more legislation in the fall.
“We strongly believe communities need to have the ability to weigh in on what is best for their residents and are open to further discussions, including considering measures to allow for moratorium decisions to be made at the local level,” he continued. “As our world continues to embrace greater access to technological advancements, the issues of energy development and national security also go hand in hand.”
Some politicians have warned that the United States needs to pursue data center development in order to compete on the global stage. 

More data center proposals keep coming to Pennsylvania. So does the outcry.


Under GRID, which critics panned for being optional, projects would need to increasingly rely on clean energy, make critical economic development investments, work with local governments, hold public meetings and hire local labor at higher-than-average wages.
In exchange, the sites would qualify for the state’s fast tracked permitting process, an option no longer available under the new executive order. 
“While fast track permitting has proven to be (an) incredible asset to helping us plan major economic development projects … what’s become clear to me is that it is not right for these kinds of data center developments,” Shapiro said. 
Dan Diorio, the executive vice president of State Policy & Government Affairs for the Data Center Coalition, advocates on behalf of such projects in the commonwealth. In a statement, he warned about changing rules “midstream” in a way that might impact “ongoing investment in verified and responsible data center projects.” 
The Montour Steam Electric Station rises above farmland the plant’s owner wants to rezone to allow Amazon to build data centers. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
“Companies have made plans, communities have prepared for economic opportunities, and workers are ready to build the next generation of digital infrastructure right here in Pennsylvania,” he continued. “Clear, predictable, and workable standards can help provide communities with confidence while allowing Pennsylvania to compete for billions of dollars in investment, create jobs, and strengthen local economies. One-size-fits-all policies that stifle investment and job creation are not the path forward.”
In 2024, the industry contributed $19.6 billion to the state’s GDP, he said, and paid $1.9 billion in state and local taxes. 
 Mixed support

Shapiro’s order was announced alongside representatives from the Pennsylvania State Association of Township Supervisors, the state Public Utility Commission and the Pennsylvania Utility Law Project, which focuses on affordability and consumer protection.
Democratic leaders from both legislative chambers shared supportive statements and squarely blamed Senate Republicans for not taking up the voluntary GRID standards.
“I am pleased that Gov. Shapiro is taking executive action to hold data center developers accountable for the impacts they have on Pennsylvania’s communities. Senate Republicans have abdicated their responsibility to protect ratepayers, deliver local control, safeguard the environment, or listen to Pennsylvanians of every county demanding the legislature’s attention,” Senate Minority Leader Jay Costa (D-Allegheny) said. 
But not everyone agreed. Food and Water Watch called it “too little, too late,” in a statement, noting that the commonwealth could lose more than $2 billion in revenue by mid-2031 due to the sales tax incentive. 
Megan McDonough, the state director of Food & Water Watch, speaks against data center development in the Capitol on June 23, 2026. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
“Shapiro is feeling our heat because Pennsylvanians have made it impossible for him to ignore us. After rolling out the red carpet for this industry, he is now scrambling. But these measures do very little to protect the people who will be left living with the consequences,” said Megan McDonough, the Pennsylvania State Director of the group. 
Tuesday’s action doesn’t “erase” his record, she continued, characterizing it as “his attempt to save face.”
“If Governor Shapiro actually believes these projects pose enough risk to require special rules, then he should stop pretending the answer is to manage the damage while continuing to permit this destructive industry,” she continued. “The only solution to addressing AI data center’s many woes is by placing a mandatory moratorium on all new data center development.”

title: Cattle and conservation program expands through Des Moines watershed
description: The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship announced Tuesday an expansion of a popular cost-share conservation program that helps farmers convert cropland to pasture.  The program has existed since 2016 in select southwestern Iowa counties where it has helped farmers convert more than 16,000 acres of less-productive cropland into pasture. Now, w[...]
text:
The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship announced an expansion to a popular cattle and conservation program. (Photo by Scott Bauer/USDA)The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship announced Tuesday an expansion of a popular cost-share conservation program that helps farmers convert cropland to pasture. 
The program has existed since 2016 in select southwestern Iowa counties where it has helped farmers convert more than 16,000 acres of less-productive cropland into pasture. Now, with funding from the state’s “farm to faucet” program, farmers in nearly 30 Iowa counties are eligible for the Cattle and Conservation Working Lands Program. 
Farmers sometimes have areas of land that aren’t suited to grow crops, either because they are too sloped, or dry, or the soil is too rough. The cattle and conservation program helps farmers convert these acres to pasture and to add features like fencing and water so the area can be grazed.  
As pasture, versus planted with row crops, the area will do a better job at holding on to soil and nutrients, according to IDALS. Ranchers who have participated in the program have said it allowed them to tackle projects they would not otherwise have had the funds to accomplish.  
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig made the announcement at the Iowa State Fair and said he hopes the program’s success in Iowa can be a “model” for reforming the federal conservation reserve program, or CRP, which pays farmers to maintain vegetative cover on erodible land. 
“The Cattle and Conservation Working Lands Program is truly a win-win, balancing productivity while improving Iowa’s water quality and soil health,” Naig said. “By converting underperforming cropland into grazing land for cattle and other livestock, we can put every acre to its best use and keep working lands working.” 
The program was established in Adams, Carroll, Cherokee, Guthrie, Ida, Page, Woodbury and Taylor counties, but is now available to producers in Audubon, Boone, Buena Vista, Calhoun, Clay, Dallas, Dickinson, Emmet, Greene, Hamilton, Hancock, Humboldt, Kossuth, Palo Alto, Pocahontas, Polk, Sac, Webster, Winnebago and Wright counties. 
The newly added counties are part of the “Greater Des Moines watershed,” which is a target of expanded conservation efforts in the newly enacted farm to faucet program that aims to improve water quality through conservation incentives and water treatment upgrades. 
According to a news release from IDALS, the expansion also includes the addition of two program coordinators to help with “outreach and engagement” to local cattle producers. 
Naig was joined by Bryan Whaley, CEO of the Iowa Cattlemen’s Association, for the announcement. Whaley said the program allows Iowa producers to “enhance current practices and implement new efforts even quicker.” 
“Cattlemen have been stewards of the land for generations, and we take that responsibility seriously,” Whaley said. “The health of our soil and water, and improving them, has always been part of that responsibility.”

name: VTDigger
title: Green Mountain Care Board set modest rate increases for 2027 Vermont health insurance marketplace plans
description:
This year’s rates represent efforts towards keeping premiums lower, while still aiming to account for insurers’ ability to pay out the costs of healthcare in Vermont. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Green Mountain Care Board set modest rate increases for 2027 Vermont health insurance marketplace plans.
text:
Insurance plans available on the state marketplace through Vermont Health Connect are displayed on a monitor on Monday, August 17, 2026. Photo by Noel Clark/VTDigger

Individuals and small businesses that buy health insurance on the state marketplace will see their premiums rise between 1% to 6% next year.
The Green Mountain Care Board, Vermont’s independent health care regulator, set rate increases late Monday night for coverage sold on Vermont Health Connect, the state’s Affordable Care Act marketplace. Each summer the board issues binding orders for how much the insurers can raise those plans’ premiums.
BlueCross BlueShield of Vermont and MVP Health Care are the only two insurers that sell health insurance plans on Vermont Health Connect. Employers with no more than 100 workers can buy small group plans on the marketplace, and individuals can buy coverage directly.
On Monday, the care board said that in 2027, it expects BlueCross BlueShield of Vermont’s individual plans to increase 2.2%, and its small group plans to increase 1.2%. MVP’s individual plans are set to increase 3.9%, and its small group plans are expected to go up 6.2% 
All four increases are less than what the insurers had originally asked regulators for.
Kaj Samsom, the commissioner of the Department of Financial Regulation, which regulates insurers, said that both the requested and granted rates “really reflect the progress that the regulated hospitals, the care board, insurers and the legislature” have made on affordability. 
Still, those increases are on top of already high premiums. Since 2021, Vermont’s premium increases for individual plans have compounded to be 74.6% more expensive than they were four years ago. The small group plans’ prices have gone up 51.5% in the same amount of time, according to the office of the Health Care Advocate.
In 2026, Vermont had some of the highest premiums in the nation for plans bought on the Affordable Care Act marketplace, according to health policy group KFF. The loss of some federal tax credits has made the ACA plans even harder to afford for some Vermonters.
Nationwide, the loss of those credits, the increasing cost of healthcare and the decreasing size of insurance pools have caused other states to catch up to Vermont. An August KFF study of preliminary rate filings across the U.S. found that most small group market insurers are increasing rates 10%-20% above last year’s rate.
The increased cost and use of pharmaceutical drugs, especially weight loss drugs, were a “primary driver” of both MVP’s and BlueCross BlueShield’s rate increase, according to the care board’s decision. In its decision, the board noted that BlueCross had removed some brand-name drugs from its coverage and instead replaced them with less expensive alternatives, bringing rates down. 
Both insurers’ rate increases account for a small percentage of premium dollars to go towards the administrative costs of running an insurance company — both of which were at levels lower than most insurers in the country, the care board’s actuaries noted.  
Still, hospital costs are the largest share of what premium dollars go towards.
As such, the care board issued two additional orders on the insurers, aimed at bringing down the price they pay for care. First the board requires the two insurers to prepare for a 2025 law that aligns hospital charges with a percentage of Medicare. They also order insurers to review what they pay to non-Vermont hospitals and whether they align with the state’s affordability objectives. 
In a first for him, care board chair Owen Foster dissented from the decision of the other four board members, arguing that it allows the insurer to unfairly move more Vermont dollars to out-of-state hospitals. He recused himself from the BlueCross BlueShield decision, citing personal reasons.

READ MORE

The board noted that while MVP expects payments to Vermont hospitals to decrease, the insurer predicts an increase in what it pays for care not regulated by the board (meaning non-hospitals and out of state hospitals). The board authors lightly pushed MVP to be “more effective” at limiting what it pays out-of-state hospitals.
Foster took this a step further than his board colleagues in his dissent. He said that allowing a decrease in overall payments to Vermont hospitals while allowing an increase for non-Vermont hospitals “misreads” the board’s duty and “takes precious Vermont healthcare dollars from Vermonters and Vermont providers, moves them out of state and favors large out-of-state hospitals.” He called the move “irrational.”
Samsom caveated that the decreases to in-state payments represents some Vermont hospital costs coming down from dollar figures that were already “demonstrably high – and in some areas, offensive – costs,“ while the out-of-state increase is a more steady trend. As a result of legislative work and the care board’s actions, Vermont’s hospital charges are “finally being tackled” and coming down, he added. 
Last year, the Green Mountain Care Board set the lowest premium increases that Vermont’s ACA insurers had seen in years after a series of legislative actions that were expected to measurably reduce the cost of care that insurers needed to pay out.
BlueCross BlueShield has also tried to strike this balance. For years, the insurer struggled to remain solvent and relied on a $30 million loan from its affiliate in Michigan. Just last year, the insurer began to build back its reserves and repaid that loan. 
Still, BlueCross BlueShield asked the care board to keep in mind the continuing need to rebuild its reserves, which also accounted for part of its requested premium increase.  
In comments to VTDigger on Tuesday, BlueCross BlueShield said it appreciates how the board has tried to strike this balance between affordability and meeting the “true cost of care” that the insurer needs to pay out to Vermont’s hospitals. 
“While these approved rates represent the lowest premium increase (to BlueCross) in five years, they are still an increase at a time when too many Vermonters are struggling to afford healthcare,” Teresa Anderson, the director of brand and engagement for the insurer, wrote to VTDigger.
She added that lasting affordability will take systemwide work.
“That underscores a simple reality: if we want lower premiums, we must lower the cost of care. Hospital costs make up a large share of healthcare spending, and BlueCross VT, hospitals and providers need to continue to work together on long term solutions to lower costs.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: In visit to a vital battleground district, Johnson said he’s “bullish” on Republicans’ 2026 chances
description: Joining U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett in downtown Lansing, U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) called on residents of one of the nation’s most competitive House districts to send the Charlotte Republican back to Washington for a second term.  “We came in to support Tom because this race is critically important,” Johnson told reporters Tuesday. “We […]
text:
U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) during a visit to Lansing, Mich. held by U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte). Aug. 18, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan AdvanceJoining U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett in downtown Lansing, U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) called on residents of one of the nation’s most competitive House districts to send the Charlotte Republican back to Washington for a second term. 
“We came in to support Tom because this race is critically important,” Johnson told reporters Tuesday. “We need this guy. He is a workhorse for the people of Michigan.”
Barrett is seeking reelection to Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, a swing district and key target for Democrats looking to build their ranks in the U.S. House. He faces William Lawrence, a Lansing-area housing advocate and founder of the Sunrise Movement, which advocates for climate justice.
Johnson told reporters he was “very bullish” on the outcome of the election, though he acknowledged Republicans would need to “defy history” as only two Presidents in the last 90 years had gained representation in the House and Senate during a mid-term election.
He touted Republicans’ accomplishments in Congress, including tax cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and efforts to cut back on regulations. He also said Republicans “have much stronger candidates.”
“The Democrat Party is almost in a stage of open civil war right now, the Marxist radical insurgent left is taking over the party, and I’m sad to say this is not our father’s Democratic Party,” Johnson said. “They are leaving the people behind. And so hardworking Americans of every stride, of every background, need to understand this is a high-stakes election.”
U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) during a visit to Lansing, Mich. held by U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte). Aug. 18, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance
He contrasted Barrett, who he portrayed as the “common-sense” candidate, with Lawrence, a former member of the Democratic Socialists of America, who he accused of working to abolish the presidency and Senate to establish “one unicameral body of the House to run everything,” referencing a policy platform developed by the DSA’s Workers Deserve More platform.
“Tom Barrett and his DC allies Mike Johnson and Donald Trump cut healthcare for Michiganders, raised our gas and grocery bills, and gave tax breaks to data center developers while working families pay more,” Lawrence said in a statement. “They can lie about me all they want, but I’ll put my policies up against theirs any day – Medicare for All, stopping AI data centers, ending the senseless wars, and taking on the corporations and billionaires driving up costs for Michiganders.”
Johnson rejects Data Center Moratorium
Beginning in the primary and heading into the general election, Lawrence has made data centers a key issue for his campaign, calling for a 12-month federal moratorium on data centers in order to develop policies to protect natural resources and neighboring properties. 
When asked whether he would support the federal government taking over control of local zoning with regard to data centers, Johnson said it’s important that community concerns are taken into account, but said that a broad moratorium against data centers is “kind of a dangerous prospect right now.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We’re in a race with China on that AI race, and if they’re able to leapfrog us in that race, it’s a very dangerous thing for everybody around the country,” Johnson told reporters, saying that corporations need to work with state and local officials to make sure they’re developing data centers in a responsible way. 
Barrett says it should be up to communities and their officials to determine whether they do or do not want a data center, with Barrett campaign strategist Jason Roe telling Michigan Advance “Tom wants to maintain their authority to do that and not turn it over to politicians in D.C.”
Lawrence’s camp has criticized Barrett’s data center stance, arguing it doesn’t reflect the reality that some communities don’t have the resources to fight back against data center developers. 
“Don’t buy this nonsense about local control as an alternative to a data center moratorium. Local control amounts to the right to get bulldozed, intimidated, bullied, and beaten by these trillion-dollar corporations,” Lawrence said in a video shared to social media. “In order to have real local control, we need to have a moratorium now.”

title: South Dakota governor expands rural fire response amid drought
description: South Dakota Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden authorized state firefighting resources to support local governments in fire suppression. Volunteer fire departments, often supported in part by local governments and fundraising, supply the first responders for blazes across most of South Dakota’s land area. “As a volunteer firefighter, I understand that every secon[...]
text:
The Qury Fire near Custer, South Dakota, pictured on March 12, 2026. (Courtesy of Qury Fire information page)South Dakota Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden authorized state firefighting resources to support local governments in fire suppression.
Volunteer fire departments, often supported in part by local governments and fundraising, supply the first responders for blazes across most of South Dakota’s land area.
“As a volunteer firefighter, I understand that every second counts when attacking a fire. And as a lifelong rancher, I recognize the difficulty feeding livestock during this ongoing drought,” Rhoden said in a news release Tuesday. “Supplementing local resources with approved state assistance will improve response time, saving lives and property.”
Rhoden’s executive order, signed Tuesday, expands South Dakota Wildland Fire’s resources to areas outside the Black Hills Forest Fire Protection District. That region starts at the Wyoming-South Dakota border and runs east through parts of the Black Hills region, but does not include any area within any nearby city limits.
Wildfire near Custer damages 10 properties, authorities say

A majority of the state is in abnormally dry to severe drought conditions, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor. Parts of southwestern South Dakota are under extreme drought conditions.
Wildfires in western parts of the state burned through thousands of acres this year — including the Qury Fire in Custer County which burned more than 9,000 acres. The False Bottom Fire near St. Onge burned 242 acres over the weekend. The Bear Butte Fire burned 400 acres the week before in Meade County, where the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally was taking place.
Rhoden also extended a July order that eases restrictions on hay haulers, allowing producers to move hay two hours before sunrise and two hours after sunset. That measure is meant to make sure livestock have enough food in spite of parched grasses and depleted feed supplies.
In May, Rhoden activated the Drought Task Force, a group of state agencies that evaluates potential drought impacts on agriculture, fire management and water supply.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Judge promises fast ruling on ballot status of Missouri amendment to protect initiatives
description: A Cole County judge will decide Wednesday on whether a proposed constitutional amendment goes too far or if state law directs him to allow it to go to a November vote. At the end of an hour of arguments Tuesday, Circuit Judge Daniel Green promised he would deliver his ruling in one day. Then the […]
text:
Attorney Chuck Hatfield addresses reporters after arguing Tuesday in Cole County Circuit Court that the Respect MO Voters petition to limit legislative authority to change measures passed by initiative should be on the Nov. 3 Missouri ballot (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).A Cole County judge will decide Wednesday on whether a proposed constitutional amendment goes too far or if state law directs him to allow it to go to a November vote.
At the end of an hour of arguments Tuesday, Circuit Judge Daniel Green promised he would deliver his ruling in one day. Then the case will go to the Western District Court of Appeals before possibly finishing with a final decision from the Missouri Supreme Court.
All litigation must be completed Sept. 8, the deadline for court-ordered additions to the ballot.
If it is on the ballot, it will be Amendment 6. Proposed by a political action committee called Respect MO Voters, it would severely limit the ability of lawmakers to alter the provisions of laws and constitutional amendments placed on the ballot by initiative. 
If passed, lawmakers would have to muster an 80% majority in both chambers to change anything in a measure passed by initiative. And if they achieve that majority, it would be subject to a statewide vote to ratify the changes.
Respect MO Voters turned in 335,000 signatures and local election authorities found there were enough to qualify for the ballot. But Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins issued a decision that it improperly addresses more than one subject and more than one article of the Missouri Constitution and refused to put it on the Nov. 3 ballot.
Relying on an analysis from Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, Hoskins also said the measure improperly infringes on the ability of the legislature to enact laws and that the summary he wrote in 2025 is flawed and should not be used.
In court on Tuesday, attorney Chuck Hatfield said Hanaway’s analysis is wrong and the secretary of state did not have the power to block the initiative from the ballot.
“I cannot find a single case or a time when the secretary of state has issued a certificate of insufficiency for something other than the lack of signatures,” Hatfield said.
Arguing to uphold Hoskins, Kathleen Hunker of the attorney general’s office said the limits on future actions are too strict and undermine the state’s legislative representatives. It improperly binds future legislatures, she said.
“It elevates the will of today and yesterday’s voters over those of tomorrow,” she said.
The Missouri Constitution limits initiative proposals to a single subject and requires all provisions to fall within a single article of the constitution. All the provisions in the initiative are in the legislative article, with exceptions that point to other articles and provisions the new language would supersede.
“It actually has the effect of changing provisions that were previously in different articles,” Hunker said. “It’s using clever law crafting in order to hide its wide scope.”
The courts dealt with a similar issue on Amendment 5, the income tax measure defeated on Aug. 4. While the provisions of Amendment 5 were all in the taxation article, it included language that addressed provisions of other articles.
The Western District Court of Appeals decided that Amendment 5 did not violate the single subject rule and allowed the statewide vote. Hatfield was the losing attorney and he said arguing that a proposal alters other articles by implication is an almost impossible task.
“I’ve argued many of them and lost them all,” Hatfield said.
Many of the questions about constitutionality of the initiative are legal questions that should wait until after voters have decided whether to enact Amendment 6, Hatfield said.
He urged Green to allow Amendment 6 to be on the ballot and let the courts determine if every provision should be allowed to stand if it passes.
“This is about the power of the people to decide what they want to do,” Hatfield said. “The legislature just asked to curtail the power of the people to do initiatives in Amendment 4 and that got voted down. Now a group of people are asking to expand and protect the power of the people.

title: Walter Edward “Ted” Tedford
description:
Back in 1956, Ted met the love of his life, Marie Flaim O’Brien. They were married a year later in Fort Lee, New Jersey. He and Marie were married for 66 years, bringing up six children.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Walter Edward “Ted” Tedford.
text:
Born: 08/13/1927
Manchester, Connecticut
Died: 07/14/2026
Underhill Center, Vermont
Details of service:
A Celebration of Life Memorial Service is planned for Ted on Saturday, August 29, from 1:00 p.m. to 3:00 p.m., at the St. Thomas Church Parish Hall on Green Street in Underhill Center. All welcome.

A Celebration of Life Memorial Service is planned for Ted on Saturday, August 29, from 1:00 p.m. to 3:00 p.m., at the St. Thomas Church Parish Hall on Green Street in Underhill Center.
Please come to remember Dad and say our good-byes to him among friends and family. And bring your memories to share!
Here is the Obituary that Dad — ever the journalist — filed away for us to use “when the time comes.”
Dad’s Obit — Walter Edward “Ted” Tedford of Underhill Center died on July 14, 2026, after a short illness. He was 98 years and 11 months old.
Ted was born at home in Manchester, Connecticut on August 13, 1927, the youngest of Walter and Margaret (McKinney) Tedford’s four children. Ted’s parents moved the family to Andover, Connecticut, in 1939 where he graduated from Andover Grammar School, and later from Windham High School in Willimantic, Connecticut, in 1945.
He immediately joined the Navy for four years, serving part of that time aboard the USS LST 512. Upon his discharge, he attended what was then Willimantic State Teachers College, now Eastern Connecticut State University. His college time was interrupted during the Korean War, when he was ordered back into the Navy in 1951 for one year, being discharged in 1952.
He returned to college, receiving his bachelor of science degree. But he wanted to be a reporter and was oﬀered a job reporting for the afternoon daily newspaper, the Willimantic Chronicle. He later joined the Manchester Herald as state editor.
After five years, he moved to the Hartford Times as assistant state editor, then to the (Bergen) Record in Hackensack, New Jersey, as chief copy editor, and later as day editor in charge of the staﬀ of reporters.
He moved his family to Milton in 1968, to serve as news editor at the Burlington Free Press, as editorial writer, and later as a reporter, retiring after 21 years. He immediately began writing news part time for the weekly Mountain Villager. When the paper was sold, Ted became editor, business manager and columnist for six years. When that paper’s owner ceased publication, Ted began writing for the Mountain Gazette, finally retiring after more than 50 years of editing and reporting news.
Back in 1956, Ted met the love of his life, Marie Flaim O’Brien. They were married a year later in Fort Lee, New Jersey. He and Marie were married for 66 years, bringing up six children.
While living in Connecticut, Ted served as a member, and one year as chairman, of the Coventry School Board and member of the Coventry Board of Welfare. In Underhill, he served six years and eight months as a member of the Underhill Selectboard and was a member of the Underhill Historical Society. He and friend Grant Corson founded the Jericho-Underhill Marching and Chowder Society Writers Group, still meeting weekly in Jericho.
While at the Burlington Free Press, Ted’s three-part series, “Aging in Vermont” was published. He received a first-place award from the New England Press Association. He wrote a book, “Incident at St. Albans,” which was published by The Tamarac Press. He was writing short stories right up to the time of his death.
During his first newspaper job as a novice, his editor instructed him to “write tight,” meaning convey the news in his stories in as few words as possible. This obituary sticks to that.

title: Morrisey names former member of WV House to lead state tourism agency
description: Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Tuesday that Kayla Kessinger, a former member of the West Virginia House of Delegates, will take over as secretary for the state’s Department of Tourism following the departure of Chelsea Ruby.
text:
Kayla Kessinger speaks at a news conference Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026, following her appointment by Gov. Patrick Morrisey to head the state’s tourism agency. (West Virginia Office of Gov. Patrick Morrisey video screenshot)Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Tuesday that Kayla Kessinger, a former member of the West Virginia House of Delegates, will take over as secretary for the state’s Department of Tourism following the departure of Chelsea Ruby.
Ruby resigned from the position last month after serving as tourism secretary since 2021. Ruby stayed with the office through the end of July and Curtis Capehart, Morrisey’s director of policy, has served as the acting secretary since Aug. 1.
Kessinger previously served in the state House of Delegates representing Fayette County. She was first elected to the body in 2014 when she was 21-years-old, and served until 2022 when she did not run for reelection. 
During her time in the House, Kessinger was a devout anti-abortion advocate, speaking regularly on the floor and in committee meetings in favor of legislation to limit access to abortion.
She previously voted against making exceptions in state code for victims of rape and incest to receive abortions, sponsored numerous bills throughout her tenure in the House limiting access and funding for abortion patients and, ultimately, voted in support of legislation in 2022 that ended the right to most abortions in the state of West Virginia.  
Kessinger currently works as the state program director of Her PLAN, an anti-abortion organization that serves people facing unexpected pregnancies through its “pro-life safety net.”
Last August, Kessinger was appointed by Morrisey to join the state’s Ethics Commission. In May, Morrisey also named her to his America 250 Task Force, which assisted in planning the America 250 festival held over 4th of July weekend at the state capitol.
In a news release Tuesday, Morrisey said Kessinger is “the right person” to build on the state’s “tremendous” momentum in tourism.
“She knows West Virginia, understands our communities, and shares our commitment to telling the story of what makes this state so special,” Morrisey said. “Kayla will bring strong leadership and a fresh perspective to an outstanding team that is already producing record results.”

title: Suspect surrenders and faces second-degree murder charge in downtown Burlington stabbing
description:
Hassan O. Haji, 24, of Winooski, pleaded not guilty and was ordered held without bail at his arraignment Tuesday afternoon.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Suspect surrenders and faces second-degree murder charge in downtown Burlington stabbing.
text:
The Burlington Police Department on North Avenue in Burlington on Thursday, August 13, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
A suspect has turned himself in and faces a charge of second-degree murder in a fatal stabbing over the weekend in downtown Burlington.
Hassan O. Haji, 24, of Winooski, surrendered at the Burlington police headquarters Tuesday morning. He pleaded not guilty Tuesday afternoon to the murder charge in Chittenden Superior criminal court in Burlington, according to Burlington police.
Police allege that during a fight early Saturday also involving a third person, Haji stabbed 24-year-old Deng Dau once in the groin, killing him.  
Judge Robert Katims granted a prosecution request Tuesday to hold Haji without bail.
“There are several witnesses to the fight, and the stabbing was caught on video, as was Mr. Haji’s movements after the event,” Chittenden County Deputy State’s Attorney Ryan Richards wrote in a court filing Tuesday. 
“They provide clear, identifiable images of him and show that he went to his brother’s apartment, where blood was found on the door and on shoes in the garbage consistent with the shoes Mr. Haji was wearing in the video,” the filing added. “Also, when Mr. Haji was arrested three days later his hand had an injury consistent with a slip-up wielding a knife.”
Margaret Jansch, Haji’s attorney, asked that the court set a hearing as soon as possible to further consider the hold-without-bail order. Katims then set that hearing for Aug. 27.
Police said that around 4 a.m. Saturday several Burlington officers were in the area of Church and Main streets when they came upon a disturbance behind the Main Street courthouse. 
Officers found that a man, later identified as Dau, had suffered a stab wound in a parking area behind the building, according to police. Dau was taken to the University of Vermont Medical Center, where he died from his injuries, police said. 
An affidavit filed in support of the charge stated that a video taken from a nearby property showed Haji and Dau shoving each other at one point.
“Haji is observed taking a step back from Dau and then lunging forward with the right side of his upper body swinging his right arm toward Dau’s right hip,” the affidavit stated. “Dau immediately puts his right hand to his right hip and says something to the effect of, ‘Yo, he stabbed me.’”
The fatal stabbing occurred during a weekend when the city also reported another stabbing that left one person injured, and two instances of gunfire where no one was injured.

READ MORE

An online post in Dau’s memory says that he “was known for his incredible sense of humor and kind heart.”
“He had a way of bringing laughter and joy to the people around him. He was supportive, caring, and always willing to be there for the people he loved,” continues the post, which is on a GoFundMe page that says it will help pay for Dau’s funeral expenses and support his family.
Chittenden County State’s Attorney Sarah George said in a statement Tuesday afternoon that she was grateful for the quick work of the Burlington Police Department in investigating the case. 
“Our office met with Mr. Dau’s family and will work diligently to connect them with the essential
services available to help them cope with this tragedy and provide them with everything they need to navigate the legal system and the daunting process that lies ahead,” George added.
If convicted of the second-degree murder charge, Haji faces up to life in prison.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: An independent candidate is fighting to stay on the ballot in a Bucks County state House race
description: The objection was brought by two voters who are being represented by Adam Bonin, an attorney who primarily works with Democrats on election-related cases.
text:
Bob Fabina talks with fellow poll workers at Fabina Hall in Johnstown May 19, 2026. Fabina owns the former church hall that dates back to the early 1900s. (Photo by John Beale for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)In a Bucks County state House race, independent Chris Gambino is fending off a challenge to boot him from the ballot.
While Democratic and Republican candidates vie for places on the ballot through state-funded primary elections, independent and small party candidates must collect signatures and submit nomination papers. Gambino appeared in court to defend his filing Tuesday, but no final ruling was issued.
Gambino told the Capital-Star that he believes the objection to his nomination papers is politically motivated, intended to clear potential competition to major party candidates.
The objection was brought by two voters, Michael Herman and Lloyd Randall Faulkner, who are being represented by Adam Bonin, an attorney who primarily works with Democrats on election-related cases.
Bonin declined to comment when reached by the Capital-Star.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“If we continue to just have two parties, this country will continue to become more and more divided,” Gambino said. “It’s shortsightedness. Is this election important? Absolutely. But is what happens in this election going to completely destroy our world? Absolutely not.” 
The Bucks County seat in the 143rd Legislative District is currently held by Republican Shelby Labs. But Democrats are eyeing the race as a potential chance to expand their slim majority. The Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee lists the 143rd as one of its “target races,” backing Democrat Tim Hayes.
The objection to Gambino’s filing papers challenges 269 of the 667 signatures he collected. He needs 488 valid signatures in order to appear on the ballot.
The challenge also alleges Gambino’s identification with the “Forward Independent” party violates state rules prohibiting political parties from adopting names similar to one another’s.
Because another candidate had already filed to run as a member of the “Independent Party” in an adjacent state House district, the objection argues “Gambino could not lawfully include ‘Independent’ as part of the name of his political body.”
“The risk of voter confusion in these adjacent districts is considerable if Gambino is permitted to employ a political body name which he is not legally permitted to use,” the petition continues.
Gambino describes himself as fed up with the two-party system, and hopes his campaign could open the door to more third-party and independent candidates like him.
“I saw that neither party was trying to bring people back together,” he said. “The goal should be bettering communities and in a lot of ways it’s not anymore. It’s about attaining and retaining power.”
He said he wonders if fear of an independent siphoning votes from a major party candidate spurred the challenge to his nomination papers, as opposed to a genuine concern about election integrity.
“We hit the pavement. We were knocking on doors. We were talking to people and got people excited,” he said. “They were willing to step out on a limb and sign this [petition], and now their voices are being thrown out.”

In a year of high stakes elections, numerous hopeful candidates have dealt with challenges to their nomination papers since the filing deadline earlier this month, along with accusations that third party candidates may serve as spoilers.
In eastern Pennsylvania’s 7th Congressional District, Both Democrats and the progressive Green Party of Pennsylvania are trying to boot Green Party candidate Andrew Tupone off the ballot. 
While the Democratic challenge is on technical grounds, the Green Party is warning that Tupone, who was registered as a Republican until earlier this year, is attempting to trick voters by claiming affiliation with their party.
Democrats and liberals view the 7th Congressional District race as a critical one in their efforts to flip the U.S. House. It’s currently represented by Republican Ryan Mackenzie and believed to be among the most competitive districts in the country.
In Western Pennsylvania’s 60th Legislative District, Libertarian Brian John Peltier requested to remove his name from the ballot after a challenge to some of the signatures he collected.
Bonin is also involved in a petition to challenge the nomination papers for Green Party candidates for Governor and Lt. Governor.

Ron DeSantis. According to a redacted affidavit released by the governor’s office, he has been charged with kidnapping, lewd or lascivious molestation, lewd or lascivious exhibitio[...]
text:
Rep. Mike Caruso (Photo by Christine Sexton, Florida Phoenix)Palm Beach County Clerk of Court Michael Caruso was arrested Tuesday morning and charged with five felony counts of child molestation and immediately suspended from office by Gov. Ron DeSantis.
According to a redacted affidavit released by the governor’s office, he has been charged with kidnapping, lewd or lascivious molestation, lewd or lascivious exhibition, luring or enticing a child, and child abuse involving a family member who was under 12 at the time.
Caruso, 67, was appointed Palm Beach County clerk of court last year by DeSantis, resigning his state House seat for the post.
He didn’t face an opponent in the Republican primary and wasn’t on Tuesday’s ballot. He was running for election to his clerk’s job in November.
DeSantis’ executive order bans Caruso from performing any official act, duty, or function of public office; from receiving any pay or allowance; and from entitlement to the emoluments or privileges of public office during his suspension.
Following his suspension, Shannon Ramsey-Chessman, Caruso’s chief of staff, was sworn in, the Clerk’s Office announced.
The affidavit was redacted in part but former state Sen. Lauren Book, a leading child-protection advocate and sexual abuse survivor, issued a statement condemning the DeSantis administration for not better protecting the child’s identity.
“It is unacceptable that in releasing documents detailing horrific allegations of child sexual abuse by recently-removed Palm Beach County Clerk of Courts Mike Caruso, the State failed to adequately protect the identity of the child victim,” Book said in a press release. “The redactions left enough deeply personal identifying information to effectively ‘out’ this child — including his relationship to the accused and other incredibly sensitive details.”

Caruso was a DeSantis loyalist while in the state House, and was removed from a leadership post after he voted against an immigration enforcement package championed by former House Speaker Daniel Perez but opposed by the governor.
Appearing at New College of Florida in Sarasota, DeSantis said his office vetted Caruso before appointing him and nothing came up.
However, Beverly Caruso accused Michael Caruso of sexually assaulting one of their children during 2012 divorce proceedings, the Tampa Bay Times reported.
“He had a clean vet, he was well regarded in the community. There was a lot of people that wanted him to be appointed to that position, and there was none of that information that was in any of the vetting materials,” DeSantis said Tuesday afternoon.
Once the case was made and the state announced the arrest, “it was a very easy decision for me to yank him from that position,” DeSantis said.
As a member of the Florida House in 2023, Caruso voted in favor of imposing the death penalty against those convicted of sexual battery against someone younger than 12 years old. 
DeSantis referenced the law saying,  “And if he’s convicted, he is going to be in for a world of hurt.”
 Details from the affidavit

The affidavit shines light on alleged acts of abuse occurring between November 2024 and August 2025..
According to the affidavit, the abuse came to light in October 2025.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Ahern’s new ad invokes praise from Rhode Island’s outgoing AG. But he endorsed her rival.
description: Kim Ahern’s latest campaign ad in the four-way Democratic primary for Rhode Island’s next attorney general begins with her reading from a plaque she was given on her final day as a prosecutor in 2019. “Your unwavering dedication to the mission of the department and victims of crime is an inspiration to all of those […]
text:
Kim Ahern, a Democratic candidate for Rhode Island attorney general, holds a plaque she received on her final day as a prosecutor in Peter Neronha’s office. Neronha has endorsed one of Ahern’s opponents. (Screenshot/Kim Ahern for Rhode Island)Kim Ahern’s latest campaign ad in the four-way Democratic primary for Rhode Island’s next attorney general begins with her reading from a plaque she was given on her final day as a prosecutor in 2019.
“Your unwavering dedication to the mission of the department and victims of crime is an inspiration to all of those who have worked with you,” Ahern intones in the 40-second video posted to Facebook and Instagram. “Your ability to happily forge ahead in the face of obstacles will be your lasting trademark.”
The camera pans to the bottom of the plaque engraved with the name of the presenter: Peter F. Neronha, attorney general. It’s a detail that caught the term-limited Neronha off guard when someone shared the video with him Monday.
“I was watching it and I’m like, ‘All right, well, like where does this end?’” Neronha said in an interview Monday evening. “And I’m like, ‘oh yeah, that’s my name.’”
Neronha said he wasn’t shocked that his name was there, he did give it to Ahern after all — as he has for other lawyers who have left the attorney general’s office. What surprised him was that the campaign chose to draw viewers’ attention to him at all.
“What she decides to do with this post, I’ll leave to her,” he said. “But there shouldn’t be any mistake or misunderstanding as to who I’ve endorsed.”
That chosen successor is Keith Hoffmann, Neronha’s former chief of policy and senior counsel who previously headed the office’s civil rights unit. The outgoing AG described Hoffmann as a proven leader ready to oversee the office of 125 attorneys, even if he lacks Ahern’s criminal trial experience.
“The public safety mission is very, very important,” Neronha said. “But the civil side of what we do — consumer protection, energy, energy regulatory work, environmental work, healthcare — those are all things that I think are critically important to the lives of Rhode Islanders.”
Neronha has also been an outspoken opponent of Ahern’s candidacy on social media, criticizing her tenure as the first chair of the Cannabis Control Commission. 
Hoffmann’s campaign called the focus on Neronha’s name in her social media ad “desperate and dishonest.”
“This is an attempt to mislead voters about her actual record in the office,” spokesperson Evan England said in an emailed statement Tuesday. “We need an AG who is committed to being honest and transparent with voters.”
Josh Block, a spokesperson for Ahern’s campaign, said the video was never intended as an endorsement — just another way to showcase her nine years of prosecutorial experience.
“Kim is enormously proud of her service as a frontline prosecutor under the past three attorneys general, and the plaque she received at the end of her near-decade in the AG’s office attests to her experience and dedication to the job,” Block said in an email to Rhode Island Current.



Quotation







What she decides to do with this post, I'll leave to her. But there shouldn't be any mistake or misunderstanding as to who I've endorsed.


– Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha, who is term-limited


Matt Ulricksen, an associate professor of political science at the Community College of Rhode Island said the use of Neronha’s name in the ad was a “slick move,” allowing Ahern to benefit from the outgoing attorney general’s political standing without explicitly claiming his support.
“Most people form impressions visually, not textually or aurally,” he wrote in a text message. “Voters are moved by emotive cues, not evidence-based appeals to reason. Images offer powerful emotive cues.”
Neronha too understands the sentimentality behind the plaque. He keeps a framed badge from his time as a state prosecutor between 1996 and 2002 outside his office. 
“When people are recognized in that way, it’s great to send them off and with a good moment,”  Neronha said.
Ulricksen said the Ahern campaign has most likely found Neronha’s endorsement carries weight with undecided voters who could determine the outcome of the Democratic primary.
“Given the level of spending by the Ahern and Hoffmann campaigns — especially Hoffmann — both should be polling much higher than they are,” Ulricksen said.
A poll released Tuesday by Salve Regina University shows Ahern with 23% support from 857 likely primary voters, a 10-point edge over Hoffmann in the four-way race. Rep. Joe Solomon Jr. saw 10% support from likely voters and Rep. Jason Knight sat at 5%. The poll was conducted Aug. 3 to 11 by Embold Research.
Almost half of likely Democratic primary voters surveyed — 46% — remain undecided on the AG’s race.
Early voting starts on Aug. 20 ahead of the Sept. 9 primary. The Democratic nominee will face Republican Alan Gordon in the Nov. 3 general election.
