title: Trump administration appeals dismissal of criminal charges against Kilmar Abrego Garcia
description: The Trump administration on Monday appealed a district court judge’s dismissal of its Tennessee criminal case against Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the 30-year-old man living in Maryland who drew national attention to the administration’s immigration enforcement practices after he was wrongly deported to El Salvador last year. U.S. District Court Judge Waverly Crens[...]
text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia stands outside U.S. District Court in Greenbelt with his wife, Jennifer Vasquez Sura, left, and Lydia Walther-Rodriguez with CASA, after a federal judge ruled earlier this month he was allowed to remain free. (File photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)The Trump administration on Monday appealed a district court judge’s dismissal of its Tennessee criminal case against Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the 30-year-old man living in Maryland who drew national attention to the administration’s immigration enforcement practices after he was wrongly deported to El Salvador last year.
U.S. District Court Judge Waverly Crenshaw dismissed human smuggling charges against Abrego, as he is identified in court documents, in May, calling the administration’s prosecution “vindictive and selective.” Crenshaw ruled that the executive branch reopened a years-old investigation into a Tennessee traffic stop and charged Abrego with two counts of human smuggling only after Abrego successfully challenged his deportation to El Salvador and the U.S. Supreme Court ordered the administration to facilitate his return.  

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
“The objective evidence here shows that, absent Abrego’s successful lawsuit challenging his removal to El Salvador, the Government would not have brought this prosecution,” Crenshaw, an Obama appointee, wrote in the opinion.
The Trump administration notified the court of its intent to appeal in June.
In an opening brief filed in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth District Monday, the administration argues that the district court’s presumption of vindictiveness was “improper” and the charges brought against Abrego were “supported by legitimate prosecutorial concerns surrounding the defendant’s return to the country.”
Crenshaw’s ruling “marks a dramatic expansion of the power of courts to dismiss serious criminal charges based on subjective assessments of a prosecutor’s motivations and is an unwarranted intrusion into the Executive’s powers and responsibility to protect the public,” the U.S. Attorney’s Office in the Middle District of Tennessee stated in a news release.
Abrego entered the United States illegally as a teen after fleeing from El Salvador, where he said he feared gang violence. A 2019 order from an immigration judge barred his deportation back to the country. Abrego was deported to El Salvador in March 2025, a move a federal attorney later admitted was made in error.
Abrego returned to the U.S. in June 2025 and was immediately sent to a Tennessee detention center, where he was held on a two-count human smuggling indictment. The charges stemmed from a 2022 traffic stop for speeding by state troopers in rural Tennessee. Federal attorneys alleged that Abrego served as a driver in an ongoing conspiracy to transport immigrants without legal status throughout the United States. Abrego pleaded not guilty to the charges.
He remains free while his immigration case continues in Maryland.
In Nashville, a federal judge dismisses indictment against Kilmar Abrego Garcia

Following Crenshaw’s dismissal of the criminal charges, national watchdog group Campaign for Government Accountability filed a complaint with the New York Bar requesting an investigation into Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s conduct related to Abrego’s case. A Department of Justice spokesperson called this complaint “baseless” in an emailed statement to the Lookout in May.
Crenshaw’s opinion honed in on the reopening of the traffic stop case against Abrego, and the scrutiny applied to federal prosecutor Rob McGuire’s handling of the case by Associate Deputy Attorney General Akash Singh. Singh was working in the office of Blanche, who was serving as deputy attorney general at the time. 
Blanche was confirmed as U.S. Attorney General in early August.
Singh pushed for Abrego to be charged, calling it a “top priority for us” in an email to McGuire in early April and closely monitored the case’s progress, reviewing drafts of complaints, according to findings detailed in Crenshaw’s opinion. 
“Blanche’s now unrequited public statements tying the reopened investigation to Abrego’s successful lawsuit taints the investigation with a vindictive motive,” Crenshaw wrote, and McGuire’s testimony to the contrary was “subjective” and did not rebut the presumption of vindictiveness, though the court did not find sufficient evidence of actual vindictiveness.
In its Monday filing, the administration argued that the finding of presumptive vindictiveness requires the prosecutor — in this case, McGuire — to have a “personal stake” in Abrego’s removal lawsuit. 
“It is undisputed that McGuire himself had no stake in Abrego’s removal suit, and there is no evidence — despite the district court’s (unfounded) authorization of extensive discovery — that anyone else in the government pressured or induced McGuire to charge Abrego,” the filing states. “Second, there was nothing unreasonable about indicting Abrego for the serious crimes charged.”
Anita Wadhwani contributed.

title: Hospital executive resigns as state auditor alleges misuse of public funds on golf, ‘lavish’ fun
description: LINCOLN  — The top administrator of Nebraska’s first designated “rural emergency hospital” has resigned amid financial abuse allegations from the state auditor that he used hospital funds for “lavish personal entertainment.”  Auditor Mike Foley, in a 28-page letter Tuesday, laid out more than $38,000 in questionable purchases that his team found the chief ex[...]
text:
Nebraska Auditor of Public Accounts Mike Foley testifies before the Legislature's Government, Military and Veterans Affairs Committee. Feb. 5, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN  — The top administrator of Nebraska’s first designated “rural emergency hospital” has resigned amid financial abuse allegations from the state auditor that he used hospital funds for “lavish personal entertainment.” 
Auditor Mike Foley, in a 28-page letter Tuesday, laid out more than $38,000 in questionable purchases that his team found the chief executive and financial officer charged to cards covered by his employer at the time, the municipal hospital in Friend, Nebraska.
Expenses in the letter addressed to the city’s mayor and Warren Memorial Hospital board included airline ticket upgrades, “extraordinary” Ritz-Carlton hotel room service charges, purchases at an ice cream shop and a pizza parlor and streaming subscriptions for Hulu and YouTube TV.
Foley said his team found thousands of dollars in golfing expenses in Nebraska, as well as Florida, Colorado, Nevada, Illinois and Tennessee, which were reimbursed with hospital funds.
“It’s always infuriating to see public money being misused,” Foley said in a related media statement. “But depriving an important medical facility of scarce funds, solely for extravagant personal aggrandizement, is especially disturbing.”




Quotation







Depriving an important medical facility of scarce funds, solely for extravagant personal aggrandizement, is especially disturbing.


– Mike Foley, Nebraska State Auditor



The implicated chief executive and financial officer was identified in the auditor’s letter as Jared Chaffin. According to a hospital response included in the auditor team’s findings, Chaffin has repaid the city’s healthcare system for personal and other charges identified as improper.
The hospital board, whose members are appointed by the city’s mayor and approved by the city council, noted that it previously submitted documentation regarding certain disputed transactions, including Dietary Department purchases that served legitimate hospital business purposes. The board said it was committed to ensuring the hospital is “made whole for any improperly expended funds” and said interim leadership is in place as it searches for Chaffin’s replacement.
Foley said his office turned over its findings to appropriate law enforcement agencies.
The audit team provided a historical backdrop in its report: Friend’s Warren Memorial Hospital, established in 1930, provides emergency, outpatient and clinic services primarily to residents of Saline and Seward counties in southeast Nebraska. Prior to 2024, the hospital, also known as Friend Community Healthcare System, was designated as a “critical access hospital.” 
Around that time, Foley’s team wrote, hospital representatives made public statements that the hospital was reaching a breaking point due to exhaustion of federal pandemic relief money. Other rural hospitals across the state and country reportedly faced similar difficulties.
In January, 2024, the hospital changed its status to become Nebraska’s first rural emergency hospital — a designation created by Congress in 2021 to assist rural hospitals by providing dedicated federal funding to maintain access to emergency and outpatient hospital services in communities that might not be able to sustain a critical access hospital or a small rural hospital. 
Foley said that rural hospitals in Nebraska are “teetering under budgetary pressures,” so financial misconduct “can be enough to push them over the edge of insolvency.”




Quotation







The corrective measures … strengthen the institution so it may continue serving its community with integrity.


– Warren Memorial Hospital leadership 



Foley alleges that Chaffin apparently tried to “deceive” the audit team by claiming he opened a second credit card account for the hospital under his own name because the prior card was cancelled due to lack of payment. 
Other questionable expenses among “hundreds” the auditor alleged to have been incurred by Chaffin included hotel alcohol charges, fees at wholesale clubs, such as Costco, and purchases at a local Dollar General store and a Rocket Car Wash.
The hospital administrators and board, in their response, said they were conducting a comprehensive review of all financial policies, including controls over purchasing cards. 
“The corrective measures … strengthen the institution so it may continue serving its community with integrity,” the hospital leadership wrote.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Congress is playing politics with Mississippi’s disaster recovery, nonprofit watchdog says
description: Devastating flooding in 2019, lasting from spring through July, flooded about 700 homes in the south Mississippi Delta, and left more than 500,000 acres underwater.
text:
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful Mississippians to share their ideas about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.    

In the U.S., the number of billion-dollar disasters is increasing each year. Wildfires, hurricanes, floods, tornadoes and extreme weather events are hitting communities with increasing frequency and severity, placing more Americans at risk of losing their homes, livelihoods and financial stability.
Mississippi offers a clear example of this growing threat. Over the past decade, the state has faced a steady drumbeat of tropical storms and hurricanes, not always direct hits, but often just as damaging. In 2020 alone, multiple storms, including Hurricane Zeta, Hurricane Sally and Tropical Storm Cristobal, brought flooding, storm surge and widespread power outages. In 2021, Hurricane Ida tore through the region, causing severe flooding and fatalities even after making landfall in Louisiana. 
These are not rare, once-in-a-generation events. They are recurring disruptions that strain infrastructure, delay recovery and test the limits of state and local response systems.
In recent years, Mississippi also has been hit with other disasters, ranging from tornadoes to ice storms to droughts.
Yet, instead of preparing for this reality, the Trump administration stopped tracking these disasters to advance an alternate-reality narrative and an out-of-touch ideology cooked up by a Beltway think tank. Dismantling the Federal Emergency Management Agency or FEMA, the very system millions of Americans rely on when disaster strikes, is not something a president can do alone. Congress has the power to stop it, and right now, too many members are choosing not to.
Brian Lowery stands before what remains of his home, which was ripped apart by a tornado, in Tylertown, Miss., on Thursday, May 15, 2025. (AP Photo/Sophie Bates) Credit: AP Photo/Sophie Bates
This follows a familiar pattern. Promises to put Americans first have repeatedly translated into gutting programs that actually serve the public, while costly, high-profile political priorities move forward unchecked. The rhetoric may win headlines. The consequences, however, fall squarely on American communities.
FEMA is not an abstract federal agency. It is one of the most widely relied upon forms of federal support in the country.  Around 94% of Americans live in a county that has received FEMA assistance since 2011. From 2017 to 2023, $267.7 billion in disaster aid and reconstruction supported communities across rural and urban areas, in red states and blue alike.
 If FEMA disappears, what happens to your community after the next wildfire, flood, hurricane, tornado or terrorist attack?
Last year, Trump said, “I’d say after the hurricane season we’ll start phasing [FEMA] out.” Interesting delay from an administration so confident that FEMA is not essential. The same overconfidence already resulted in multiple “fire-first-then-realize-the-wrong-people-were-fired” moments. Let’s remember that there is no serious plan to replace FEMA’s capabilities.
Without FEMA, disaster response responsibilities shift to state and local governments that are already stretched thin and to families who cannot afford to wait for help that may never come. 

Ben Smilowitz, of Rockville, Maryland, witnessed the bungled Hurricane Katrina response while managing a Red Cross Client Service Center in Gulfport. Soon after, he launched Disaster Accountability Project – SmartResponse, an independent watchdog, to confront the root causes of the failed Katrina response and maximize the impact of billions of dollars of disaster relief and humanitarian aid.
DAP – SmartResponse has successfully advocated for the release of millions of dollars of disaster relief and recovery funds after Superstorm Sandy, investigated deficiencies in emergency planning surrounding 19 commercial U.S. nuclear power plants and improved the transparency of nearly $2 billion dollars of disaster relief donations after disasters in the U.S., Haiti and Nepal. DAP’s reports, advocacy and op-eds have been covered by global news media 
Prior to starting DAP – SmartResponse, Ben had a background in civic engagement and issue advocacy. He wrote successful legislation in Connecticut and created a youth cabinet in Missouri. Ben is an Echoing Green fellow, studied political science and nonprofit management, and holds a law degree from the University of Connecticut School of Law.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: The bill that threw low-income Colorado students under the bus
description: I just had a difficult conversation with one of my favorite students. A brilliant, motivated and focused first-generation college student from Denver, she relies on work-study to help fund her education. As a college professor, I had planned to hire her as a research assistant using her work-study funding, both supporting my research and building […]
text:
Members of the Colorado House of Representatives work on the final day of the 2026 legislative session, May 13, at the Colorado Capitol in Denver. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)I just had a difficult conversation with one of my favorite students. A brilliant, motivated and focused first-generation college student from Denver, she relies on work-study to help fund her education. As a college professor, I had planned to hire her as a research assistant using her work-study funding, both supporting my research and building her resume for law school.
In undergraduate mentoring, I’ve leaned on work-study as a way to compensate for the inequities that are built into the internship process. Wealthy students with parental support can pursue unpaid internships that build their resumes without having to worry about how to pay the rent or fill their gas tank. Low-income students often need to split their time between schoolwork and off-campus jobs to pay their bills and help their families. Work-study research and teaching assistantships can help fill the resulting resume gap.
This summer I had to tell my student that our research assistantship wasn’t happening. The work-study funds that she counts on vanished in a single line of the 22-page Colorado House Bill 26-1345 as part of a late-stage floor amendment that bypassed any public hearing. The amendment stripped state funding for Colorado Work-Study at private institutions, including Regis University, where I am a professor.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ordinarily, a major cut to need-based CWS would require advance public notice, expert testimony, and dedicated committee debate before lawmakers. It also would have forced the legislators who favored sacrificing need-based student aid to defend their priorities in an open debate.
Instead, lawmakers opted to exploit a procedural loophole stripping these students of aid in a late-stage amendment appended without public notice or dedicated committee debate. Low-income Colorado college students at private universities found themselves stripped of the support they relied on, left to absorb the blow in silence.
The budget trade-offs faced by the state Legislature were real: Increases in Medicaid costs needed to be absorbed, and the TABOR straightjacket demanded reciprocal cuts. What’s indefensible is which group the Legislature chose to sacrifice. While throwing low-income students under the bus, the state leaders opted to protect tax loopholes that lavish millions of dollars of state funding into the pockets of the state’s richest and most privileged millionaires and billionaires, illuminating their own values in the process.
Consider the Colorado tax code loophole that allows corporations to deduct massive, multi-million-dollar salaries of their CEOs as a routine operating expense, like paying for raw materials or factory rent. This legal trick allows corporations to manipulate a tax subsidy intended to encourage corporations to direct profits back into production and, ideally, innovation. Instead, the loophole incentives corporations to do the exact opposite: rather than plow those millions back into innovation, the law rewards corporations to line the already bloated pockets of their shareholders and CEOs.
What’s worse is that they do so at public expense. A tax deduction is fiscally indistinguishable from a cash handout in which the state directly subsidizes gargantuan CEO salaries. Don’t let the technical language fool you: This is welfare for the rich, amounting to tens of millions of dollars per year.
Progressive statehouse Democrats attempted to close this notorious loophole in the same 2026 legislative season during which work-study was axed. The reform bill was relatively meek, restricting state tax deductions for executive compensation exceeding $250,000 rather than closing the loophole altogether. Roused by this threat to his favorite constituency, however, Gov. Jared Polis and his corporate allies leapt into action. Polis threatened to veto the bill, working with his allies in the Senate to kill it.
The political economist Joseph Schumpeter once wrote that “the budget is the skeleton of the state stripped of all misleading ideologies.” Polis and his centrist Democratic allies bloviate about meritocracy and equal opportunity, but when faced with a choice between state subsidies for millionaires and billionaires and support for low-income students working their way through college, they threw my student, and thousands like her, under the bus. Hundreds or possibly thousands of students across the state will not return to their studies this year because of the state Legislature’s decision to shield the wealthy and powerful at their expense.
If Colorado can afford tax breaks for wealthy corporate CEOs, it can afford work-study for students trying to work their way through college. This January, Colorado lawmakers must restore CWS to all Colorado colleges and universities.

title: Unions ask Supreme Court to affirm judge who found Act 10 unconstitutional
description: The unions that won a circuit court ruling to overturn Wisconsin’s Act 10, the 2011 law stripping most public employees’ collective bargaining rights, are asking the Wisconsin Supreme Court to reinstate that ruling after an appeals court reversed the lower court. The plaintiffs filed their state Supreme Court appeal Monday. They include unions affiliated wit[...]
text:
Act 10, one of the signature laws passed early in former Gov. Scott Walker’s two terms, ended collective bargaining rights for most state and local employees, making an exception for certain public safety employees. The law survived a series of court challenges in the years immediately after its passage. (Photo by Emily Mills. Used by permission)The unions that won a circuit court ruling to overturn Wisconsin’s Act 10, the 2011 law stripping most public employees’ collective bargaining rights, are asking the Wisconsin Supreme Court to reinstate that ruling after an appeals court reversed the lower court.
The plaintiffs filed their state Supreme Court appeal Monday. They include unions affiliated with the Wisconsin Education Association Council, the American Federation of Teachers, the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, the Service Employees International Union and the Teamsters.
Act 10, one of the signature laws passed early in former Gov. Scott Walker’s two terms, ended collective bargaining rights for most state and local employees, making an exception for certain public safety employees. The law survived a series of court challenges in the years immediately after its passage.
In December 2024, however, Dane County Circuit Court Judge Jacob Frost ruled  that the law made an arbitrary distinction between the public safety employees who kept their union rights under Act 10 and other public safety employees who lost those rights.
State Capitol Police, University of Wisconsin Police, and state conservation wardens were “treated unequally with no rational basis for that difference” when they were denied collective bargaining, Frost ruled, and for that reason, Act 10 violated the Wisconsin Constitution’s equal protection clause.
The law remained in place pending appeals, and more than 18 months later, the 2nd District Court of Appeals overturned Frost’s ruling in a 2-1 decision July 29.
The Legislature’s reasoning for making the distinction wasn’t an issue, so long as there are “any reasonably conceivable state of facts that could provide a rational basis for the classification,” Judges Mark Gundrum and Shelley Grogan wrote.
Judge Lisa Neubauer dissented, arguing that the unions that kept their bargaining rights had all supported Walker’s election in 2010 just months before he took office and signed Act 10 into law. Excluding them from the law while subjecting other public safety employees to its restrictions “is not based on any identified ‘substantial distinction’ that makes the first group really different from the other,” Neubauer wrote.
The new appeal quotes Neubauer’s dissent in arguing for the justices to take up the case.
“This Court should accept review and reaffirm that, as Judge Neubauer put it in her dissent, ‘rational-basis review is not a rubber stamp,’” the unions’ motion states. “Here, because Act 10’s classification between ‘public safety’ and ‘general’ employees cannot survive anything greater than rubber-stamp-level scrutiny, that classification violates Article I, Section 1 of the Wisconsin Constitution.”
The new appeal also challenges a finding from the appeals court majority, which found Wisconsin’s equal protection clause was identical to the federal equal protection clause and that a 2013 federal appeals court ruling had already found Act 10 constitutional.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Amazon’s data center network in Northwest Louisiana is going to get bigger
description: A third facility, not officially part of Amazon’s original $12 billion investment announced in February, will bring the total project value to $18 million.
text:
Fireworks and confetti fill the Shreveport Municipal Auditorium for Amazon's announcement Monday, Feb. 23, 2026, of it plans to build three connected data centers in Bossier and Caddo parishes. (Photo by Elise Plunk/Louisiana Illuminator)  Amazon and state officials announced Tuesday the company’s data center hub under construction in Northwest Louisiana will be expanded. 
A third facility, not officially part of Amazon’s original $12 billion investment announced in February, will bring the total project value to $18 million. 
The plans now call for three data centers spanning Caddo and Bossier parishes, with the new location set for Resilient Tech Park in Shreveport. 
“Amazon’s decision to increase its investment in Louisiana so quickly sends a clear message about what they have experienced here,” Gov. Jeff Landry said in a news release. “Amazon came to our state with an ambitious vision, and Louisiana has shown we can deliver at the scale and speed that vision demands.” 
The expansion is expected to add 210 permanent direct jobs to the 540 announced earlier this year, according to Louisiana Economic Development. Amazon will continue to partner with development company Stack Infrastructure to build the data centers. 
Stack, which will own the data centers, anticipates construction jobs for the data centers to increase from 1,500 to 2,250. 
Amazon’s expansion comes as debate continues in Louisiana over data centers’ natural resource and electricity use. Questions are also growing about the prevalence of elected officials signing nondisclosure agreements to limit scrutiny of the state and local subsidies offered to entice industrial development to the state. 
In a bid to assuage local concerns over water and power needs, Amazon has pledged to invest up to $400 million in improving public water infrastructure to support its three campuses. The company has also “coordinated with local utilities to ensure sufficient capacity for both its facilities and existing customers,” according to Louisiana Economic Development. 
Amazon has also promised to fund all water and wastewater improvements its projects require and minimize its use of water to cool the data centers. 
Amazon is working with Southwestern Electric Power Co. to power its data centers, promising to fully fund the new energy infrastructure and grid upgrades it needs. 
“We’re ready to serve and ready to deliver the reliable energy our communities need to support new investment while protecting existing customers from the costs of that growth,” SWEPCO president Brett Mattison said in the state news release. 
Amazon’s expansion plans come just months after Meta announced it would nearly double the expected size of its Hyperion campus in Northeast Louisiana. Meta has faced pushback against its deal with Entergy to build seven new natural gas power plants to supply the electricity it will need. 
The Louisiana Public Service commission recently decided to allow Meta to keep its calculations for job creation and electricity needs concealed, against the wishes of consumer rights and environmental advocates pushing for transparency.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: The Jericho Road in SC: But for the grace of God go I
description: There is a saying repeated so frequently that few of us stop to consider its implications: “People just don’t want to work anymore.” It is often said offhandedly, as though it explains why some people struggle while others do not. Beneath the phrase is an assumption that poverty reflects something about a person’s willingness to […]
text:
"For far too many of our neighbors, the line
between stability and crisis is one missed paycheck, one broken-down car, one rent increase," writes author Jessica Kaneft. (Photo illustration by mohd izzuan/Getty Images Plus)There is a saying repeated so frequently that few of us stop to consider its implications: “People just don’t want to work anymore.”
It is often said offhandedly, as though it explains why some people struggle while others do not.
Beneath the phrase is an assumption that poverty reflects something about a person’s willingness to work, and perhaps even something about their character. The neighbor facing eviction, the mother at the food pantry, or the man sleeping beneath the overpass are not victims of circumstance. In this telling, they are simply living with the consequences of their own choices.
Our brains crave order and coherence. Something is right or wrong, fair or unfair, people are deserving or undeserving.
This “just world hypothesis” reassures us that if we work hard, make good choices, and follow the rules, our lives will turn out well.
The more people I meet and the more experiences I have, the harder it becomes to believe that success and stability are simply rewards for good choices.
This is not to dismiss that choices matter. Of course they do. But so do the circumstances in which those choices are made.
Some of us grew up in stable homes free of violence, attended good schools, lived with financial security, and benefited from strong social networks. Others experienced trauma, lived with poverty, experienced housing instability, attended underfunded schools, and grew up in communities where opportunities were scarce or nonexistent.
Advantages compound and so do disadvantages. The gap between people is rarely the result of one decision.
We know this: good people suffer all the time. For far too many of our neighbors, the line between stability and crisis is one missed paycheck, one broken-down car, one rent increase.
We even have a name for many of these families: ALICE, an acronym for Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed.
According to United for ALICE, a family of four in South Carolina needed roughly $77,000 a year in 2024 just to cover basic household expenses. Yet many of the jobs that support our communities, such as childcare workers, home health aides, retail employees, and food-service staff, pay far less than that.
Sometimes earning more does not mean having more. As a low-income parent’s earnings rise, government help through Medicaid, the Women Infants and Children Nutrition Program, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (commonly known as food stamps), housing assistance, and childcare assistance may shrink or disappear at different income levels.
A small raise can actually leave a family no better off, and sometimes worse off, than before. Turning down a raise or additional hours may look irrational from the outside. From the inside, it can be a careful calculation about how to keep the rent paid, the children fed, and the family insured.
These stories matter because they shape how we see our neighbors. They determine whether we approach someone with curiosity or condemnation, compassion or judgment.
Jesus repeatedly challenged this instinct to judge. He warned people to remove the plank from their own eye before pointing out the speck in someone else’s. When a crowd gathered to stone
a woman caught in adultery, he asked which of them was without sin. One by one, they walked away.
I keep picking up my stone. We all do.
When someone we love loses a job, makes a poor financial decision, or struggles to keep life together, we know the context. We know the divorce, the illness, the grief, the addiction, the hard season they have been carrying. We extend grace because we know the whole story.
When we encounter someone outside our circle, we often fill in the missing pieces with assumptions instead.
“There, but for the grace of God go I” is another saying I have heard so often that I rarely stopped to think about what it meant. To me, it is not an expression of pity. It is a recognition that the
distance between my life and another person’s may be far smaller, and far less earned, than I would like to believe.
Grace, however, cannot end with recognition. Recognition must lead to responsibility, to change.
Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. once said that it was not enough to help the wounded traveler along the Jericho Road. Eventually, he argued, “the whole Jericho Road must be transformed.”
That statement has stayed with me.
Right now, all across South Carolina, roads and bridges are under construction. Traffic slows.
Detours frustrate us. Yet we endure the inconvenience because we understand that infrastructure cannot be repaired without disrupting what already exists.
The same is true of our communities.
The question is not only whether we will stop for our neighbor when she is suffering beside the road. It is whether we love her enough to help make the road safer.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Former Democratic Party of New Mexico official says party leaders broke rules to force her out
description: A new lawsuit from a former Democratic Party of New Mexico secretary accuses top party officials of wrongfully pushing her out of the position after she voiced concerns about “discrimination against Navajos within” the party.
text:
Former Democratic Party of New Mexico Secretary Brenda Hoskie, second from right, poses for a photo with Chair Sara Attleson, Vice Chair Cam Crawford and former Treasurer Julie Rochman. In a new lawsuit, she accuses party leaders of violating internal rules to push her out after she voiced concerns about discrimination against Navajo party members. (Courtesy photo)A new lawsuit from a former Democratic Party of New Mexico secretary accuses top party officials of wrongfully pushing her out of the position after she voiced concerns about “discrimination against Navajos within” the party.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Former party secretary Brenda Hoskie, who is Navajo, alleges that, since early 2025, she has repeatedly voiced concerns to party leaders about discrimination, harassment and retaliation against Navajo members of the party. In a Facebook video earlier this year, for instance, she accuses party officials of telling her to “be a brown face in the photo, but not a strong voice at the table” and “to stay on my reservation.”
In the video, posted at the end of March, Hoskie said she was “being bullied to resign from my statewide position as secretary of the Democratic Party of New Mexico because I will not go along with how they run the part,” and said that she witnessed DPNM members refer to Indigenous people as “effing Navajos” and “stupid Indians” at party events.
She said that the party “recklessly mishandled” investigating reports of the alleged discrimination.
In the suit itself, Hoskie alleges DPNM Chair Sara Attleson and Executive Director Sean Ward booted her as secretary without following the party’s internal rules. According to the lawsuit, Attleson and Ward convened a Committee on Discipline meeting in May, for which Hoskie was absent, and subsequently sent an email on Aug. 7 to the party’s State Central Committee which said that the office of secretary had become vacant.
The lawsuit alleges that the party’s Committee on Discipline is not mentioned in the party’s internal rules and that the State Central Committee is supposed to handle disciplinary matters.
The lawsuit, filed in the Second Judicial District Court in Bernalillo County, asks a judge to restore Hoskie to her position as party secretary.
A spokesperson for the state Democratic Party did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Infighting similarly plagued the Republican Party of New Mexico in the months leading up to this summer’s primary election.
Republican officials across the state accused Party Chair Amy Barela of violating party rules by staying in her post even though she was running against a fellow Republican in a contested primary and called on her to step down. A judge ultimately ordered Barela to resign as party chair and she lost her appeal to the New Mexico Supreme Court.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Governor appoints justice to Idaho Supreme Court to fill upcoming vacancy
description: Idaho Gov. Brad Little named an Idaho Supreme Court justice to fill a vacancy left by the retiring chief justice. Little appointed Fourth District Judge Jason Scott to fill outgoing Chief Justice Richard Bevan’s seat on the state’s highest court, the governor’s office announced Tuesday.  Scott is an Idaho native who earned an accounting degree […]
text:
The exterior of the Idaho Supreme Court building in Boise as seen on Jan. 14, 2026. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Idaho Gov. Brad Little named an Idaho Supreme Court justice to fill a vacancy left by the retiring chief justice.
Little appointed Fourth District Judge Jason Scott to fill outgoing Chief Justice Richard Bevan’s seat on the state’s highest court, the governor’s office announced Tuesday. 
Scott is an Idaho native who earned an accounting degree at Idaho State University before graduating from Duke University’s School of Law in 1997. After law school, he returned to Idaho — clerking for a U.S. district judge and working for 15 years at the law firm Hawley Troxell, including seven years as a partner at the firm. His legal practice focused on civil litigation.
Justice Robyn Brody to become chief justice of Idaho Supreme Court 

“Judge Scott has dedicated his career to the law and to serving the people of Idaho,” Little said in a written statement. “His experience as a practicing attorney and a district judge gives him a strong understanding of both the courtroom and the broader legal system. I am confident he will bring thoughtful judgment, a strong work ethic, and a deep commitment to the rule of law to the Idaho Supreme Court.”
In 2014, Scott was first appointed as a district judge in Idaho’s Fourth Judicial District, which includes Ada County. As a judge, he has presided over high-stakes lawsuits — including a legal challenge to the state’s strict abortion ban and an open meetings lawsuit over University of Idaho’s attempted purchase of the University of Phoenix. He also serves as presiding district judge in Valley County.
“For twelve years, I’ve given my all to serving the people of Idaho as a district judge,” Scott said in a written statement. “I’m grateful to Governor Little for entrusting me with the opportunity to continue in public service as a justice of the Idaho Supreme Court. I will always perform the duties of the office to the best of my ability, and I look forward to collaborating with my new colleagues on the Court to decide cases with the utmost care and fidelity to the law.”
Scott is set to fill the seat upon Bevan’s retirement on Oct. 30. Idaho Supreme Court justices recently elected Justice Robyn Brody to succeed Bevan as chief justice.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Manhattan’s $1.25 billion animal disease research facility not fully operational, report says
description: TOPEKA — The $1.25 billion biocontainment facility in Manhattan developed for cutting-edge research on the most dangerous animal diseases is not fully operational three years after its ribbon-cutting, a federal report determined.  The Office of Inspector General published a July report stating the National Bio and Agro-Defense Facility isn’t able to perform[...]
text:
The National Bio and Agro-Defense Facility in Manhattan isn't using its two labs designated for handling the most dangerous animal diseases, an Office of the Inspector General Report found. (Photo by National Bio and Agro-Defense Facility)TOPEKA — The $1.25 billion biocontainment facility in Manhattan developed for cutting-edge research on the most dangerous animal diseases is not fully operational three years after its ribbon-cutting, a federal report determined. 
The Office of Inspector General published a July report stating the National Bio and Agro-Defense Facility isn’t able to perform the high-level animal disease science it was designed for. 
The facility wasn’t appropriately configured by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, the report said. 
DHS transferred the facility to the U.S. Department of Agriculture in February 2024, which accepted it without a complete commissioning report, a move that ultimately cost the USDA $75.8 million as it fixes issues that hadn’t been addressed, the report said. 
The USDA expects additional costs may be incurred to finish the 574,000-square-foot facility. 
The OIG report recommended multiple steps to bring the facility to full operational status, including repairs and upgrades to configure spaces to appropriately house animals and completing the commissioning process that allows the facility to handle dangerous diseases. 
NBAF was built to replace New York’s Plum Island Animal Disease Center, where the USDA conducted high-level animal disease research. Plum Island was billed on its website as “the nation’s premiere defense” against accidental or intentional introduction of animal diseases into the United States. 
It was considered a coup for Kansas when Manhattan was selected as the site for the facility in 2009, and a groundbreaking was held in 2015 for the laboratory. The facility was expected to employ about 325 permanent workers and to have a $3.5 billion economic effect on the state in its first 20 years of use, according to a 2015 announcement from Kansas State University. 
The state committed $105 million in matching state funds to NBAF and $35 million of research funding, the announcement said. 
In May, NBAF director Alfonso Clavijo told the Greater Manhattan Area Chamber of Commerce that the lab would soon be hiring 150 people, to bring total employees to about 400. 
NBAF was designed to handle large animals in areas that allowed for high-level containment to study hazardous diseases, the report said. 
The facility is meant to support research at multiple biosafety levels, ranked from BSL-1, which allows scientists to work with microbes and biological agents that are considered minimal biosafety hazards, up to BSL-4, which are rated as dangerous, the report said. 
Currently, NBAF is operating its BSL-1 and -2 levels but is not operating the BSL-3 and -4, which require “more robust protective and decontamination equipment, and being airtight under certain circumstances (BSL-3) or always (BSL-4),” the report said.
DHS said the commissioning process was finished and distributed a commissioning report to USDA in July 2023, but the USDA knew there were deficiencies in the facility, the OIG report said. 
In May 2023, the USDA asked an outside organization for an independent review. Issues discovered in the facility include air supply continuity issues, problems with sealing rooms and lack of gates to keep animals from moving around. 
USDA said in a response to the report that it will have the BSL-3 lab operational by the end of 2026 but didn’t set a date to open the BSL-4 lab.
The NBAF communications department did not immediately answer phone and email requests about how research on animal diseases was affected by the delay between closing Plum Island and getting NBAF labs operational.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ health officials urge parents to ignore Trump order on childhood vaccines
description: New Jersey's health commissioner wants residents to ignore President Donald Trump's call for childhood vaccines to be cut from 17 to 11.
text:
New Jersey's health commissioner wants residents to ignore President Donald Trump's call for childhood vaccines to be cut from 17 to 11. (Photo courtesy of Scott Housley/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)New Jersey health officials want parents to ignore an executive order President Donald Trump issued last week calling for fewer childhood vaccines, warning it likely will increase the risk of preventable illness and death nationally.
In an Aug. 10 order, Trump said children should get vaccinated against 11 diseases, instead of the 17 immunizations previously recommended, and called for splitting the vaccine for measles, mumps, and rubella — long administered as a single combined shot — into three shots given during separate medical visits.
But that order does not invalidate or supersede New Jersey’s vaccine requirements, which parents and guardians here should continue to follow, said Dr. Raynard E. Washington, the state’s health commissioner.
Trump’s order departs from decades of evidence, Washington added.
“Protecting children from preventable disease is one of the most fundamental responsibilities we hold, and it is one we take seriously,” he said in a statement Tuesday. “Families deserve clear, science-based guidance, not confusion. The evidence behind childhood vaccines is clear, it has not changed, and New Jersey will continue to make sure every family can access the vaccines that keep their children safe.”
New Jersey is a founding member of the Northeast Public Health Collaborative, a multistate coalition that also rebuked Trump’s order and exhorted parents and guardians to follow the childhood and adolescent immunization schedules issued by the American Academy of Pediatrics.
“These schedules reflect the current scientific evidence on vaccine safety and effectiveness and are based on the specific disease risks and healthcare delivery context in the U.S.,” the collaborative said in a statement. “Undermining confidence in the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine — used for over five decades — during the largest measles outbreak in decades will lead to additional measles cases and, potentially, deaths. Immunizations save lives, and parents should be able to trust that the health recommendations they receive are based on science.”
Last week, Trump said his new order would align the United States “with common sense and knowledge” when it comes to vaccines for children.
Trump has repeatedly linked vaccines to autism and did so again last week when he announced his order, despite studies debunking any link.
“The claim that they cause autism has been studied exhaustively and disproven. Reviving it does not help families; it draws attention away from the work of keeping children healthy,” Tuesday’s statement from the state Department of Health says.
Tuesday wasn’t the first time state health officials have warned residents against following the Trump administration’s health advice.
Health officials under former Gov. Phil Murphy urged parents in December to ignore the Centers for Disease Control when it reversed its decades-long recommendation that all newborns get hepatitis B vaccines at birth to protect Americans from the incurable liver disease. State lawmakers also passed a law in January meant to bolster the state’s vaccine recommendations and ensure insurance coverage.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas launches universal application portal for state colleges and universities
description: The Arkansas Department of Education launched a universal application system Tuesday for colleges and universities in the state. The portal launched a little over a year after Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders signed the Arkansas ACCESS Act, which directed the department to create a “uniform application” for college admissions in the state. Thirty-four public univ[...]
text:
Education Secretary Jacob Oliva speaks at a press conference on Feb. 14, 2025 as Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders listens. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)The Arkansas Department of Education launched a universal application system Tuesday for colleges and universities in the state.
The portal launched a little over a year after Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders signed the Arkansas ACCESS Act, which directed the department to create a “uniform application” for college admissions in the state.
Thirty-four public universities and colleges, and eight private schools, are currently accepting applications submitted through the ACCESS Portal, according to its website. The portal will communicate provisional admissions decisions to the students, as well as financial aid information.
The portal is currently available to enrolled public and charter school students applying for admission for the 2027-2028 academic year. Students attending private schools can begin using the portal when applying for the 2028-2029 academic year, with home schooled students and GED recipients gaining access the year after that.
Students can apply to up to five participating schools at no cost through the ACCESS portal. The portal will also “automatically populate” transcripts, grade point averages and test data for applying students.
“The Arkansas ACCESS Portal takes what used to be a confusing, repetitive college application process that would overwhelm students and families and streamlines it into a simple process,” Arkansas Secretary of Education Jacob Oliva said in the release.
The Arkansas ACCESS Act introduced several changes to higher education. The measure overhauled how higher education is funded, including a return-on-investment metric. Through rules created by the state’s Division of Higher Education, the metric links state funding for schools to factors like whether the schools have success in serving underrepresented students, and whether the credentials awarded to students are “aligned with state economic and workforce needs.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma Secretary of State arrested for public intoxication
description: OKLAHOMA CITY –The Governor’s Office would not say Tuesday whether Oklahoma’s secretary of state will remain on the job following an arrest for public intoxication. Gov. Kevin Stitt’s office did not respond to a request for comment regarding the Friday arrest of Secretary of State Benjamin M. Lepak, who Stitt appointed to the post in […]
text:
Oklahoma Secretary of State's Office is pictured on July 21, 2026. (Photo by Janelle Stecklein/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY –The Governor’s Office would not say Tuesday whether Oklahoma’s secretary of state will remain on the job following an arrest for public intoxication.
Gov. Kevin Stitt’s office did not respond to a request for comment regarding the Friday arrest of Secretary of State Benjamin M. Lepak, who Stitt appointed to the post in October. 
Lepak, 42, of Edmond, was arrested Friday on a municipal charge of public intoxication after Edmond police said they encountered him at about 10:45 p.m. on foot outside the drive-through window of a McDonald’s, according to a police report.
Benjamin Lepak (Photo provided by the Edmond Police Department)
An officer wrote in his report that Lepak had “extremely slurred speech” and could smell alcohol on his breath, according to the police report.
Lepak seemed to struggle to remove his identification from his wallet, the report said.
Lepak told officers he had driven to the McDonald’s, but later said he had not, according to the police report. His car was parked at the  restaurant, the report said.
Lepak said he had been to a church event earlier. He said he had consumed less than one beer after telling police he had consumed no alcohol and offered to get an Uber home, the report said.
He told officers that he had been eating healthy, and it was his night to get McDonald’s, the police report said.
“Based on Lepak’s extremely slurred speech, the odor of alcoholic beverage coming from his breath, and his inability to maintain a coherent train of thought when responding to officers’ questions,” Lepak was arrested for public intoxication and taken to the Edmond jail, according to the report.
A spokesperson for Lepak said in a statement Tuesday that he was waiting outside the McDonald’s for dinner.
“He was not given a breathalyzer test,” the spokesperson said. “Mr. Lepak will address the ticket appropriately through the legal process.”
The spokesperson did not respond to a question about his employment status.
Lepak had previously served as Stitt’s general counsel.
Typically considered Oklahoma’s top clerical official, the secretary of state is responsible for a variety of tasks, including overseeing the state’s initiative petition process, maintaining the record of legislative and executive actions and keeping a database of registered businesses.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana Republican senators endorse Garten as chamber’s next top leader
description: The question of who’ll be the next leader of the Indiana Senate is essentially decided as GOP senators are backing Sen. Chris Garten for the president pro tem position. The Senate Republican caucus announced that it had “endorsed” Garten during a private meeting Tuesday to replace current President Pro Tem Rodric Bray. Garten was the […]
text:
Sen. Chris Garten, R-Charlestown, speaks in support of the congressional redistricting bill during Senate debate on Dec. 11, 2025. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The question of who’ll be the next leader of the Indiana Senate is essentially decided as GOP senators are backing Sen. Chris Garten for the president pro tem position.
The Senate Republican caucus announced that it had “endorsed” Garten during a private meeting Tuesday to replace current President Pro Tem Rodric Bray.
Garten was the only senator to publicly announce a bid for the top Senate position after Bray said July 31 he would give up the job he’s held for eight years.
Bray’s decision followed President Donald Trump-endorsed challengers winning primaries over at least six current Republican senators who defied Trump over congressional redistricting last year.
Garten was unopposed and received unanimous support from the Republican senators, caucus spokeswoman Molly Swigart said.
Garten’s rise to president pro tem won’t be official until the full Senate votes following the November election, but the Republican caucus said he was taking over leadership of its campaign operation and planning for the 2027 legislative session.
Trump’s Indiana redistricting revenge aims to topple state Senate’s leader

Garten is a favorite of strident Trump supporters and backed the redistricting push. That split Garten from Bray and other top Senate Republicans on the issue.
“Leading this caucus is a profound honor, and my commitment to my colleagues and the people of Indiana is simple: unapologetic conservatism, decisive action and absolute transparency,” Garten said in a statement. “We have an incredible, talented team of conservative leaders ready to do the work. As we approach the upcoming budget session, we will operate in the daylight – scrutinizing every dollar, safeguarding taxpayer resources and executing a bold agenda that keeps Indiana strong, free, and prosperous.”
The president pro tem has authority to pick Senate committee chairs, direct bills to particular committees and broadly set the Senate’s agenda.
Bray made Garten his top deputy by appointing him majority floor leader in August 2022 but Garten resigned from that position in June, saying he no longer had “seamless alignment with the current strategic direction of leadership.”
Garten, of Charlestown, was first elected to the Senate in 2018. He was unopposed in the Republican primary as he is seeking reelection to a third term this year. He faces Democrat Nick Marshall and Libertarian Larry Mahaney in the fall. 
Garten previously announced he would appoint Sen. Eric Koch of Bedford as majority floor leader.
Bray says Garten will lead “with conviction”
Republicans currently hold a 40-10 Senate majority. 
Twenty-two Republican-held seats are up for election this year, with at least nine current Republican senators not returning for the 2027 session either because of retirements or primary defeats. Most of those open seats, however, are in strongly Republican districts.
Bray will continue to run the daily operations of the Senate until the formal vote for president pro tem is taken on the Legislature’s Organization Day in November, a news release said.
Bray said in the statement that he believed Garten would “lead the caucus with conviction and boldness.”
“I look forward to working with Sen. Garten to ensure a smooth transition, and I wish him well in this role,” Bray said.
Another Senate leadership contest remains
Republican senators still face a contest for the other top leadership position of majority caucus chair.
Sen. Scott Baldwin of Noblesville and Sen. Tyler Johnson of Leo have announced bids to replace Sen. Travis Holdman of Markle, who was among the current senators defeated in the May primary.
Swigart, the caucus spokeswoman, said the caucus chair election will occur after the November elections.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: AG Keith Ellison sues Texas governor for failure to extradite ICE agent charged with assault
description: Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison is suing Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, alleging that Abbott is holding up the extradition of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer charged with assault in the shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in Minneapolis on Jan. 14. The agent, Christian Castro, was arrested in Cameron County, Texas, on May 29 by […]
text:
Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison announces a lawsuit with Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty on March 24, 2026 against the Trump administration seeking evidence in the shootings of three people by federal immigration agents. (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer) Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison is suing Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, alleging that Abbott is holding up the extradition of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer charged with assault in the shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in Minneapolis on Jan. 14.
The agent, Christian Castro, was arrested in Cameron County, Texas, on May 29 by the Texas Rangers, a state law enforcement agency. He is still incarcerated in Texas. 
Castro is charged with four counts of second-degree assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime. He is accused of firing his gun through the closed front door of a Minneapolis home, hitting Cesar-Solis in the leg. Three other people were inside the house, Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said, and one of the bullets was found embedded in the wall of a child’s bedroom. 
Castro is also charged with falsely reporting a crime because he accused Sosa-Celis and another Venezuelan immigrant of assaulting him with a broom and a snow shovel before Castro opened fire. The U.S. Department of Justice charged the two immigrant men with assaulting a federal agent, but the charges were dropped after surveillance footage disproved Castro’s claims.
A federal law prohibits law enforcement agencies from detaining fugitives awaiting extradition for longer than 90 days. That means Castro could be released from custody as soon as Wednesday, Aug. 26, Ellison said. His office is asking a federal judge to compel Abbott to instruct Cameron County authorities to hand over Castro to the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehensions and to block Castro’s release if he is not extradited before the 90-day deadline.
“Christian Castro is not above the law, and Greg Abbott isn’t either,” Ellison said.
A spokesperson from Abbott’s office said the governor would not comment on pending extradition matters. 
Ellison and Moriarty, whose office charged Castro, emphasized that extradition is a routine task and a settled point of law. 
The U.S. Constitution mandates that states facilitate the extradition of people charged in other states. 
A unanimous 1987 Supreme Court ruling said “the commands of the Extradition Clause are mandatory, and afford no discretion to the executive officers or courts of the asylum state.”
Moriarty said Texas has facilitated the extradition of three defendants to Minnesota since Gov. Tim Walz sent the extradition paperwork for Castro to Abbott’s office on June 2 — only Castro’s case has been delayed during that time. 
“It is an administrative process. It is not controversial,” Moriarty said.
Texas Democrats, who hold a minority in the state Legislature, are also pushing Abbott to hand over Castro.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Appeals court allows class action lawsuit over ‘noxious’ Scott County landfill to move forward
description: The Kentucky Court of Appeals is allowing a class action lawsuit to move forward against a shuttered Scott County landfill that local residents have lodged complaints against for years over allegations of pervasive and noxious odors coming from the site.  In an Aug. 7 decision, Court of Appeals Judge Will Moynahan wrote Scott County Circuit […]
text:
A lawsuit against a Scott County landfill has stretched for years. (Stock photo by Greenleaf123/Getty Images)The Kentucky Court of Appeals is allowing a class action lawsuit to move forward against a shuttered Scott County landfill that local residents have lodged complaints against for years over allegations of pervasive and noxious odors coming from the site. 
In an Aug. 7 decision, Court of Appeals Judge Will Moynahan wrote Scott County Circuit Judge Kathryn Gabhart did not err in her ruling that a lawsuit against Waste Services of the Bluegrass met the legal requirements to be class action — meaning that the plaintiffs can represent a larger group of people in the case. 
Scott County residents brought a lawsuit against Waste Services of the Bluegrass in 2019 following years of odor complaints connected to the company’s Central Kentucky Landfill in northern Scott County. 
The Kentucky Energy and Environment Cabinet received complaints about alleged “noxious” odors on an almost daily basis when the approximately 33-acre landfill was operating, according to the July 2025 ruling by Gabhart that certified the lawsuit as class action. Complaints described the alleged odors as “sulfuric or chemical in nature” impacting people working both outside and indoors, causing physical symptoms including irritated eyes and nausea. 
The landfill stopped accepting waste in 2022 following an agreed-upon order with the cabinet, which had inspected the landfill site at least 104 times between 2017 and 2022 and had found “reported odor exceeding regulatory thresholds” on 42 occasions, according to the ruling by Moynahan. 
Attorneys for Waste Services of the Bluegrass had argued the plaintiffs’ individualized complaints against the landfill did not meet the legal requirements to be defined as class action. Attorneys for the defendant also argued that plaintiffs had asked for the lawsuit to become class action in 2024, an unreasonable delay that was years after plaintiffs filed the suit. 
Moynahan wrote that the case has “progressed slowly” but he didn’t find any fault with the years of delays. 
Attorneys for Waste Services of the Bluegrass did not respond to a Tuesday email asking if they would appeal the appeals court decision to the Kentucky Supreme Court. An attorney representing Scott County residents declined to comment on the decision.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Kentucky has a measles outbreak
description: The best protection against measles is the measles vaccination, which is generally available at pharmacies and through medical providers.
text:
Health officials urge Kentuckians to talk to their health care provider about getting the the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine.(Getty Images)Kentucky has a measles outbreak, with a total of 19 confirmed cases this year and 11 of those discovered in August alone, according to the state’s Department for Public Health. 
That’s more than any recent year, according to state data that goes back to 2019. All 19 cases from this year are in individuals who are either unvaccinated or their vaccination status is unknown, according to the state’s measles dashboard. An outbreak is defined as three or more related cases by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. 
According to the dashboard, 10 cases were discovered in Christian County. Other counties with confirmed cases are Jessamine, with four cases, Trigg County, with two, and Owen, Todd and Washington, which have (or had) one case each.
Of the 19 known cases this year:

Five are/were in children 5 years old or younger. 
Ten are/were in children between the ages of 5 and 17.  
Four are/were in people 18 years old and older. 

There have been two measles hospitalizations and no deaths this year. Measles is extremely contagious and spread through the air from coughs or sneezes, according to the CDC. One infected person can infect nine in 10 unprotected people around them. 
Symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes and a rash. The best protection against measles is the measles vaccination, which is generally available at pharmacies and through medical providers. The CDC recommends the measles vaccination series at 12-15 months and then at 4-6 years old. 
Vaccinations have declined recently even as the United States is facing an outbreak larger than any since measles “was declared eliminated in the U.S. in 2000,” the Cabinet for Health and Family Services previously said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Prado plans to turn vacant Jackson YMCA into mixed-use housing and recreation site
description: Gabriel Prado, CEO and president of PraCon Global Investment Group, speaks at a press conference in Jackson on Wednesday, April 22, 2026.
text:
The Jackson City Council has approved rezoning for the long-vacant YMCA on Fortification Street.
The council approved the rezoning from light industrial to community mixed use. The plan is to eventually approve a mixed-use housing and recreation site called Prado Conservatory according to the developer Gabriel Prado, president and CEO of PraCon Global Investment Group.
“Their vote gives us the opportunity to save a property that has been dilapidated for years and transform it into something meaningful for Jackson. Our commitment to this city is long-term, and we believe Prado Conservatory can become a signature example of what is possible when vision, persistence and private investment come together,” Prado said in a statement.
The YMCA closed in 2017 and has sat empty since. PraCon plans to convert the existing YMCA building into about 60 multifamily units and add approximately 100 more units in a new five-story building. 
The YMCA building sits along the Pearl River and PraCon said that part of the property’s appeal will be its proximity to the river, which could be revamped in the coming years thanks to a proposed flood-control lake project
For decades, Jackson Metro area officials have debated how to address flooding along the Pearl River. While indicating support for a version of the controversial project, federal officials recently said that a final environmental impact study is needed before any final decision is made about the design. Environmental groups have criticized the project saying it would destroy wildlife habitats downstream, and have also pointed to much cheaper flood control alternatives.
However, advocates of the project say that in addition to better controlling the river’s flooding, the project would open up new recreational and economic development opportunities.
“Prado Conservatory is an incredible fit along with the Pearl River Flood Control Project and the larger vision creating Jackson’s riverfront. Bringing new housing, recreation and private investment to a long-vacant property on the Pearl River creates exactly the kind of momentum that can help turn the riverfront into a destination and a catalyst for growth,” said Jeff Rent, President & CEO of the Greater Jackson Chamber Partnership
PraCon has become one of the Jackson Metro area’s most prolific developers with projects including Topgolf in Ridgeland, Prado Lofts in Jackson and a potential foray into data centers.
“Prado Conservatory is another demonstration of our confidence in Jackson and our determination to complete projects that others may have already given up on,” Prado said.

name: VTDigger
title: Parker’s career took several turns before he settled into a job that works for him and his family
description:
When a slowdown pushed him to look for his next opportunity, Parker set his sights on a Class A CDL. He completed his training at Stafford Technical Center and landed a job at Lamell Lumber in Essex within 45 minutes of walking in the door—proof, as his VSAC counselor put it, that "life often shows us possibilities if we're willing to pay attention."
Read t[...]
text:
Parker has a strong sense of purpose, and he’s remained flexible throughout his working life—a skill that has enabled him to pivot when necessary and explore opportunities when they’ve come knocking. 
After he graduated from Harwood Union Middle and High School, he attended Castleton State College (now Vermont State Castleton) to pursue a business degree. He realized that wasn’t his path and left after two semesters. He spent the next few years working at Green Mountain Coffee Roasters in his hometown of Waterbury. After a few years, he applied to Vermont Technical College (now Vermont State Randolph), where he was able to return to school full time. 
Parker graduated at 25 with an associate’s degree in mechanical engineering. Superior Technical Ceramics in Saint Albans hired him before he’d even graduated to work as a R&D material technician. For the next few years, he helped develop porous ceramic materials, ceramic armor plating, and similar mixes. 
During that time, when his mother was moving, she found a picture of a wind turbine Parker drew in second grade. It said, “green energy is the future.” For a while, Parker had been feeling like his career in ceramics wasn’t quite what he wanted. The picture was a catalyst. He decided to look for a career in green energy and joined Vermont Energy Investment Corporation (VEIC) as an energy associate. Over the years he worked his way up to metering specialist. Working on the measurement and verification side meant he was helping incentivize people to invest in more energy-efficient equipment. 
“I was proving the math on energy efficiency installations and showing that energy savings were verified,” he said. “I was there almost a decade, but like so many people was laid off when COVID hit.”  
He took a variety of farm labor and masonry jobs for the next few years, and it was during this time that he saw a new opening. He started his own company, Hobs Hauling LLC with a dump truck, backhoe, and trailer. He made a name for himself digging ponds, retention ditches, laying concrete, and doing stone and tiling. 
 “I saw a need to be a CDL licensed driver.”
During a sudden slowdown in his business, Parker saw yet another opportunity instead of a dead end. He began working toward getting his CDL license at Stafford Technical Center in West Rutland, ensuring his options were open as his business began to take a turn. 
But financing the class proved to be a challenge, especially as Parker’s business was winding down. “Most people just don’t have that kind of tuition money sitting in the bank,” he said.
Parker filled out the contact form on VSAC’s website and was connected with Martha McCaughin, an outreach counselor in VSAC’s Educational Opportunity Center (EOC). VSAC’s EOC helps adults access college and career training. He was looking for some financial aid for the class, and Martha was able to help him apply to the program and get his paperwork in order, as well as offer guidance to help Parker select a program that would support his goals. 
“I chose Stafford because they have a great reputation and because they teach manual transmission trucks,” he said. “Safety is really important to me too, and they have a reputation for graduating safe, responsible drivers.” 
Parker was ultimately awarded money to cover tuition at Stafford through VSAC’s Vermont Trades Tuition Benefit Program. “The financial aid from VSAC was what made it so I could take the class and get my Class A CDL,” he added. 
It was a tough few months. The class started in the dead of winter on Saturdays, and required Parker to leave home before sunrise and return after sunset. “I’d be there all day on Saturday, leaving at 5am to drive the two hours to Rutland, where I’d be in class until 4:30pm, and then would need to drive the 2 hours home,” he said. Luckily, it was only four months, and he had his Class A CDL by April. 
Making the transition to driving 
While at Lamell Lumber in Essex one day to pick up material for a job, he noticed the trucks in the yard that the business uses to haul wood chips, sawdust, and other materials. 
Parker saw the opportunity and decided to pursue it. “I actually went in and asked them for a job on the spot. I filled out an application and they hired me within 45 minutes. I started the next Monday.”
He’s been working for Lamell Lumber for over a year now. And, he and his wife, Claire, a preschool teacher, welcomed a son earlier this year. 
When Parker reflects on the turns his career has taken, he expresses gratitude for the opportunities he’s had that led him to where he is today. And, he’s grateful for Martha. “Bless her, what a wonderful person,” he said. 
For her part, Martha shared that what she loves about Parker’s story is his curiosity and tenacity. “He paid attention, got an idea how to make himself more employable and then got the training he needed,” she said. “Life often shows us possibilities if we’re willing to pay attention.” 

The Vermont Student Assistance Corp. was created by the Vermont Legislature in 1965 as a public nonprofit agency. We advocate for Vermont students and their families to ensure that they have the tools they need to achieve their education and training goals. We create opportunities for all Vermont students, but particularly for those—of any age—who believe that the doors to education are closed to them. Growing families save for education with VT529, Vermont’s official 529 savings program. To help Vermonters plan and pay for college or job training, our counselors work with students in nearly every Vermont middle school and high school, and are also available to work with adults. Our grant, scholarship, and workforce development programs create opportunity, help students re-skill or learn new skills, and grow the economy. VSAC’s loan, loan refinance, and loan forgiveness programs provide competitive education financing to students and families. Find us at www.vsac.org or visit Facebook, Instagram, or LinkedIn.
