name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Another year, same ranking: Utah still last for women’s equality
description: For the 12th consecutive year, Utah has been ranked as the worst state in the nation for women’s equality. Each August, WalletHub releases its “Best & Worst States for Women’s Equality” report, and every year I’m asked whether Utah’s last‑place ranking is a surprise. It isn’t. At the Utah Women & Leadership Project (UWLP), we […]
text:
The Capitol and downtown Salt Lake City are pictured at dusk on Monday, Nov. 10, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)For the 12th consecutive year, Utah has been ranked as the worst state in the nation for women’s equality. Each August, WalletHub releases its “Best & Worst States for Women’s Equality” report, and every year I’m asked whether Utah’s last‑place ranking is a surprise. It isn’t. At the Utah Women & Leadership Project (UWLP), we have tracked these metrics for more than a decade, and in 2021 we published an extensive analysis explaining why Utah ranks last and what can be done to change it.
WalletHub’s 2026 analysis again highlights how uneven women’s equality remains across the country. Hawaii, Maryland, Alaska, Maine, and Vermont lead the nation with strong performance across workplace, education, health, and political empowerment metrics. These states have significantly narrowed gaps in pay, leadership representation, unemployment, educational attainment, and political participation. Their scores — ranging from 69 to nearly 78 out of 100 — demonstrate what is possible when states prioritize gender equity across multiple systems. At the other end of the spectrum, Utah once again ranks 50th, with a total score of just 32.18. We fall far behind states like Texas, Oklahoma, and Idaho. The contrast between the top and bottom states underscores the urgency of addressing structural barriers that continue to limit women’s opportunities and outcomes.
WalletHub’s index draws on national datasets like the U.S. Census Bureau, Bureau of Labor Statistics, Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, so the numbers typically lag by a year or two. Even so, the pattern is unmistakable. Utah’s scores have fluctuated over the past five years, but the state has remained firmly in last place. And while WalletHub’s metrics do not capture every dimension of women’s experiences, they align closely with the extensive research conducted by UWLP and our partners.
WalletHub groups its findings into three main categories — workplace environment, education and health, and political empowerment — using 17 weighted indicators. With a total of 100 possible points, Utah has consistently remained at the bottom: 29.85 points in 2021, 31.22 in 2022, 19.43 in 2023, 23.04 in 2024, 29.93 in 2025, and now 32.18 in 2026. The gap between Utah and the next lowest state has varied over time: 7.52 points behind Idaho in 2021; 12.77 behind Georgia in 2022; 22.11 behind Texas in 2023; 16.71 behind Texas in 2024; 11.96 behind Texas in 2025; and now 8.76 behind Texas in 2026. Even with slight improvements, Utah remains significantly behind.
I was able to get more in-depth data from WalletHub than was published in their recent report. Let me share what I found.
Workplace Environment
Utah currently ranks 47th in the “Workplace Environment” category (we were 50th in both 2024 and 2025), which is worth 40 of the 100 points. Below are the rankings (1 = best, 50 = worst):

Income Disparity: 2024=50, 2025=49, 2026=50
Higher-Income Disparity: 2024=50, 2025=50, 2026=50
Disparity in Share of Executive Positions: 2024=48, 2025=47, 2026=48
Disparity in Share of Minimum-Wage Workers: 2024=1, 2025=1, 2026=1
Unemployment-Rate Disparity: 2024=43, 2025=49; 2026=1
Entrepreneurship-Rate Disparity: 2024=34, 2025=41; 2026=42
Disparity in Average Number of Work Hours: 2024=50, 2025=50; 2026=50
Job Security Disparity: 2024=50, 2025=1; 2026=1
Economic Security Disparity: 2024=3, 2025=3; 2026=3
Disparity in Poverty Rate: 2024=5, 2025=3; 2026=4

The most concerning areas include income disparity (gender pay gap), higher‑income disparity, and executive position disparity. Our rankings also drop when other states make progress.
Education & Health
Utah ranks 50th in “Education & Health” (40 points), a position we have held for many years. This category includes:

Disparity in Advanced Educational Attainment: 2024=50, 2025=50, 2026=50
Disparity in Math Test Scores: 2024=50, 2025=33, 2026=33
Disparity in Doctor-Visit Affordability: 2024=37, 2025=41, 2026=39

Although I’m concerned about all of these, I hope the progress seen in math test score disparity is not just a temporary blip. Even so, girls remain significantly lower than boys on math scores compared to other states.
Political Empowerment
Utah now ranks 29th in “Political Empowerment” (20 points), reflecting some recent improvements. We were 41st in 2024 and 28th in 2025:

Disparity in Share of Lawmakers in the U.S. Senate: 2024=22, 2025=22, 2026=23
Disparity in Share of Lawmakers in U.S. House of Representatives: 2024=23, 2025=23, and 2026=23
Disparity in Share of Lawmakers in State Legislature: 2024=39, 2025=32, 2026=30
Disparity in Share of State-Elected Executives: 2024=38, 2025=15, 2026=16

Research continues to show that women in political office are more likely to advocate for public policies around education, health, poverty, and family issues. Things change when there are more equal percentages of men and women serving in elected office at all levels.
The value of these rankings is not in the number itself, but in what they reveal about where Utah must focus its efforts. They align closely with the research UWLP and our partners have tracked for years: progress requires intentional, statewide action. The good news is that Utah has the talent, commitment, and collaborative spirit to change these numbers. When we invest in women and girls, we strengthen every part of our state. Now is the time for all Utahns to help build a future where equality is not an aspiration but a reality.

name: VTDigger
title: Time limits on teacher licensing tests measure the wrong thing
description:
A five-point miss on a timed exam nearly ended a decades-long teaching career — until extra time told a different story.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Time limits on teacher licensing tests measure the wrong thing.
text:
This commentary is by Ben Mitchell, a reading interventionist at Riverside Middle School in Springfield and the publisher of Divergents Magazine.
In January I found myself at my computer, watching a digital clock aggressively count down the seconds. As a reading teacher in a Vermont public middle school, I love my job; this work challenges me to be my very best. Nevertheless, because I am on a provisional license, my entire career hinges on a number. Vermont requires a score of 164 on the Middle School English Praxis exam to be a candidate for licensure. That winter day, I scored a 159.
According to the remote workers who score the tests, I was five points short of being qualified to do the job I was already doing every day. The problem wasn’t my knowledge. After nearly 40 years of teaching, I know the material inside and out. The problem was that I ran out of time on each section. My brain processes information differently: I have dyslexia and ADHD, so under the frantic sprint of a strict time limit, my executive function faltered. Determined to stay in my classroom, I used the official Praxis appeal process. I was denied. I appealed again. Denied a second time. They wanted me to get $3,000 worth of testing just to secure a basic accommodation: 50% more time.
In July I took the same exam — new questions, same standards — with that extra time. The result? I scored a 171. When given the space to breathe and actually demonstrate what I know, I passed the 164 mark easily. The only variable that changed was the clock. My story is proof of a systemic flaw: Time limits on professional licensing exams do not measure competence. They measure processing speed, anxiety management and privilege. It is time to eliminate them entirely.
Professional licensing should ensure subject-matter expertise, whether for the classroom or the courtroom. It should not just be some kind of appreciation circle for the fast processors. Time-limited testing rests on the flawed assumption that speed equals mastery. In the real world, a professional’s effectiveness is rarely measured by a stopwatch. In reading instruction, decoding, student engagement and perseverance take time and patience; they cannot be rushed. No actual educational scenario requires a teacher to answer dozens of complex pedagogical questions in a frantic, high-pressure sprint. Instead of evaluating true competence, strict time limits simply measure how quickly a person can regurgitate information.
For professionals with ADHD, dyslexia or other processing differences, these timed tests act as a barrier to entry rather than a metric of quality control. Capable, passionate individuals are systematically locked out of professional careers due to these rigid, arbitrary structures. To make matters worse, forcing candidates through grueling bureaucratic appeal processes just to secure basic accommodations is exhausting and becomes an exclusionary barrier. The systemic absurdity is clear: Any framework that labels a teacher “unqualified” in January and “highly qualified” in July simply because they were granted a time extension is fundamentally broken.

READ MORE

To build a just and effective educational system, evaluations should focus on what a candidate knows, not how fast they can click a mouse. Allowing everyone to finish the test is a fundamental principle of universal design and widely considered best practice in contemporary education theory. Eliminating time constraints standardizes equity, allowing all candidates to demonstrate their true capabilities without having to jump through bureaucratic hoops. Testers can still record how long an individual takes to complete the assessment, allowing timeliness to be considered by employers.
I ask the state of Vermont to pass a law banning time limits for professional testing. Removing these artificial bottlenecks will not only promote equity in the workplace but also help qualified, dedicated individuals enter critical fields like education, resolving labor shortages in areas where talent is needed.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: ‘Smack dab in the middle:’ Kansas candidates for U.S. Senate stake out ground for general election
description: TOPEKA — From Lebanon, Kansas, the geographic center of the contiguous United States, the Rev. Adam Hamilton began his general election campaign for U.S. Senate. Before launching on Tuesday his debut general election ad, Hamilton visited Lebanon, a physical embodiment of a campaign that hinges on “meeting in the middle.” “Here in Kansas, we’re right […]
text:
The Rev. Adam Hamilton, pastor of the largest United Methodist Church in the country, announces his candidacy for U.S. Senate on April 30, 2026, in Prairie Village. The Democrat faces incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — From Lebanon, Kansas, the geographic center of the contiguous United States, the Rev. Adam Hamilton began his general election campaign for U.S. Senate.
Before launching on Tuesday his debut general election ad, Hamilton visited Lebanon, a physical embodiment of a campaign that hinges on “meeting in the middle.”
“Here in Kansas, we’re right smack dab in the middle of the country,” Hamilton says in the ad, which is scheduled to appear on TV markets in Wichita and Topeka. “The West Coast about 1,600 miles that way. The East Coast 1,100 miles that way. I’m Adam Hamilton, and here in Kansas, we’re proud of being in the middle politically, too. That puts us about a million miles away from the extreme politics of Washington that are tearing us apart and driving up prices.”
Hamilton, a Democrat and United Methodist pastor, will compete against Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall in November, and until then, healthcare, the rising cost of living and the president are expected to be major issues on the campaign trail. While Hamilton is aiming for the middle, Marshall is firmly positioned on the right.
Hamilton’s ad is the first individual campaign ad of the race for the general election, but outside groups waded into the Kansas ad market following the Aug. 4 primary.
On Marshall’s behalf, political action committees the Main Street Fund and Main Street Defense Fund have aired ads touting his “pro-farmer” record and ties to Trump. Another classified Hamilton as a “woke megachurch pastor,” with clips from old sermons.
“They take little pieces of sermons — so I’ve got 30 years of sermons out there, 36 years — take little pieces of them, sew them together, and try to make me say things I didn’t say, which is by itself sad and tragic,” Hamilton said during a press call Monday.
Glynnis Harvey, a spokesperson for Hamilton’s campaign, said he will be a “different kind of leader” than Marshall.
“Kansas is smack dab in the middle of the country, and so are the voters here,”she said.
U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) criticized Hamilton’s theology on the social media platform X.
“Why do Democrats keep nominating ‘preachers’ who reject the central tenets of Christianity?” Cruz wrote. 
In response, Marshall thanked Cruz for “bringing this up.”
“This is only one of hundreds of examples. … Wait until you hear about the ‘hundreds of mistakes in the Bible’ my opponent claims to have found,” Marshall wrote.

title: Bureau of Elections report recommends against approving citizens-only voting measure for the ballot
description: A proposed amendment to the Michigan state constitution requiring residents to prove their citizenship when voting may not make the ballot, with the Michigan Bureau of Elections issuing a report determining it may not have submitted enough valid signatures. While Americans for Citizen Voting – Michigan submitted 709,841 signatures on its petitions, well over[...]
text:
Kurt O'Keefe, one of the organizers behind Americans for Citizen Voting Michigan, a ballot committee dedicated to enacting voter ID and citizen-only voting in Michigan, lords over several boxes of petition signature sheets as the group prepares to deliver them to the Michigan Department of State. The group said it collected more than 750,000 signatures, which still need to be reviewed for validity by the state's Bureau of Elections. March 4, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan AdvanceA proposed amendment to the Michigan state constitution requiring residents to prove their citizenship when voting may not make the ballot, with the Michigan Bureau of Elections issuing a report determining it may not have submitted enough valid signatures.
While Americans for Citizen Voting – Michigan submitted 709,841 signatures on its petitions, well over the 446,198 needed to make the ballot, the Bureau of Elections estimates only 434,423 signatures are valid after reviewing a random sample of 1,000 signatures.
After considering a challenge to the signatures filed by Promote the Vote Action and attorney Bob Labrant, former general counsel to the Michigan Chamber of Commerce, the Bureau of Elections determined that 612 of the signatures were valid.
The bureau advises against certifying the petition if a review of the sample returns 628 or fewer valid signatures.
 The Board of State Canvassers will meet on Aug. 24, where the bipartisan, four-member board will determine whether the petition is sufficient, though canvassers typically follow the bureau’s recommendation.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The measure would require residents to show a photo identification before casting their ballot and establish new voter roll verifications, requiring the Secretary of State to review the rolls and remove any noncitizens. It would also add language to the state constitution noting that only U.S. citizens can vote in local, state and federal elections.
In a statement, the initiatives’ organizers criticized the bureau’s findings, calling on the Board to let voters have the final say on their proposal. 
“Our petitions were submitted more than four months before the deadline, yet here we are at the last minute being told they should not be certified,” said Kurt O’Keefe, the initiative’s treasurer. “We spent months reviewing these petitions, removing duplicates and discarding signatures we believed might not comply with Michigan law. We are confident we submitted significantly more than the 446,198 valid signatures required.”
However, Promote the Vote Action, which has argued the citizens-only voting proposal would create additional barriers that could keep some citizens from casting their ballot, celebrated the bureau’s findings. 
“The attacks on Michiganders’ access to the ballot are far from over, but today we celebrate that one of them has stalled,” Promote the Vote Executive Director Micheal Davis Jr. said.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Mazzei, Drummond talk campaign spending, endorsements ahead of Oklahoma runoff
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – As the Aug. 25 primary runoff approaches, the top Republican gubernatorial candidates are engaged in a war of words over campaign funding and a presidential endorsement. Rancher and attorney Gentner Drummond, the state’s Attorney General, is hoping his Hominy upbringing and military service will appeal to enough Republican rural voters to put[...]
text:
Oklahoma State Capitol Building (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – As the Aug. 25 primary runoff approaches, the top Republican gubernatorial candidates are engaged in a war of words over campaign funding and a presidential endorsement.
Rancher and attorney Gentner Drummond, the state’s Attorney General, is hoping his Hominy upbringing and military service will appeal to enough Republican rural voters to put him on top.
He faces former state senator Mike Mazzei, a Tulsa financial planner who garnered the coveted endorsement of President Donald Trump, a man who took all of the state’s 77 counties.
Mazzei is hoping that endorsement will help him win the election.
Both men were the top vote getters in the June GOP primary and advanced to a runoff, which typically has low turnout.
Recent polling indicates the men are in dead heat just days before the election. 
Primary spending, meanwhile, has reached historic levels.
Mike Mazzei addresses his supporters on Tuesday, June 16, 2026, during Mazzei’s watch party in Bixby, Okla. Supporters gathered to watch results in the Republican primary election.(Photo by Ace Cuervo/Oklahoma Voice)
Mazzei had loaned himself  about $11.6 million dollars, a record amount for an Oklahoma gubernatorial candidate, according to state ethics commission records. Drummond has loaned himself $3 million, according to the most recent campaign finance reports.
The Oklahoman in June reported that Mazzei put his business assets up as collateral.
In an interview with Oklahoma Voice, Drummond said there should be a restriction on how much candidates can loan themselves because it prevents qualified, but non-independently wealthy candidates from getting into the race.
“We have well-qualified men and women out there that just simply can’t afford to run, or they run, and when you have to put in more money  to be competitive, they don’t have the ability to, therefore, they drop out,” Drummond said.
Mazzei, though, told Oklahoma Voice that he views his loans as a “good investment” in Oklahoma that would result in more prosperity if he is elected by increasing literacy rates and changing tax policy.
“My wife and I decided it was a good investment,” Mazzei said.
Though Mazzei said he didn’t know if he could raise enough money from donors to retire the debt, he does not believe there should be limits on loans. He said that campaign spending is a free speech issue.
Trump’s endorsement
Trump’s endorsement of Mazzei has shaken up the race and given Mazzei a boost at the polls.
Drummond said he believes if Trump hadn’t endorsed Mazzei, his opponent would not have made it out of the primary.
Gentner Drummond visit with guests on Tuesday, June 16, 2026, during Drummond’s watch party at VFW Post 577 in Tulsa, Okla. Supporters gathered to watch results in the Republican primary election. (Photo by Ace Cuervo/For Oklahoma Voice)
He said Trump’s endorsement ahead of Oklahoma’s June primary cut the legs off fellow Republican contenders Charles McCall, a former House speaker, and businessman Chip Keating, because they both put all their cards on the Make America Great Again movement.
But while Mazzei might have gotten the Trump endorsement, Drummond said he’s secured support from Oklahomans.
“I think that carries a lot of weight,” Dummond said. “Now, to the uninformed that sit in their La-Z-Boy with a six-pack of beer, I think the president is very powerful.”
Drummond said he believes Mazzei obtained the endorsement because he employed a Trump adviser and friend on his campaign team.
Mazzei disputes that.
“Everybody and their brother knows that Donald Trump makes his own decisions and billionaire Donald Trump doesn’t give a whiff about a few thousand dollars from any of his, you know, contacts,” Mazzei said.
Drummond never had a shot at a Trump endorsement, Mazzei said.
He said his economic plan aligns more with Trump’s.
Early voting begins Thursday. Polls open at 7 a.m. and close at 7 p.m. on Aug. 25.

description:

text:
Born: 08/28/1952
Pittsford, Vermont
Died: 08/09/2026
Columbus, Ohio
Details of service:

Michael Burditt Cadwell, son of John and Mary Cadwell, died peacefully on August 9, 2026 after along illness. Michael enjoyed an idyllic childhood on the family farm in Pittsford and attended Otter Valley Union High School ’70, Williams College ’74, and the Yale School of Architecture ’81. He then worked for the firms of Turner Brooks, Cesar Pelli, and Wiemann and Lamphere.
There followed scholarly pursuits in architecture at The Ohio State University, where he spent 31 years, eventually becoming Director of the Knowlton School of Architecture, Landscape Architecture, and Planning before retiring in 2020. Michael published widely, most notably with his books Small Buildings and Strange Details. He was awarded Fellow of the American Institute of Architecture, and fellowships to the American Academy in Rome, the MacDowell Arts Colony, and the Woodstock Art Colony.
Throughout he was lovingly supported by his wife Jane Murphy, his son Gus Murphy, his dog Manny and his brothers Ashley, Steven, Jared, Alden, and Jason and their families.
Michael was blessed with a full and rich life, manifested in a unique combination of low comedy and high endeavor. He enjoyed guitar playing, skiing, soccer, and triathlon. Most of all, he enjoyed time with Jane and Gus and his extended family at gatherings in Maine and Vermont. There was love and laughter.
In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to the Pittsford Village Farm at https://www.pittsfordvillagefarm.org/donate or The Michael B. Cadwell Endowed Scholarship Fund – Fund # 483652. https://giveto.osu.edu/makeagift/details/483652

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Jolly promises campaign $ will come in after the primary, but says he can win despite being outspent
description: TAMPA — David Jolly likes his chances of becoming the first Democrat to win the governor’s race in Florida in more than three decades this November. You read that correctly. The 53-year-old former GOP Congressman and MSNBC pundit’s confidence appears off the charts even though there are 1.5 million more registered Republicans than Democrats in […]
text:
Florida Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly speaking in Ybor City in Tampa on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)TAMPA — David Jolly likes his chances of becoming the first Democrat to win the governor’s race in Florida in more than three decades this November.
You read that correctly. The 53-year-old former GOP Congressman and MSNBC pundit’s confidence appears off the charts even though there are 1.5 million more registered Republicans than Democrats in the state; he is being outspent by likely GOP gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds by 10:1; and no Democrat has won anything at the state level since 2018.
According to Jolly, in this election year money doesn’t buy popularity.
“We need resources to reach the mark. I don’t want to be naive about that,” he said on Monday night after finishing a primary election eve rally in Tampa. “But this is a cycle where you can get outspent 10:1 and still win. Now I will tell you I think that you’re going to see money come in.”
Jolly and Democrats believe that while Donald Trump’s endorsement for Donalds last year meant everything for his success in Tuesday’s primary, it could prove to be an albatross around his neck in the general, as the president’s approval ratings are now at an all-time low nationally.
“Byron Donalds has spent more than $50 million dollars and his number are getting worse. His numbers are getting worse!” he thundered to a crowd estimated at around 300 people in a cavernous outdoor patio space in Tampa’s Ybor City entertainment district Monday night.
“There’s this thing in politics,” he continued. “There are some candidates that the more you see of them, the more you learn about them, the less you like them. Think about Ron DeSantis in Iowa, folks.”
Campaign finance records show Donalds has spent a combined total of $55.8 million through his regular campaign and political committee since entering the race in February 2025, blowing away the entire field of candidates who have entered both the Republican and Democratic races for governor this year. Jolly has raised around $10 million overall, and has less than $4 million cash-on-hand right now.
The assertion that Donalds’ poll ratings are tanking isn’t backed up by the data (as questionable as they might be these days). Donalds has a nearly 32-point lead over his closest opponent in Tuesday’s GOP primary, according to an average of polls by RealClearPolitics. A polling average compiled by the election website 270 to win has Donalds up by six points over Jolly in a general election matchup, 45.5%-39.5%.
In addition to former Hillsborough County State Attorney Andrew Warren, the only elected official who took the stage before Jolly’s entrance was Hillsborough County state Sen. Brian Nathan. Nathan defeated a Republican who vastly outspent him in a district won by the previous Republican by nearly 10 points in 2022, winning support from Republicans and non-party-affiliated voters. Jolly has been explicit that the only way he can win in November is by duplicating Nathan’s winning formula.
Attacking trans people
Donalds began airing an ad hitting Jolly on transgender rights last week — a particularly potent issue for Republicans and specifically Donald Trump over Kamala Harris in 2024.
Jolly has previously announced for support for transgender youths’ access to medical care and participation in sports.
“I think what Byron Donalds is doing across the state right now is ugly,” Jolly said of Donalds’ focus. “It’s downright mean and it’s ugly, dividing people based on who they love.”
“Punching down on marginalized communities has never lowered your insurance bill … has never improved education … has never delivered affordable healthcare,” he said.
Jolly has previously addressed Donalds’ criticism of transgender rights by arguing Floridians can’t afford to be distracted by “culture wars” rather than addressing the affordability crisis. He told reporters after his speech Monday night that he remains an “old-school Republican who thinks that government should stay out of your lives, should stay out of your doctor’s offices, stay out of your bedroom. Respect your medical privacy.”
He went on to say, “I do think that local communities know how to set the rules for their sports leagues. I’m not going to try to change the current law. I’m going to leave that to the courts.”
Florida has attempted to ban access to medically necessary gender care for minors and limit access for adults. Although a federal court temporarily enjoined the ban, a federal appeals court lifted the stay while it considers arguments. The ban remains in effect as the court deliberates.
Jolly took aim at Donalds in his speech for some of the big-money donors who have contributed to his campaign. That includes dozens of contributions from artificial intelligence groups and donors as well as from companies hoping to build data centers, as reported by POLITICO.
“Byron Donalds has been bought by every special interest in the state,” he said. “Data centers in your neighborhood. Utility companies spiking your rates. For-profit schools. Defunding your local schools. Byron Donalds profits off of all of that. And you know what the difference between me and Byron Donalds is? He will sell you out for a buck as your next governor and I’m going to be there fighting for you.”
Jolly will host his election night watch party in Miami Lakes Tuesday. He intends, he said, to spend a few days there this week preparing for the general election before making a tour of most of the major media markets across the state.

name: Delaware
title: Human trafficking summit aims to turn awareness into action
description: Delaware’s inaugural statewide summit will bring survivors, national experts, professionals and concerned citizens together to improve prevention, identification and survivor support. By George Rotsch, Editor of Delaware LIVE DEWEY BEACH — Human trafficking can remain hidden in plain sight, leaving teachers, medical professionals, police officers, business l[...]
text:
The Delaware Coalition for Human Trafficking Survivors hopes to close those knowledge and coordination gaps through Delaware’s inaugural Human Trafficking Awareness, Prevention and Action Summit on Friday, Oct. 2, at Hyatt Place Dewey Beach.
Delaware’s inaugural statewide summit will bring survivors, national experts, professionals and concerned citizens together to improve prevention, identification and survivor support.
By George Rotsch, Editor of Delaware LIVE

DEWEY BEACH — Human trafficking can remain hidden in plain sight, leaving teachers, medical professionals, police officers, business leaders and concerned residents uncertain about how to recognize the warning signs or respond safely.
The Delaware Coalition for Human Trafficking Survivors hopes to close those knowledge and coordination gaps through Delaware’s inaugural Human Trafficking Awareness, Prevention and Action Summit on Friday, Oct. 2, at Hyatt Place Dewey Beach.
The summit is open to professionals, organizational leaders and members of the public who want to better understand human trafficking and help Delaware build a more informed and coordinated response.
“It’s for everybody,” said Jennifer Cooper, the coalition’s Community and Continuing Education Committee chair and one of the summit’s organizers. “It’s not just for people doing the work. It’s for people who may want to learn a little bit more.”
Cooper, a registered nurse and forensic coordinator at Nemours Children’s Health, said the program will explain trafficking, challenge common misconceptions and help participants understand how exploitation occurs in Delaware.
“We’re going to break down the myths, dispel the myths and talk about what trafficking looks like in Delaware,” Cooper said.
Public engagement is part of the response
Marcia Ferranto, board chair of the Delaware Coalition for Human Trafficking Survivors, said public involvement is essential because human trafficking cannot be addressed solely by law enforcement agencies or organizations serving survivors.
“Human trafficking affects Delaware communities, but too often it remains unseen or misunderstood,” Ferranto said. “We need residents, business leaders, educators, health care professionals, faith communities and policymakers to understand the warning signs and recognize that each of them can play a role in prevention.”
Ferranto said trafficking affects Delaware even when victims are not immediately identified and cases are not publicly described as trafficking.
“Trafficking does not happen only somewhere else; it is affecting people here in Delaware,” Ferranto said. “When the public understands what exploitation looks like and knows how to respond, we become better able to protect vulnerable people, support survivors and make Delaware a much more difficult place for traffickers to operate.”
Delaware needs its own summit
Cooper has worked with the forensic team at Nemours since 2012 and became its coordinator in 2019. Through that work, she began seeing more young patients affected by or vulnerable to exploitation.
Her involvement in Delaware’s anti-trafficking efforts also showed her that professionals frequently had to travel outside the state to receive advanced training.
“I went to a lot of conferences, and I realized that I wasn’t going to anything in Delaware,” Cooper said. “I was traveling. And I said, ‘Delaware needs its own.’”
That realization helped lead to the October summit.
National experts and local authorities are expected to participate as keynote speakers, panel moderators and breakout-session presenters. The program will include learning tracks focused on survivors, law enforcement, mental health, direct-service workers and medical providers.
Continuing education credits for eligible medical and other professionals are planned, with additional details to be announced.
Bringing Delaware’s response together
Cooper said the summit has two immediate goals: raising awareness among leaders and bringing together the professionals and organizations already working with vulnerable people and survivors.
“I want to bring together the people who are doing the work,” Cooper said. “There are organizations doing phenomenal work, and right down the street there may be another organization doing something a little differently. They really could benefit from each other.”
Better coordination could help Delaware identify trends, determine where services are missing and direct resources toward needs involving young people, labor trafficking, health care, housing and other areas.
“By bringing all of the people together, we can see what our trends are in Delaware and where we need more services,” Cooper said.
The summit also is intended to support professionals engaged in emotionally demanding work.
“From a trauma perspective, this is very challenging and very tough work,” Cooper said. “Making sure that everybody has their own resources and people to bounce things off of is really important.”
A private executive roundtable will precede the public summit Thursday, Oct. 1. Attendance at the roundtable is by invitation only.
The roundtable is expected to bring Delaware leaders and decision-makers together to review state-level information and consider potential policy, training and legislative responses. The public summit the following day will focus on education, professional development and building connections among participants.
A problem that can be difficult to identify
Cooper said one of the challenges involving young people is that victims may not identify themselves as having been trafficked. They may believe they willingly participated in an exchange or may not recognize food, housing, drugs, alcohol or other items of value as part of commercial sexual exploitation.
Under federal and state law, proof of force, fraud or coercion is not required when a minor is induced to perform a commercial sex act. A commercial exchange also does not have to involve cash.
Cooper said 80 juvenile cases were referred to Delaware’s Juvenile Trafficking Oversight Team last year. Those cases involved young people identified as being at risk of trafficking, suspected of being trafficked or confirmed as victims.
The National Human Trafficking Hotline has identified 301 trafficking cases involving 662 victims in Delaware since 2007. The hotline received 51 signals from Delaware in 2024, including eight from victims or survivors.
Hotline figures reflect only situations reported to the organization and should not be interpreted as representing the full extent of trafficking in the state.
Survivors and experts lead the program
Opening keynote speaker Kevin McNeil is a retired police officer, trafficking and sexual-abuse survivor and motivational speaker. His presentation, “Stuck in Traffic,” will compare the experience of being trapped in vehicle traffic with the sense of being trapped in exploitation.
Marty MacGibbon, a trafficking survivor, therapist, author and comedian, will discuss the intersection of human trafficking and substance abuse. She also will close the program with a presentation addressing mental wellness, self-care and trauma-informed practices.
Breakout sessions will address trafficking fundamentals, myths and realities; care for survivors; familial trafficking; legal and law enforcement considerations; trauma among children and adults; and the development of multidisciplinary response teams.
The program also will include survivor perspectives and discussion of vulnerabilities affecting boys and members of the LGBTQ community.
Why leaders and residents should attend
For leaders in government, health care, education, law enforcement, hospitality, nonprofits and other community institutions, the summit offers an opportunity to examine whether their organizations have adequate training, policies and referral relationships.
Front-line professionals can learn more about recognizing possible exploitation, interacting with survivors without causing additional trauma and coordinating with other service providers.
For parents, faith leaders, volunteers and concerned residents, the summit offers a clearer understanding of what trafficking can look like, which warning signs deserve attention and how to report concerns without placing a potential victim at greater risk.
Established in 2014 as Meet Me at the Well Delaware, the Delaware Coalition for Human Trafficking Survivors provides individualized assistance to survivors seeking to leave sex trafficking and rebuild their lives. Its work includes education, street outreach, advocacy, mentoring and connections to housing, employment and treatment resources.
The larger objective of the summit is to create a more unified statewide response capable of recognizing exploitation sooner, supporting survivors more effectively and making Delaware a more difficult place for traffickers to operate.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Union members, activists defiant in the face of federal surveillance
description: Unions, progressive organizations and churches that were the subjects of a wide-ranging surveillance operation by the Department of Homeland Security are presenting a unified message: We will not be intimidated. The leaders spoke at a press conference Tuesday morning alongside three of the 15 people indicted in an alleged conspiracy to impede or assault fede[...]
text:
Gabriel Van de Water Davis, one of the 15 people federally indicted for conspiracy to impede or injure federal officers, talks to Unidos executive director Emilia González Avalos after speaking during a press conference condemning federal surveillance Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Unions, progressive organizations and churches that were the subjects of a wide-ranging surveillance operation by the Department of Homeland Security are presenting a unified message: We will not be intimidated.
The leaders spoke at a press conference Tuesday morning alongside three of the 15 people indicted in an alleged conspiracy to impede or assault federal agents. 
“The (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) and Border Patrol agents who murdered Renee Good and Alex Pretti have been hidden away and protected, while DHS turns its attention towards spying on union members, civil rights organizations, churches and individuals who stood up for their community in whatever ways they were able,” said Gabriel Van De Water, an artist and community organizer who was among the 15 people indicted in June.
As part of its surveillance operation during Operation Metro Surge, Homeland Security agents secretly obtained financial records from organizations, including the labor unions Service Employees International Union and Communications Workers of America; Voices for Racial Justice, a longstanding racial justice training organization; and Sunrise Movement, an environmental justice organization. Undercover agents attended meetings of anti-ICE organizers as they planned protests, including the Jan. 23 general strike and march, and food distribution for immigrants who were in hiding. 
The tactics were revealed by a defense attorney representing one of the 15 defendants in federal court documents last week. Filings included reports filed by undercover agents, copies of subpoenas and descriptions of messages on the encrypted messaging app Signal.
“These shams of political investigations — these are just acts of retribution and intimidation,” said Rev. Jennifer Crow, senior minister of the First Universalist Church of Minneapolis, one of the churches where undercover agents infiltrated a meeting. 
The speakers gathered outside the Target headquarters in downtown Minneapolis, and called on Target and other Minnesota-based corporations to use their political power to demand accountability for federal agents’ actions during Operation Metro Surge.
“Every single corporation that claims to be here for the right reasons is going to have to show it through,” said Marcia Howard, president of Minneapolis Federation of Educators Local 59. 
ICE and Target did not immediately respond to the Reformer’s emailed questions. 
The Minneapolis Federation of Educators Local 59 is one of nearly 20 organizations accused by the U.S. Department of Justice of forming part of a wide-ranging conspiracy to impede and assault federal agents. A diagram presented to the grand jury as part of the indictments shows the teachers’ union alongside several other unions, the ICE-tracking group Monarca, Democratic Socialists of America and “Left Jab,” a community martial arts group, among others.
Labor leaders and union members said their solidarity with their immigrant members, and with each other, was indispensable as they worked together to defend immigrants from ICE during Operation Metro Surge.
Howard said she’s proud to be affiliated with other institutions that stood up to the swarm of federal agents in Minnesota this winter. 
“Kinda chic to be on that list,” she said.
Marcia Howard, president of Minneapolis Federation of Educators Local 59, speaks during a press conference condemning federal surveillance Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Legislature scraps $288,000 contract with company linking lawmakers to constituents
description: A council representing the Kansas Legislature votes to abandon the contract with a company hired to help lawmakers connect with constituents.
text:
The Legislative Coordinating Council, which assumes responsibility for legislative business when the Kansas Legislature isn't in session, votes to end a $288,000 annual contract with Indigov, which provided software to improve lawmaker interaction with constituents. (Screen capture from Legislature's YouTube livestream/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The bipartisan leadership of the Kansas Legislature ordered cancellation of a contract with a company that offered lawmakers a software service to manage relationships with constituents.
Instead of renewing the $288,000 annual deal with Indigov that was initiated in December 2024, the Legislative Coordinating Council voted to end the contract. The LCC, comprising Republicans and Democrats serving in leadership roles in the House and Senate, works on behalf of the legislative branch when the full Senate and House aren’t in session.
The LCC was responsible for approving the contract nearly two years ago and unanimously voting Monday to kill the agreement with Indigov. The platform was brought online in anticipation it could help senators and representatives better respond and reach out to constituents. Complaints among legislators about poor usability and low adoption rates for the online system doomed the subscription.
House Speaker Dan Hawkins, a Wichita Republican, presided at the LCC meeting at the statehouse and invited colleagues to make a motion regarding the future of Indigov’s contract.
“Is there a motion? Motion to terminate?” Hawkins whispered to Senate Majority Leader Chase Blasi, also a GOP lawmaker from Wichita.
“I do,” replied Derby Republican Rep. Blake Carpenter. “I make the motion that we not move forward with our current subscription agreement and we cancel that subscription at this time.”
Hawkins invited colleagues to debate the issue, but none volunteered to talk about the contract.
“The termination is delivered,” he said.
In October 2024, members of the LCC reviewed a collection of proposals from companies offering software designed to make it more efficient for legislators to interact with the public. At that time, members of the LCC scrutinized a handful of bids before recommending Indigov.
At that time, Carpenter encouraged others on the LCC to support Indigov because the company had more experience working with state legislatures than rival bidders.
“They’re actually in 12 state legislatures,” Carpenter said when the LCC originally agreed to the contract. “For me, as we move forward, Indigov has what we need and is the right tool for us at the time. I think Indigov is the right choice.”
Hawkins and Senate President Ty Masterson, R-Andover, recommended a “soft rollout” of the program during the initial year. The LCC secured user licenses for 150 legislators and staff under an agreement that allowed expansion to 400 people. There are 165 senators and representatives, but all have temporary or full-time staff who engage the public.
In the second year of the contract, the LCC negotiated to retain the 150-license cap and hold the an annual cost at $288,000.
Legislatures and government agencies have sought software programs to improve interaction with constituents, build trust and promote civil communication.
House Majority Leader Chris Croft, a Republican from Overland Park, said the Legislature outsourced the communications system after a frustrating attempt to create its own.
“We tried to develop a program from scratch,” he said. “It’s really hard to do.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: University of Michigan taps Vanderbilt vice chancellor as next president
description: Cybele Raver, Vanderbilt University’s provost and vice chancellor for academic affairs, will serve as the next president of the University of Michigan, the university’s Board of Regents announced Tuesday morning. Raver is recognized as a national leader in higher education with a strategic mind for university administration, the university said in a news rel[...]
text:
C. Cybele Raver, currently provost and vice chancellor for academic affairs at Vanderbilt University, has been selected by the Board of Regents to serve as the next president of the University of Michigan. (Photo courtesy of Vanderbilt University)Cybele Raver, Vanderbilt University’s provost and vice chancellor for academic affairs, will serve as the next president of the University of Michigan, the university’s Board of Regents announced Tuesday morning.
Raver is recognized as a national leader in higher education with a strategic mind for university administration, the university said in a news release. U-M also said Raver was “instrumental in strengthening all aspects” of Vanderbilt’s “research and academic enterprise.”
Raver’s accomplishments include helping Vanderbilt surpass $1 billion in annual research expenditures and the launch of Vanderbilt’s College of Connected Computing, the university’s first new college in over 40 years. Raver also expanded Vanderbilt’s academic footprint to New York City, San Francisco, Chattanooga, Tennessee, and West Palm Beach, Florida.
“Dr. Raver has a proven record of building strong teams, expanding research excellence, and strengthening every institution she has served,” Michael Behm, chair of the U-M Board of Regents, said in a statement. “She understands what it takes to lead a complex, world-class university — and she shares our unwavering belief that Michigan has been, is now, and must remain the best university in the country. We are confident she is the right leader for this moment and we look forward to the board’s formal vote.”


The U-M Board of Regents has scheduled a special meeting at 11 a.m. on Sept. 1 to take a formal vote on Raver’s appointment. If approved, Raver’s term with U-M will begin on Dec. 1.
Raver said in a statement that it was an “extraordinary honor” to be the next leader of U-M “at this pivotal moment in higher education.”
“Michigan’s scale and impact across research, education, economic growth, and public service are unmatched and I’m eager to build on its remarkable legacy,” Raver said. “I look forward to working alongside faculty, staff, students and alumni to lead Michigan forward with clarity and confidence.”
Current U-M President Domenico Grasso will lead the university until Nov. 30 and will assist with Raver’s transition into the role of president.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana shifts $130M to replace road funding lost during gas tax holiday
description: Indiana officials directed more than $130 million Tuesday to state and local road programs, replacing revenue lost in June amid Gov. Mike Braun’s continued suspension of the state’s gasoline taxes. The State Board of Finance approved three transfers totaling $130.45 million from the State Highway Fund’s existing balance — not directly from Indiana’s broader[...]
text:
Indiana officials approved more than $130 million in transfers to replace June road funding lost during the state’s gasoline tax holiday. About $58.3 million is designated for local governments. (Getty Images)Indiana officials directed more than $130 million Tuesday to state and local road programs, replacing revenue lost in June amid Gov. Mike Braun’s continued suspension of the state’s gasoline taxes.
The State Board of Finance approved three transfers totaling $130.45 million from the State Highway Fund’s existing balance — not directly from Indiana’s broader budget surplus.
Each replaces June revenue that would normally flow to a different road account through Indiana’s gasoline use tax or 36-cent-per-gallon gasoline excise tax.
“I made a commitment that we would provide gas tax relief to Hoosiers without leaving our local communities to foot the bill,” Braun said. “I’m grateful to the Board of Finance for their partnership in once again helping us keep that promise. Right now, local leaders across Indiana are focused on cleaning up from historic storms, repairing damaged infrastructure and helping their neighbors recover, and they can continue to direct their efforts there.”
The largest transfer sent $89.39 million to the Motor Vehicle Highway Account, including $9.65 million in gasoline use-tax revenue and $79.75 million in gasoline excise-tax revenue.
Braun announces new energy emergency, continues Indiana’s gas tax suspension

The board separately directed $26.58 million in excise-tax revenue to the Highway, Road and Street Fund and $14.47 million in use-tax revenue to the Local Road and Bridge Matching Fund, which supports matching grants to local governments.
After the money moves through the normal distribution process, State Budget Director Chad Ranney told the Indiana Capital Chronicle, $72.17 million will return to the State Highway Fund for use by the Indiana Department of Transportation.
The remaining roughly $58.3 million is designated for local road funding.
That local share includes the $14.47 million matching-fund transfer and approximately $43.8 million that the state comptroller’s office will distribute directly to local governments within days, Ranney said.
Braun first suspended the state’s 7% gasoline use tax in April as fuel prices surged during the war with Iran. He added the gasoline excise tax to the suspension in May and has continued the tax holiday through subsequent energy emergency declarations.
His administration pledged to protect local road budgets from the resulting revenue losses.
The transfers keep scheduled road distributions intact but do not provide new money or address Indiana’s longer-term infrastructure funding needs.
State officials previously projected the months-long tax holiday would reduce revenue for INDOT and local governments by a combined $533 million. That was before Braun initiated a second emergency starting in August.
Another Board of Finance transfer could be considered in September as delayed gas-tax distributions continue.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi Today’s work on podcast honored with prestigious journalism award
description: The project, in partnership with Reveal from the Center for Investigative Reporting and The New York Times, features more than 70 interviews with former inmates and officers at the Rankin County jail.
text:
Mississippi Today, in partnership with Reveal from the Center for Investigative Reporting and The New York Times, has won a National Edward R. Murrow Award for the podcast “Abuse of Power: Beyond the Goon Squad.”

The project features more than 70 interviews with former inmates and officers at the Rankin County jail. Reporters from Mississippi Today and The New York Times discovered a system in which guards ordered beatings, inmates who participated were rewarded, and those trying to raise an alarm about the system for more than a decade were ignored. 
The podcast allowed people who experienced abuses by the Rankin County Sheriff’s Department to tell their stories in their own voices. 
“Mukta Joshi, Brian Howey and Nate Rosenfield took their in-depth and impactful reporting about abuses at a Mississippi sheriff’s office to another platform, allowing listeners into the world they witnessed and wrote about,” said Debbie Skipper, Justice Team and Special Projects Editor at Mississippi Today. “Their podcast demonstrated the hurdles they had to overcome and their concern for protecting the people who dared to challenge a system stacked against them. It opened the eyes of a community to what was going on behind the walls of the sheriff’s office and jail and empowered residents to seek solutions.” 
The Radio Television Digital News Association (RTDNA) oversees the Edward R. Murrow Awards, which honors work in broadcast and digital journalism. Among the most prestigious in news, the Murrow Awards recognize local and national news stories that uphold the RTDNA Code of Ethics, demonstrate technical expertise and exemplify the importance and impact of journalism as a service to the community. 
The award will be presented at the Edward R. Murrow Awards Gala on Oct. 12 at Gotham Hall in New York City.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: ‘Future-proof’ or ‘a strategic mistake’? Inside the MBTA’s effort to electrify its commuter rail system
description: The first battery-powered trains will start running on the Fairmount Line more than a decade after MBTA overseers called for electrifying the system, and they’ll be eye-wateringly expensive. Is that just the price and pace of a transformative project?
text:
THE MOOD WAS CELEBRATORY when MBTA oversight board members unanimously declared their support for transforming the commuter rail system, a blue-sky vision featuring zero emissions and more frequent service using electrified trains.
Transit advocates cheered the November 2019 move — even if the board votes came in the form of nonbinding resolutions with no funding attached — as a win. T leaders at the time said that new trains could arrive in two to four years. The votes were described at the time (by this reporter) as “historic.”
Then the COVID-19 pandemic hit, safety failures threw the T into chaos, and a new governor took office and set about transforming the agency. It seemed like the vision of a clean, frequent commuter rail system that did not rely on fossil fuels would have to wait, shifted to the back burner in favor of putting out fires and repairing those infuriating slow zones that suddenly seemed to be everywhere.
Today, the MBTA is again thinking about big commuter rail upgrades and is now inching toward a major early milestone that could serve as a proof of concept for the agency’s broader ambitions: acquiring battery-powered trains for the shortest route in the commuter rail system, the 9.2-mile Fairmount Line that runs almost entirely within Boston city limits.
It’s a project years, if not decades, in the making, one that could bring more frequent transit service and slash greenhouse gas emissions in parts of the city with significant Black populations saddled with few connectivity options. But the first new vehicles will not arrive for testing of their cutting-edge technologyuntil a full decade after the vote to forge ahead with electrification, and the cost for the new vehicles on a single commuter rail line will exceed an eye-poppingthree-quarters of a billion dollars.
Did something go haywire, or is this just the price — and pace — of a fundamentally transformative project?
To Sen. Brendan Crighton, one of the co-chairs of the Legislature’s Transportation Committee, the work has “absolutely taken longer than I hoped.”
“But you also have to look back. The previous administration, I don’t believe, prioritized electrification,” Crighton said, referring to former Gov. Charlie Baker’s team. “In fairness, COVID hit, which delayed some things. So it’s frustrating, but I don’t think it’s a lack of will of this current administration.”
Today, all of the MBTA’s roughly 100 commuter rail locomotives run on diesel fuel. The fleet also features about 400 passenger coaches, which have no power sources of their own. Replacing all of those with infrastructure that can run on electric power has long been viewed as an effort that could cost tens of billions of dollars.
In June, the MBTA’s board of directors approved a 15-year, $765 million deal to lease 28 battery-powered vehicles for the Fairmount Line. The first battery electric multiple unit (or BEMU, in industry parlance) train from Swiss manufacturer Stadler is set to arrive for testing by the end of 2029, and passenger service will begin the following year.
Electric trains do not produce any greenhouse gas emissions, and officials say they’ll be able to operate with shorter headways between trips, reducing waits for passengers.
Crucially, the new trains for the Fairmount Line do not require the constant presence of overhead catenary wires or electrified third rails for power. That infrastructure is absent from most of the commuter rail system, though the Providence Line has catenary wires because it uses the same stretch of rail as Amtrak’s electrified Northeast Corridor service.
Depending on who you ask, the new technology is either the chief upside or the biggest risk in the electrification strategy.
MBTA officials say embracing battery power avoids the hassle of installing catenary along anentire line, which can be costly and can also fuel political spats in areas where neighbors view them as eyesores. Instead, they can focus on building charging infrastructure at endpoints and hanging shorter lengths of wires in select places.
Because they can run for roughly 50 miles on a single charge, the battery electric multiple units also have more flexibility, and the T could more easily expand them to other lines with less up-front infrastructure work.
Mike Muller, the T’s executive director of commuter rail, called the approach “scalable and future-proof.”
“The technology has evolved to a point now where you don’t need to put up 650 miles of overhead catenary,” Muller said in an interview, referring to the combined length of commuter rail tracks across the system. “You can put it in strategic locations of maybe less than half of that,” he said, where the overhead wires are needed for battery recharging.
Some advocates worry, however, that the technology is unproven locally. Three years ago, California’s Caltrain signed an agreement with Stadler to procure a single bi-level BEMU train for a first-in-the-nation pilot. In 2024, Chicago’s Metra system also struck a deal with Stadler to procure similar trains. Vehicles are years away from being delivered in both cases.
“It’s a little bit untested in the United States, and that gives me great pause, great concern,” said Brian Kane, executive director of the MBTA Advisory Board, which represents cities and towns who help fund the T. “It’s also going to take a lot longer to procure, and it’s going to take a lot longer to test and make sure it works. I just think there’s a better alternative staring us in the face.”
Catenary wires, Kane said, are a “tried and true” technology. He argued the Fairmount Line that runs from South Station to the Readville neighborhood of Hyde Park is an ideal stretch for the power cables, too, because it is not interrupted by any grade crossings where automobiles drive over the tracks, nor does it travel directly though any Main Street-type areas where the wiring would disrupt local aesthetics.
He suggests that outfitting the entire line with catenary wires would allow the T to try out the battery-powered trains, but quickly pivot to more conventional electric trains powered with overhead wires if there is a problem with the new locomotives.  
“If they strung catenary along the entire Fairmont branch, they could still get battery-electric trains and test them by just not using the catenary some of the time,” Kane said. “But they’re locking themselves into this technology by not stringing catenary everywhere, and I just think it’s a strategic mistake.”
Some onlookers are frustrated by what they perceive as the lack of a big-picture plan. They worry there’s no clear vision for how the MBTA gets from a handful of battery-powered trains on one single line to hundreds of miles of commuter rail track running on electricity.
“[Electrifying] the line out to Readville is a great first step. That’s a natural fit,” said Joseph Aiello, who long chaired the Fiscal and Management Control Board, the T panel that oversaw the agency for more than six years after its creation in response to the disastrous winter of 2015. “But what happens next?”
Crighton, a Lynn Democrat, has a particular interest in electrified rail: his hometown’s fastest transit access to Boston is on the Newburyport/Rockport Line, which the 2019 MBTA board vote called for electrifying early alongside the Fairmount Line and Providence Line.
The latter is on track for some changes. T officials are procuring 10 electric locomotives, which will run using the Providence Line’s catenary wires and pull existing passenger coaches.
The interior of South Station, including the MBTA and Amtrak train schedule. (Kate Kotlyar/CommonWealth Beacon)
But electrifying the stretch of the Newburyport/Rockport Line through Lynn will take time. Muller said the T first needs to install new power infrastructure north of Boston before it can pursue electric trains on the Newburyport/Rockport Line “in a really meaningful way.”
MBTA officials have been eyeing “discontinuous” electrification, the jargon for using battery-powered vehicles that only need smaller stretches of catenary or localized equipment to recharge instead of running wires along an entire line, for at least four years. In 2024, the agency’s board approved an initial deal with commuter rail operator Keolis to start the rollout process on the Fairmount Line, projecting at the time that service would begin in early 2028.
The effort is now running about two years behind that estimate, in large part because the T wants Stadler to customize its trains to feature more wheelchair-accessible seating. The off-the-shelf design from the manufacturer features one car per train set with accessible seating, which matches federal standards for commuter rail coaches. However, the Fairmount Line today has accessible seating in all cars, and officials were hesitant to move forward on cleaner power while moving backwards on accessibility.
Muller, the T’s commuter rail chief, said the timeline has also been affected by pandemic upheaval and by major funding constraints. He noted that the 2019 resolutions from the Fiscal and Management Control Board — which dissolved in 2021 and was later replaced by the current MBTA board — were both nonbinding and unfunded.
Even as Beacon Hill steers significantly more money toward the T’s operations, the agency has little room available in its capital budget, which funds major infrastructure work and expansions.
Aiello, who chaired the board at the time of the 2019 votes, said board members “just didn’t have enough information” to dictate something more forcefully.
“We knew it was going to be complicated, we knew it was going to be expensive. We wanted to set them on a path, and we thought focusing on those first three lines with clean intent was going to put enough pressure on them to start thinking about the rest of the system,” he told CommonWealth Beacon. “This BEMU idea, which wasn’t on our radar screen, is really one of the wonderful, transformative pieces of thinking that happened subsequent to our vote.”
The new trains are also enormously expensive. Under the deal, the T will pay about $27 million per car for the 15-year lease, which would by far be the highest in a database of many North American, European, and Chinese locomotive and coach procurement prices tracked by researchers at the Transit Costs Project.
Muller attributed the high costs to rampant industry-wide inflation, and the fact that new technology is more expensive than more traditional options such as diesel trains. About $190 million of the $765 million contract also covers maintenance, which Muller said is typically not included in the sticker price of a procurement.
Under the deal, the T also has the option to procure another 96 cars. Its timeline will extend past the end of Keolis’s current tenure and into the next commuter rail operations contract, which is set to begin in July 2027.
Beyond that, next steps are murky. Muller said the T does not have funding available for expanding electric power beyond the limited Fairmount and Providence line efforts.
The T could soon be forced to put pen to paper, though. In a recent education and transportation spending bill, lawmakers tucked in language ordering the MBTA to report by July 1, 2028 a vision for a completely transformed commuter rail system featuring more frequent, electrified service, along with an explicit order of operations and projected timeline.
Crighton said the document “will be more of a game plan than a report.”
“For something this complicated, we really need to lay out very specific objectives and projections and study everything about this and make sure we have a schedule,” he said. “We need to hold ourselves to a timetable so that we don’t get in the situation we’re in now, where it’s taken seven years to make even modest progress.”
To Aiello, the outcome could hinge on how well officials are able to sell a decades-long investment. “The cost and the reality of competing interests for federal and state dollars means that the regional rail initiative needs sustained public and political support over a couple decades, and the initiative needs to be handed from one group of Beacon Hill leaders to the next and to the next,” he said. “How to build and sustain that support will be a central element to its success.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Kentucky governor wants to limit data centers, but critics say executive order has little teeth
description: During a press conference earlier this month, Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear stood firm behind the power of his executive order he issued seeking to limit the impacts of data centers eyeing Kentucky. “The executive order is fully enforceable, and if you don’t believe it, watch me,” Beshear told reporters. “Watch what happens as we […]
text:
Gov. Andy Beshear issued an executive order on Aug. 6 directing the Kentucky Public Service Commission and the Energy and Environment Cabinet to take specific actions to limit data center impacts. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)

During a press conference earlier this month, Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear stood firm behind the power of his executive order he issued seeking to limit the impacts of data centers eyeing Kentucky.
“The executive order is fully enforceable, and if you don’t believe it, watch me,” Beshear told reporters. “Watch what happens as we move forward. Watch how these companies present their plans as they have to. Watch the actions of the various agencies.”
Those agencies he’s referring to include Kentucky Public Service Commission, the state’s utility regulator, and the Energy and Environment Cabinet, which regulates water and air pollution. Among other things, he directed the agencies to deny utility rate increases and prevent negative environmental impacts from data centers.
But some people who watch energy policy in the state wonder how the executive order will be implemented and if a governor can compel an agency like the Public Service Commission, which has to follow a mandate defined in state law, to deny requests from utilities. The governor’s executive order doesn’t have the backing of any specific state law regulating data center impacts, potential legislation that the GOP-controlled state legislature has failed to take up so far.
Lane Boldman, the executive director of the environmental advocacy group Kentucky Conservation Committee, described Beshear’s executive order as a “document of intent” that makes clear to state regulators what the governor wants to see happen. But she said the regulators still have to show evidence for their decision-making with data centers.
“I think anything that starts bringing more attention to the very real impacts of these facilities and has any teeth at all is welcome. And this has a little bit of teeth, but it certainly could be enhanced more with strong legislation,” Boldman said.
Another environmental legal group agrees with Boldman. In a recent statement, the Kentucky Resources Council wrote it supports the governor’s goals but that executive branch agencies are “creatures of statute and their authority and discretion are bound and limited by law.” The organization also called on the state legislature to adopt new laws for data centers.
Boldman said she wishes state lawmakers had addressed the impacts of data centers sooner. After a bill to limit data center impacts on electricity ratepayers died during this year’s legislative session, a key GOP lawmaker told the Lantern he’s working on new legislation.
“You invite a high impact economic development industry into your state, and you are surprised now at the impact because they’re coming on so fast. That should have been anticipated,” Boldman said.
Regulator independence
Specifically, Beshear’s executive order directed the Kentucky Public Service Commission, or PSC, to deny any request from utilities to raise rates that would have other ratepayers pay for data center construction and operations.
Yet a former chair of the commission told the Lantern the executive order doesn’t have an enforcement mechanism to ensure the commission complies.
“I don’t think it has any legal weight. I don’t think it needs to necessarily have legal weight for the PSC to take it seriously,” said Kent Chandler, a non-resident senior fellow in energy and environmental policy at the think tank R Street Institute. “Either they’re going to take the governor’s public demands at face value, or they’re not.”
In quasi-judicial cases, the commission weighs whether to grant utilities a rate increase to recover cost from utility investments including power plants. The governor appoints and reappoints the five commissioners on the board, who are then confirmed by the Kentucky Senate. The PSC is guided by state law — including that utility rates be “fair, just and reasonable” —  on whether to approve or deny a request.
Chandler said parties can appeal a decision if they believe the commission didn’t follow state law or regulations. He also doesn’t believe the executive order bucks how the commission was already operating with utility cost allocation.
“I just don’t think there’s anybody out there beating the door down at the PSC saying, ‘Yes, please, let’s allow utilities to raise rates on other customers for costs they didn’t incur for the benefit of data centers,’ right?” Chandler said.
Chandler said he also doesn’t recall a time when a governor has issued an executive order dictating to the commission how to rule on utility requests.
Chandler pointed to the U.S. Supreme Court overturning a precedent giving President Donald Trump control over federal agencies that Congress intended to be independent. He also pointed to a new state law giving the Public Service Commission more independence in its operations from the rest of the state executive branch.
“I think it just goes to show how important regulator independence is,” Chandler said.
He said that new state law indicated the commission is “independent from the rest of the executive branch and that they should have the ability to do their jobs without fear or favor.”
In an emailed statement, current Public Service Commission chair Angie Hatton told the Lantern the executive order is consistent with “what the PSC has already tried to do” under its statutory mandate of setting “fair, just and reasonable” rates.
“When it comes to data centers and other very large load customers, fair cost allocation means striving to ensure those large loads pay for the costs they cause,” Hatton said. She said the regulator would conduct a “prudency review” to determine the cost allocation.
The commission recently held a conference with data center developer TeraWulf to discuss the executive order as the regulator weighs whether to approve a special contract between the developer and utility Big Rivers Electric Corporation.
Permits and energy plans
The governor also has stood firm on his oversight of environmental permitting.
When asked in a recent MS NOW interview about a massive hyperscale data center and natural gas-fired turbines being built on or near a federal site in McCracken County — a project he said he wasn’t briefed on ahead of time — he referenced the Energy and Environment Cabinet’s permitting power.
“You can’t operate without an air or water permit,” Beshear said. “If you’re going to invest $100 billion to build something, you probably ought to go talk to the person in charge of the state.”
The cabinet oversees a variety of permitting for industrial sites including for water withdrawal, floodplain construction, storm water runoff and air quality, and those permits set limits on the amount of pollution allowed by an operation. Beshear’s order directed the cabinet to deny any permit request from a data center that would “negatively impact” water, air, and natural resources.
Additionally, Beshear’s executive order requires data center developers to submit an “energy plan” to the cabinet explaining how the developer plans to protect residential ratepayers and meet its energy needs. In a PSC filing, TeraWulf said it provided on Aug. 14 an 88-page energy plan to the cabinet.  Earlier this month, Energy and Environment Cabinet Secretary John Lyons said the state has received only a few water-related permits from data center developers.
Robin Hartman, a spokesperson for the cabinet, in a statement said the cabinet is drafting “guidelines” for the energy plans.
“All related projects – past, present and future – must provide an energy plan to Team Kentucky’s Energy and Environment Cabinet, as well as meet all other requirements outlined in the executive order,” Hartman said.
