name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: After a 2-year wait, will Ohio’s largest solar project get the OK?
description: Following a key legal deadline last Friday, the stage is now set for the Ohio Power Siting Board to make a final decision about whether the state’s largest solar and energy storage project to date can move ahead. The OPSB initially approved the Oak Run Solar Project in March 2024, but the case has since been bogged down by an appeal filed by Madison County [[...]
text:
The Gavel outside the Supreme Court of the State of Ohio. (Photo by Graham Stokes for Ohio Capital Journal. Republish photo only with original article.)
Following a key legal deadline last Friday, the stage is now set for the Ohio Power Siting Board to make a final decision about whether the state’s largest solar and energy storage project to date can move ahead.


The OPSB initially approved the Oak Run Solar Project in March 2024, but the case has since been bogged down by an appeal filed by Madison County and three of its townships.


Oak Run Solar would bring 800 megawatts of solar and 300 MW of energy storage to a state that has become increasingly hostile to clean energy, even as mounting electricity demand increases power prices and threatens grid reliability.


Though the county and townships filed their appeal with the Ohio Supreme Court in October 2024, it was not until this past May that the court weighed in. A majority of the seven justices rejected all objections to the project except one.


To deal with that issue, the court sent the case back to the board with instructions for regulators to ​“more thoroughly address the Oak Run project’s visual impacts,” specifically by reviewing photo simulations or artist’s sketches of how the project’s proposed substations would look from public vantage points.


On July 28, Ohio regulators heard testimony on this narrow issue. Briefing wrapped up last Friday.


Once the full board reviews the transcript, briefs, and other filings, it will issue a decision. The OPSB’s staff has already weighed in: Its Aug. 7 brief asks the full board to confirm Oak Run’s permit.


The board is under no obligation to vote according to its staff’s recommendation, and there is no specific deadline for it to act. Any additional appeal could also eat up more time.


“The project represents a significant opportunity for long-term economic investment in Madison County while supporting Ohio’s growing energy needs,” Samantha Sawmiller, senior development manager for the Oak Run Solar Project, told Canary Media. ​“We respectfully await the Ohio Power Siting Board’s decision.”


Oak Run’s saga demonstrates the difficulty of developing clean energy in Ohio. In recent years, the state has blocked 5.3 gigawatts of wind and solar projects and garnered a reputation as the place ​“where wind and solar projects go to die.”


Since 2021, the General Assembly has enacted multiple laws that create extra hurdles for new solar and wind, but not for fossil fuel projects.
Meanwhile, the OPSB has played a central role in restricting solar’s growth, especially for grandfathered projects exempted from local government bans under those state statutes.


In March, the OPSB denied permits for the proposed 94-MW Crossroads Solar Grazing Center in central Ohio. Last month, it asked the state Supreme Court to dismiss an appeal from the developer of the planned 175-MW Kingwood Solar installation, whose permits the regulators denied in 2022. The project’s interconnection agreement has expired while it awaits a court decision — a fact the board used to justify its request for dismissal.


The Ohio Supreme Court’s multiple opinions on May 26 in the Oak Run case may also suggest a growing partisanship among some of its members. Previously, the court’s members had generally shown more deference toward the OPSB’s expertise on its factual findings.


When those opinions are pieced together, six of the court’s seven justices found fault with the OPSB’s grant of the permit because the developer’s visual evidence didn’t include renderings of the project’s three substations.


Three of those justices found that was the only shortcoming. Three others also sided with the local governments and would have required more evidence on issues dealing with water, wildlife, and fears about the safety of battery storage.


Jennifer Brunner, the court’s only Democrat, would have affirmed the OPSB’s decision in its entirety, based on the case record’s other evidence.

Taken together, the opinions ​“added more confusion to an already uncertain legal environment” for utility-scale renewables, said Karin Nordstrom, a lawyer with the Ohio Environmental Council, which is a party in the case supporting the project.


“Ohio is facing a massive energy crunch and ever-rising energy prices [and] really needs a clear substantive standard for reviewing these proposed projects,” she added. ​“And that’s not what we got from the court in this case.”


Testimony at the July 28 hearing was relatively brief. Lauren Devine, director of permitting and environmental matters for Savion, the project developer, said the company had the consulting firm EDR do additional work to show how public vantage points would look with the planned substations.


Gordon Perkins, a division manager with EDR, reported on that new work and its photo simulations with the substations included. The substations ​“would not contribute to visual impacts that were not already identified” in the group’s earlier review of the Oak Run project, he said, adding that the developer would take various steps to minimize visual impacts.


Mark Bellamy, a utilities specialist on the technical staff that advises the OPSB, reported that he had reviewed the consultant’s new report and concluded that Oak Run’s aesthetic appearance would be consistent with that of other solar farms — hence the staff recommendation to greenlight the project.


The local governments’ sole witness was Errol Gattis, a resident of London, Ohio, who said he’d be able to see the project from his yard and porch and objected to EDR’s choice of vantage points.


Ohio’s rules don’t require consideration of a project’s expected appearance from every possible angle, however. And state law doesn’t guarantee that viewsheds won’t change, said Tom Bullock, executive director for the Citizens Utility Board of Ohio, a consumer watchdog group that promotes clean energy and is not part of the case.


An Aug. 7 brief filed by the opponents’ lawyer, Jack Van Kley — a longtime renewable-energy opponent in the state — took issue with the vantage points for the visual analysis and argued that the developer should have provided the materials as a supplement to the company’s project application, complete with various steps for public participation.


Those stances are similar to arguments that the Ohio Supreme Court rejected in its Oak Run ruling in May, about the general approach for a visual analysis and whether regulators had properly found that the developer’s application was complete. Moreover, the court didn’t order a supplement to the application, just the review of additional material on a single issue.


“This was the evidentiary hearing that is very narrowly focused on the simulations for the substations,” said Christine Pirik, a lawyer for the developer, when Van Kley tried to use the argument to block admission of the additional evidence into the case record.


Administrative Law Judges David Hicks and Isabel Marcelletti sided with the developer and the siting board’s staff, noting their belief that the hearing process complies with the court’s directive.


Filings by the OPSB’s staff and the Ohio Environmental Council, which advocates for clean energy, also took issue with Van Kley’s arguments. ​“The Local Governments’ alleged procedural violations apply to service requirements for an application, not supplemental evidence submitted on remand,” lawyers Karin Nordstrom and Chris Tavenor wrote in the council’s Aug. 14 reply brief.


The clock is ticking for Oak Run, as lawyers for the developer noted in a May 18 court filing: ​“Oak Run is now in dire need to have the appeals process come to a close as soon as possible.”


Besides having spent more than $13 million already, the developer faces contractual deadlines from grid operator PJM Interconnection and others to reach commercial operation by 2030.


“Should the Project fail due to the lengthy time for considerations, Oak Run will lose its significant financial investment and the community and state of Ohio will lose the employment and financial benefits that would result from construction and operation of the Project,” including about $250 million for local governments, its filing said.


Plus, of course, the clean energy and battery storage.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: South of the Mason-Dixon Line, Maryland counties scramble to respond to data centers
description: Data centers have become a contested issue in recent years, and as local governments are facing more opposition to the facilities, many are taking time to understand how they should move forward.
text:
Del. Lorig Charkoudian (D-Montgomery) and Sen. Katie Fry Hester (D-Howard and Montgomery) were among lawmakers who rallied  to push PJM on clean-energy projects and on holding data centers accountable for their power needs. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Bryan Cornell lives in a house he built on his grandparents farm in Harford County. His parents live next door, and his daughter is in the next house over.
When he first heard a rumor in April that a golf course behind his property was being considered as a potential site for a data center campus, “he panicked” and even weighed selling his home. But then, he decided to push back.
He quickly teamed up with Krissy Flatau, who lives across the street from the golf course, and together they formed Our Land, Our Home, Our Harford – a grassroots community organization that advocated against data centers in the county. Months later, in June, Harford County became the first in Maryland to completely ban the facilities.
“I couldn’t stand the thought of my kids never wanting to visit me, my grandkids never wanting to visit me because there would be an industrial site right across the street from me,” Flatau said.
Data centers have become a contested issue in Maryland in recent years, and as local governments are facing more opposition to the facilities, many are taking time to understand how they should move forward. Currently, 13 counties have enacted temporary data center moratoriums, with two voting earlier this month, and more counties are considering a pause.
Angie McCarthy is the clean energy campaign manager at Nature Forward and the founding chair of Marylanders for Data Center Reform, a coalition of 62 environmental and community organizations that aim to ensure data center development is done sustainably and ethically.
She calls the moratoriums a “natural reaction” to all of the concerns people have about data centers impact on things like the environment, noise, community infrastructure and public health.

Several Maryland counties, from Caroline on the Eastern Shore to Montgomery, the state’s most populous, have decided to pause data center development in recent weeks. Many counties say these moratoriums will give them the time to research the potential impacts of the facilities in their communities and issue appropriate regulations for them.
A statement from the Maryland Tech Council said local governments have a responsibility to examine how data centers fit in their communities, but that many of the concerns associated with the facilities are “misunderstood or vastly overstated.”
“Rushing to enact broad policies before the facts are fully examined risks foreclosing on a generational economic opportunity rather than regulating an industry on reasonable terms set by local governments,” the statement said.
Harford is so far the only county to impose a ban. County Executive Bob Cassilly proposed the ban in response to a proposed moratorium to develop “guardrails” on data center development, according to public testimony read to the council on his behalf in June.
Cassilly said he didn’t see a reason for a moratorium because the county had already been researching the feasibility of data centers and concluded that it did not have the electrical capabilities to power hyperscale centers. He said it would be “grossly irresponsible” to allow data centers when there’s not enough power to run them.
Cassilly said he expects other counties will eventually decide to ban the centers, given the state’s limited energy capabilities.

Data center developers want to build in three Pa. communities. Each has its own experience.


“I don’t know what choices they have other than ‘Let’s inflate all the energy prices for all of our residents,’ which doesn’t seem like an appropriate thing to do,” Cassilly said. “People are already struggling with some of the highest energy costs in the country, so adding that burden doesn’t seem appropriate at all. To me, that’s just highly irresponsible to do.”
The Montgomery County Council voted recently to extend its current six-month pause on data centers to 18 months. County Executive Marc Elrich signed an executive order in June to approve the pause amid concern over a potential facility in Dickerson.
The 18-month pause was a compromise between a six-month moratorium first proposed by Council member Evan Glass and a two-year pause by Council members Will Jawando and Kristin Mink.
Glass said the extended pause will give the county more time to “get this right” and ensure that economic opportunities don’t come at the expense of the environment and the community’s needs.
“The worst thing you can do is try to rush because once it’s built and all these things are in place, you can’t go back,” Jawando said.
In Frederick County, County Executive Jessica Fitzwater signed an order July 1, pausing new data center permitting or approvals until the end of the year. The current moratorium also does not have any affect on previously approved projects.
Fitzwater created a data center pause and work group to provide recommendations for future development guidelines in June 2023, soon after coming into office. This came after developers purchased 2,100 acres of land in 2021 for a hyperscale data center campus in southern Frederick County.
“With the Quantum Frederick project, it just put us in a different position than some of the other counties who were trying to attract data centers,” said Council member Renee Knapp, who served on the work group. “We already had this really large project that we had to come up with regulations for.”
In December, the Frederick County Council voted to expand the data center zoning area surrounding the Quantum Frederick development to about 2,600 acres. Before this, 5,000 acres of the county’s industrial zoning area was available for data center development. While the change was designed to limit urban sprawl and confine the facilities to just that area, it was 1,000 acres beyond what the county’s planning commission previously recommended.

More data center proposals keep coming to Pennsylvania. So does the outcry.


This decision prompted residents to pursue a ballot referendum on the issue, with organizers collecting more than 20,000 signatures. The county’s board of elections approved the measure, but the Maryland Supreme Court ruled on June 30 that it must remain off the ballot, after data center companies challenged the petition’s legality.
Fitzwater said the current pause will give the county time to answer residents’ questions and address their concerns about the developments. Frederick and several other Maryland counties with moratoriums are waiting to receive a study on the impacts of data centers that is due to Gov. Wes Moore and the General Assembly by Sept. 1.
“These projects that are being built now already have approvals, so there isn’t a mechanism to take away approvals that were already given,” Fitzwater said. “But, we can say we’re not accepting new applications or doing any new approvals while we continue to monitor the industry [and] see what the state impact analysis tells us.”
Council member Brad Young said that while he understands why Fitzwater issued the moratorium, he didn’t agree with the decision. He said the county had already gone through the process of getting public input and agreeing on county regulations.

He said he saw having data centers in the county as a way to relieve the tax burden on residential taxpayers and still find ways to support schools and the community.
“I was for limiting it to that one area, putting tough regulations on them and taxing the heck out of them,” Young said. “And I was, and am, still confident we did a great job with that.”
Taylor Frazier McCollum, a Prince George’s County-based advocate against data centers, and Cornell both said they felt moratoriums just give counties the opportunity to open the door for future data center development, despite significant community opposition.
“It’s a hot issue, and it crosses party lines,” Frazier McCollum said. “It’s a bipartisan issue. It’s something that people are concerned about. They don’t want their sleep disrupted. They don’t want to live near diesel generators or have gas plants turned back on to run a data center in the community.”
McCarthy said it’s important for counties to think about how they will move forward once their moratoriums end. She said this won’t be a “one size fits all,” and will have to look different for each county.
This could mean strict environmental regulations, heavily taxing developers and ensuring that money is reinvested back into the community. But, McCarthy said, if county governments and their residents can’t agree on what regulations to accept, it may be time to consider a permanent ban.
Advocates, like Frazier McCollum, Cornell and Flatau say they don’t want data centers in Maryland at all, and they plan to fight to make it happen.
“We’re definitely staying involved,” Cornell said. “We know the session’s coming up, and we’re not going away.”

title: The real reason many Americans are cutting ties with their parents and siblings
description: Luna, 26, no longer speaks to her father. There was no single betrayal, no dramatic rupture. What ended the relationship was his insistence on obedience and dominance. “In his head it’s like, ‘I’m the father, you’re the daughters, we do things my way,’” she told me. Luna explained to him that she was “not willing […]
text:
(Photo by Sue Barr/Getty Images)
Luna, 26, no longer speaks to her father. There was no single betrayal, no dramatic rupture. What ended the relationship was his insistence on obedience and dominance.
“In his head it’s like, ‘I’m the father, you’re the daughters, we do things my way,’” she told me. Luna explained to him that she was “not willing to have a relationship like that,” and her terms for contact were simple: “We could only have a relationship where you understand that I’m a person, and I’m not just gonna do whatever you want me to do whenever you want me to.”
He refused to accept those terms. So after numerous attempts to make it work, she walked away.
Family estrangement has become a fixture of talk shows, advice columns and social media. It’s also the subject of my new book, “Families We Lose.”
Much of the current media coverage on estrangement tends to frame it as an epidemic that is the product of therapy culture.
My research suggests that this framing misses what is actually happening. I conducted 68 in-depth interviews with adults who went no-contact with a parent, sibling, grandparent or other relative. (All participant names, including Luna’s, are pseudonyms used to protect their privacy.)
I found that estrangement is less a story of trauma or selfishness, and more a clash between competing expectations: an insistence on loyalty, duty and forgiveness on one hand, and the longing for respect, emotional safety and personal growth on the other.
 Falling birth rates raise the stakes

Estrangement is fairly common.
In a 2022 study, my colleagues and I used national survey data that followed parent-child relationships over several decades. In that period, 26% of adult children in the U.S. experienced a period of estrangement from their fathers, and 6% reported a period of estrangement with their mothers. Our findings were consistent with what sociologist Karl Pillemer found in his 2020 national survey, which showed that 27% of Americans were estranged from a relative, or roughly 67 million people.
Headlines often treat numbers like these as evidence of a sudden crisis. But no study has tracked estrangement rates over time, and nothing in the existing data shows that it is skyrocketing.
Yet estrangement can have different consequences today. People have far fewer children than in most of human history, so the loss of one relationship may carry greater weight. Two generations ago, a parent might have had several other children with whom to maintain close ties; today, many parents have only one or two.
Smartphones, meanwhile, have created expectations of constant contact and connection within families. Even adult children who have quietly distanced themselves by moving away or limiting contact may still find themselves fielding regular requests for connection through texts, phone calls and social media. This can be stressful, emotionally taxing and make it difficult to establish boundaries.
Those I interviewed often had difficult childhoods, and some had experienced abuse. But they rarely pointed to childhood as the proximate cause of the estrangement, instead citing the poor quality of their relationships with parents and other relatives in adulthood.
 ‘Kinship culture clash’

For them, the path to estrangement was usually gradual, marked by mounting tensions and unresolved conflicts. It emerged out of the recognition that a parent or sibling would not, or could not, treat them the way they desired. For most, this looked like accountability and growth, intentional connection, mutual respect and safety.
Molly, 36, described a lack of accountability as motivation for her estrangement from her mom, Cindy, a decade ago.
Molly told Cindy: “You’ve done all these horrible things. I just need you to acknowledge it. I feel like I’m owed an apology.”
Molly felt that her desire for accountability was a basic need of any relationship, noting, “I didn’t feel like that was asking too much, but apparently it was. I put the ball back in her court, and she’s just sitting on it.”
Most of the people I interviewed recognized that they had different definitions of what family should look like and feel like. In my book, I call this a “kinship culture clash.”
Divorce offers a familiar example of this kind of shift.
For most of American history, marriage was an institution shaped by economics, law, religion and social pressure. You stayed married because that was what one did, and there were few alternatives that didn’t leave one spouse – usually the woman – socially ostracized and financially destitute.
Then, as sociologists Andrew Cherlin, Anthony Giddens and Stephanie Coontz have argued, marriage transformed into a relationship judged by its ability to provide love and support, promote ideals like fairness and lead to personal growth. Once a marriage started being thought of as an arrangement that needed to work for each spouse, divorce became thinkable, then ordinary.
 Should family ties always bind?

The family you are born into can carry the same tension.
Ties to parents and siblings are often expected to be permanent and unconditional, reinforced by cultural norms and laws that bind parents and children to one another, even when children become adults. For example, in adulthood, 27 states have filial piety laws that require adult children to bear financial and, in some cases, direct caregiving responsibility for aging parents. This is part of what I term “compulsory kinship.”
Under this framework, you show up at Thanksgiving no matter what was said last year, because your family is your family. You take your dad into your home to care for him when he gets sick, because he’s your father.
This model does help many Americans. It can ensure aging parents have adult children to care for them, while adult children may have a place to call “home,” no questions asked.
In contrast, the estranged people I talked to for my book adhere to what I call “democratized kinship,” and it generally reflects views of contemporary marriage.
Family bonds require mutual respect, reciprocity and support in order to continue. Under this model, genetics take a back seat: Anyone can become family, just like anyone can become a spouse, but no one is automatically family.
Neither family framework is new, and neither belongs to a single generation. Some people have always held family of origin relatives to distinct standards of care. Queer people have been building chosen families for generations.
But what I chart in this book is the conflict between these two ways of thinking.
Estrangement often happens when these two ideas of family collide and cannot be reconciled – when one member insists that biological or origin ties and hierarchies reinforce the family unit, and another insists that behavior does. That is Luna’s story. Her father drew on the logic of age and hierarchy – “Because I’m your father and I said so” – and she demanded to be treated as a person first and a daughter second.
 A family that works for you

People who leave their families of origin are not rejecting family altogether.
In a recent study drawing on these same interviews, I show that estrangement operates as a catalyst for what I call “redoing family.”
After cutting off contact with a family member or multiple relatives, people commonly went on to rebuild kinship networks, drawing friends, partners, in-laws and neighbors into roles once reserved for blood relatives, and constructing new family units organized around support and reciprocity.
Luna is not on her own because she no longer talks to her father. Her family today includes her sister, whom she talks to multiple times a day, and a large group of friends.
“I think you can have your chosen family, and whoever in your biological family you connect to,” she told me. “Everybody just gets to choose who they feel they have a real, intimate, deep connection with. And that’s your family.”
She didn’t want less family. She simply wanted a family that works.

Florida's Primary Election is Tuesday, Aug. 18. (Getty Images)Florida voters have until 7 p.m. local time Tuesday to cast ballots in the primary elections.
As election results become available Tuesday night, the Phoenix will provide updates on key races across the Sunshine State, including for governor, U.S. Senate, and U.S. House districts that could flip from one party to another.
A Phoenix analysis of early voting and vote-by-mail numbers published by the state indicate more than 14% of registered voters had voted in advance of the election.


Counties among the highest turnout for vote-by-mail and early voting were:

Sumter (23.85%)
Dixie (23.69%)
Liberty (22.38%)
Leon (20.98%)
Calhoun (20.23%)
Monroe (19.55%)
Lee (19.54%)
Citrus (19.46%)
Gulf (19.39%)
Sarasota (19.37%)
Flagler (19.1%)
Lafayette (19.07%)



High-population areas of the state saw early and mail-in ballots returned at rates as follows: Miami-Dade (12.14% of registered voters), Broward (11.85%), Duval (12.19%), Hillsborough (15.86%), Orange (13.84%), Palm Beach (13.99%), and Pinellas (18.54%).
Statewide, 15.53% of Republicans had voted early or by mail as of Monday morning and 19.83% of Democrats. By contrast, 6.32% of No Party Affiliation voters, the designation for about one-fourth of registered voters, had voted early or by mail.
GOP turnout for early and mail-in voters ran above 25% in a handful of counties: Liberty (27.23%), Dixie (27.02%), and Sumter (26.23%).
Democratic turnout for early and mail-in voters ran above 25% in other counties: Sumter (32.85%), Sarasota (31.71%), Monroe (29.47%), Citrus (27.57%), Flagler (27.43%), Charlotte (26.66%), Leon (26.22%), and Lee (26.14%).
To vote
A current and valid photo ID is required to vote in Florida. Acceptable formats include driver licenses, identification cards issued by the state, passport, credit card, military ID, student ID, retirement center ID, neighborhood association ID, public assistance ID, Veteran Affairs health ID, concealed carry permits, or government-issued employee ID.
A provisional ballot may be cast without a photo ID but the signature on the provisional ballot must match the signature on file with the county, as determined by the canvassing board. The vote must’ve been cast by a registered voter in his or her proper precinct.
Voters in line when the polls close are still allowed to vote.
Voters who cast ballots early or by mail can check the status of their ballot using their county’s website.
The Florida Phoenix lists voter precincts at the bottom of all of its webpages.
For other voter information or to read election-related coverage, check out the Phoenix’s Election 2026 landing page.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: A slapdash EV tax is not the answer
description: This suggested opinion piece is in response to Jim Cameron’s column regarding a proposed EV tax. The state of the air is not good. The “State of the Air” is the name of a report issued annually by the American Lung Association. And the most recent edition tells us that seven of Connecticut’s eight counties […]
text:
This suggested opinion piece is in response to Jim Cameron’s column regarding a proposed EV tax.
The state of the air is not good. The “State of the Air” is the name of a report issued annually by the American Lung Association. And the most recent edition tells us that seven of Connecticut’s eight counties get a grade of “F” for Ozone pollution (Windham gets a C). Five of eight counties get a “D” for particulate matter pollution, and 707,181 children are at risk.

Barry Kresch

Cameron notes that Connecticut wants to reduce emissions. As well it should. The transportation sector accounts for about 40% of greenhouse gas emissions and 70% of nitrogen oxide emissions, a major contributor to smog, according to the Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection.
While emissions rate only a passing mention in the column, we should not overlook the very real impact they have. The New York University Marron Institute/American Thoracic Society “Health of the Air” report attributes 163 excess annual deaths and 9,634 excess major morbidity events (e.g. heart attack, chronic bronchitis, ER visits, etc.) in Connecticut due to poor air quality.
There is a lot of controversy around vaccines and autism. Vaccines don’t cause it. But you know what might be related?  Air pollution.
A study published in The Lancet has documented measurable decreases in pollutants in places like Southern California where EV adoption is high. It further projects that with full EV adoption, nitrogen dioxide concentrations (a precursor to smog) would be reduced by 61%.
The Special Transportation Fund and EV taxes
The reasons the fund faces operating deficits are improvements in the fuel efficiency of internal combustion engine vehicles and choices made (or not made) by the legislature.
The federal Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards, augmented by the California Air Resources Board (CARB) standards, have led to an improvement in fuel efficiency of almost 40% over the past 25 years.
While transit construction costs were rising and internal combustion vehicles were consuming less fuel, gasoline taxes were not indexed to inflation or barely raised at all. There are two parts to the state gasoline tax. The first is an excise tax of 25 cents, which was last increased in 2000. The second gas tax is the gross receipts tax, which stands at 8.1% of the wholesale price and was last adjusted in 2013.
At current adoption levels, taxing EVs will in no way make up for operational shortfalls. In fact, raising the gasoline tax by 1 cent would generate 144%**(see note below)  more funds than the proposed EV tax.
There’s a war out there
The economic impact of the Iran war demonstrates our vulnerability to major disruptions in the fossil fuel supply chain. These happen regularly, if not exactly predictably, e.g. Russia invading Ukraine and the political instability around the Arab Spring. The best responses, as many countries are finding, are renewables and EVs.
People are feeling pain at the pump. Even though the Trump Administration has gutted the fuel-efficiency standards, the trend toward greater fuel-efficiency (and lower tax revenue) is likely to continue at least while high gas prices are with us. Kelley Blue Book reports sales of hybrids are up 9% for the first half of the year and by mid-2026 have reached an 18% market share.
Vehicle weight
Let’s dispense with the vehicle weight argument, which is a red herring. The vehicles that disproportionately damage our roads are fully loaded semi-trucks, which cause 1,000 times the damage that an EV would cause. 
Also, even though an EV may be 10 or 15% heavier than its combustion sibling, that doesn’t really account for the distribution of vehicles on the road. The most popular EVs are the Tesla Model Y (3920 – 4,416 pounds) and the Tesla Model 3 (3,552 – 4,072 pounds). Compare that to the most popular internal combustion engine vehicles, –the Ford F-150 (4,021 – 5,950 pounds), Chevrolet Silverado (4,410 – 6,850 pounds), Toyota RAV 4 (3,370 – 4,300 pounds), Honda CR-V (3,300 – 3,926 pounds) — and it is not clear that EVs are responsible for adding extra weight to our roads.
Fossil fuel subsidies
A much bigger subsidy than anything going toward EVs is our continued (and recently expanded) subsidies of fossil fuels. Yale Environment 360 reports that “the amount of public money the U.S. will now spend on domestic fossil fuels stands at least $34.8 billion a year.” These are direct subsidies and do not account for the indirect impacts of extracting, transporting, refining and burning the stuff.
Imposing an EV tax will slow EV adoption at a time when we should be doubling down on promoting EVs for environmental, public health and national security reasons.
Simple or simplistic
When someone buys a gasoline vehicle, they can influence their gasoline expenditures based on their option to choose a fuel-efficient vehicle and their utilization. This proposed tax is a simplistic one-size fits all design. And you have the privilege of paying for three years of it upfront.
EVs should contribute to the maintenance of our transportation system, but in a way that acknowledges the damage that burning fossil fuel causes. The subject deserves a more carefully considered approach. For example:

At what level of EV adoption should we begin to phase in some kind of tax?
There are other options besides registration fees being tried in other states. What have we learned from the results?
The current gasoline tax level is not sacrosanct. It should be raised (though this is an admittedly difficult moment).
According to Cox automotive, the purchase premium for a new EV sits at $5,500. That means EV owners pay an extra $349 to buy an EV at the standard sales tax or $426 if the vehicle is subject to the luxury tax. EV drivers using public charging in the state pay sales tax on the juice (gasoline has no sales tax).
A holistic design should take these factors, and the multiple levers available into account.

===========================================
**Here’s how I came up with the 144% number:
There are 47,441 battery electric vehicles. At $250 each, this would yield $3,953,417.There are 25,416 PHEVs. At $62.50 each, this yields $529,500. Total $4,482,917There are 2,305,954 registered vehicles in Connecticut.Deducting for EVs, that leaves 2,233,097.If they are driven an average of 12,000 miles annually, that comes to 26,797,164,000 miles. Divided by 24.5 MPG used in the column, that is 1,093,761,796 gallons. An additional 1 cent per gallon yields $10,937,618.
Barry Kresch is President of the Electric Vehicle Club of CT.

title: Bird defends state decision to submit voter data to feds
description: Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said Monday at the Iowa State Fair that the state should do everything it can to prevent illegal voting, including turning over voter data to the U.S. Department of Justice.  Bird, who is running for reelection, spoke Monday at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox where she highlighted the work […]
text:
Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird speaks at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the Iowa State Fair Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said Monday at the Iowa State Fair that the state should do everything it can to prevent illegal voting, including turning over voter data to the U.S. Department of Justice. 
Bird, who is running for reelection, spoke Monday at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox where she highlighted the work during her first term and the areas where she and her opponent differ. 
“I will fight for you,” Bird said. “I will fight to keep you and your children safe. I will uphold our law enforcement. I will support our constitution and uphold our laws.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Voter registration data
In May the state confirmed it had submitted voter registration data that included personally identifiable information like driver’s license and Society Security numbers to the DOJ, at the federal department’s request. 

Candidates speak at Register Soapbox
Monday was the third day of candidate speeches at The Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the state fair. Here’s the schedule.
Read about previous speakers:
Republican U.S. Senate candidate: Ashley Hinson
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate: Josh Turek
Republican gubernatorial candidate: Zach Lahn
Democratic gubernatorial candidate: Rob Sand
Republican secretary of agriculture candidate: Mike Naig
Democratic secretary of state candidate: Ryan Peterman
Republican secretary of state candidate: Paul Pate
Democratic state treasurer candidate: John Norwood
Libertarian U.S. Senate candidate: Thomas Laehn
Independent 1st Congressional District candidate: Michael Bridgford
Republican 2nd Congressional District candidate: Joe Mitchell
Independent 2nd District Congressional District candidate:  Dave Bushaw
Libertarian 2nd District Congressional candidate: Rick Stewart
Republican 3rd Congressional District candidate: Zach Nunn
Democratic 3rd Congressional District candidate: Sarah Trone Garriott
Republican 4th Congressional District candidate:  Chris McGowan


At the time, Secretary of State Paul Pate and Bird said Iowa was legally obligated to comply with the request which sought to investigate potential election crimes in states across the country.
Not every state, however, turned over the data. According to the Brennan Center for Justice, 30 states were sued by the administration over the refusal to hand in the data, but more than 20 of those cases have been dismissed by the court.
Bird, when asked if her legal advice to submit the data was correct, given the case dismissals, said working to prevent illegal voting is better than working to prosecute it after it has occurred. 
“Because you can’t unscramble the egg, and it’s not possible to pull that vote out later,” Bird said. “So I think everything we can do to prevent illegal voting, to prevent fraudulent voting, I think it’s important that we do that.” 
That includes, she said, working with the federal government to “make sure that the voter rolls are correct.” 
Pate was also asked Monday about turning over voter data and said he was “sensitive” about the decision, which he had to make based on the information he had at the time. 
The state’s participation in the request to turn over the data was also criticized by Democrats, including Bird’s Democratic opponent in the race, Nate Willems. 
She said during her speech that she and Willems, a former state legislator and labor lawyer, don’t “see eye to eye” on a number of issues, including “stand your ground” and voter ID laws which she supports. 
Willems campaign manager Brittan Ostby said in a statement that Bird has used the office to “push a political agenda.”
“Nate Willems is running for attorney general to hold greedy corporations accountable, take on polluters when they poison our air and water, and will always keep our communities safe,” Ostby said
In her Soapbox speech at the Iowa State Fair, Bird highlighted issues she has worked on since being elected in 2022, including efforts to increase penalties for assaults on law enforcement officers, lawsuits related to transgender participation in women’s sports, suing “scammers” and launching a cold case unit. 
Bird also said she worked to protect Iowans from “woke mandates” like California’s Proposition 12 that would stipulate production standards for certain types of livestock, or mandates from other states to prioritize electric vehicles.
“Here in Iowa, we’re governed by Iowa laws and not theirs,” Bird said.
Willems is scheduled to speak at the Soapbox Friday. The full schedule can be found here.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Polls open at 7 a.m. on Alaska’s pick-one, top-four statewide primary election day
description: Over a month ago, Shelley Cotton cast the first vote in Alaska’s statewide primary election, downloading a blank ballot and sending it quickly by mail from Texas to Alaska.  Since then, more than 31,000 other Alaskans have cast their ballots, and starting at 7 a.m. Tuesday, tens of thousands more residents will vote in an […]
text:
Voters line up on Aug. 17, 2026, at the early voting station set up in Anchorage's Midtown Mall. Voters reported waiting about an hour to cast their primary election ballots. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Over a month ago, Shelley Cotton cast the first vote in Alaska’s statewide primary election, downloading a blank ballot and sending it quickly by mail from Texas to Alaska. 
Since then, more than 31,000 other Alaskans have cast their ballots, and starting at 7 a.m. Tuesday, tens of thousands more residents will vote in an election that will start to decide who Alaska’s next governor will be.
What’s on the ballot? 
Seventeen people are vying to replace Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who is term-limited and unable to run this year. In that race and all others on the ballot, voters will pick one candidate. The top four vote-getters, regardless of party, advance to November.
There are 16 candidates for U.S. Senate, including Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan and Democratic challenger Mary Peltola. 
There are 15 candidates for U.S. House, including Republican incumbent Nick Begich III, independent challenger Bill Hill, and Democratic challenger Matt Schultz, who suspended his campaign last month and decided to back Hill.[Voter Guide: 2026 Voter Guide Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
As in the governor’s race, voters pick one candidate for each of those races, and the top four candidates advance to November.
There are 40 state House races and 10 state Senate races; each part of the state has one House race, and only half of the state has a state Senate race.
If there are four or fewer candidates for one or both of the legislative races, all candidates advance to November. Only five of the 50 legislative races have more than four candidates. 
On the back of the ballot, there’s also an up or down vote on Ballot Measure 1, which would reimpose limits on how much money that people can donate to political candidates. 
Ballot Measure 2, which has been the subject of extensive advertising, isn’t until November.
Where do I vote and what do I need to vote?
You can find your polling place by entering your information here. Bring a governmental ID; it doesn’t have to have your photo. If you don’t have an ID, bring a piece of mail with your name and address. 
If you can’t make it to your polling place on election day, you can go to another polling place and vote there, but you’ll be asked to provide additional identity information because that polling place won’t have a way to immediately check that you’re registered to vote.
What do I do if I want to vote by mail?
It’s too late to request a blank ballot. If you already have your blank ballot and need to return it, DO NOT just drop it into a mailbox. Your ballot must be postmarked by election day, and in Alaska, it may take a day or more for a ballot to be postmarked after it is mailed. Instead, go into a post office with your sealed ballot and ask the postal clerk to postmark it by hand. 
If you’re near a polling place, you can also drop your sealed ballot in the box there. 
How many people have already voted?
As of noon Monday, according to statistics published by the Division of Elections, almost 22,000 Alaskans had already voted early, in person at 10 polling stations in the Railbelt, Juneau and Nome. Another 9,000 voters had cast absentee ballots. 
That’s less than 5% of all eligible voters.
In early voting, a voter’s ID is checked when they cast their ballot, guaranteeing that the vote is counted. In absentee voting, the voter’s ID is checked later, and their ballot could be disqualified if elections officials aren’t able to verify that it was cast by an eligible voter. 
In 2020, 2022 and 2024, absentee ballots leaned Democratic, with election day results favoring Republicans and then leaning away from Republican candidates as additional votes were counted. 
This year, through Sunday, the division had received absentee ballots from 2,702 registered Republicans, 1,996 registered Democrats, and 4,467 undeclared and nonpartisan voters. 
Importantly, of the 22,838 blank absentee ballots requested by Alaska voters, only 9,232 had been returned by Sunday, indicating many more filled-out ballots could still be in the mail.
When do we know the results?
The Division of Elections has said the first partial, preliminary results will be available on its website about 9 p.m. Tuesday night. As more votes are counted, those results will be updated until early Wednesday morning, when elections officials take a break and go to sleep.
More counting may be needed on Wednesday or later this week to complete the election day tally.
Mailed ballots will be counted through Aug. 28, with results updated regularly through then. 
Any candidate who finishes in the final four can withdraw until Aug. 31. 
Governor and lieutenant governor run on a single ticket, and a governor can change out his or her lieutenant governor candidate until then as well.
Entering election day, six big questions remain unknowns.
Who will be the finalists in the governor’s race?
Pre-election polling indicated Democratic candidate Tom Begich was likely to finish first among the 17 candidates for governor. Because there are only two Democratic candidates, fellow Democratic candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins also appeared likely to finish in the top four.
What was less clear was which of the 12 Republican candidates would finish in the top four, and whether independent former Gov. Bill Walker would also make the cutoff. 
Will there be voting problems in rural Alaska?
In previous years, the Division of Elections has struggled to find election workers in rural towns and villages across Alaska. On Monday, observers tracking the division said the polling station in the North Slope community of Point Lay would open late because workers would not arrive until the morning flight.
In addition, prior elections saw elections officials reject an unusually large number of absentee ballots cast in rural Alaska. It isn’t yet clear whether that trend will continue this year.
On Saturday, the early voting station in Nome failed to open on time, an issue that helped prompt the Alaska Federation of Natives — in conjunction with other groups — to issue a statement saying they were deeply concerned by potential staffing issues and any effects on rural voters.
How enthusiastic are Democratic voters this year?
In other states that have already held their primary elections, Democratic voters turned out in large numbers, motivated by the desire to vote for candidates who oppose Republican President Donald Trump.
If the number of votes cast for statewide Democratic candidates exceeds or approaches the number of votes cast for statewide Republican candidates, that could indicate strong Democratic enthusiasm in Alaska as well, something that could affect the November result.
Two years ago, Democratic candidates posted unusually strong results in the August primary — but Alaska still voted for Trump by six percentage points and elected Republicans to statewide office.
Will any incumbents be voted out early in the Alaska Legislature?
Of the 50 state House and Senate races on the ballot Tuesday, there are only five with more than four candidates. Three of those races — two in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough and one in Eagle River — have incumbents. 
Incumbent lawmakers traditionally have an advantage in crowded primary elections because of name recognition and popularity, but it’s possible that one or more could lose. 
Rep. Garret Nelson, R-Sutton, was appointed to his office by Gov. Mike Dunleavy and is running for election for the first time against five challengers. Rep. Jamie Allard, R-Eagle River, is facing four challengers, as is Rep. Kevin McCabe, R-Big Lake.
In Bristol Bay, Speaker of the House Bryce Edgmon, I-Dillingham, is competing with four other candidates to replace Sen. Lyman Hoffman, D-Bethel, who is retiring as the longest-serving state legislator in Alaska history.
Seven people are competing to replace Edgmon in the state’s most crowded legislative race. 
Will donation limits return to Alaska’s state political campaigns?
In 2006, 73% of participating voters approved a ballot measure that limited the amount of money that a political candidate can receive from a person or group. 
A three-judge panel of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals overturned those limits in 2021, and the Dunleavy administration declined to fight the issue further.
Now, voters will be asked to reimpose some limits. The new measure isn’t as comprehensive as the last measure, in part because the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 2010 that states cannot limit third-party spending by groups acting independently of campaigns.
Those groups have flooded Alaskans’ mailboxes with mailers ahead of the primary, but stanching the flow could require an amendment to the U.S. Constitution or a new ruling by the Supreme Court.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: No pause on data centers but North Dakota special session to debate non-disclosure deals
description: North Dakota lawmakers will consider a temporary ban on non-disclosure agreements for data centers and other industrial developments during a September special session.  Legislative leaders also voted Monday to consider a line of credit for a stalled Military Gallery project, advance a technical correction to a property tax credit and debate two bills relate[...]
text:
Members of Legislative Management meet Aug. 17, 2026, to hear proposals for the upcoming special legislative session. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota lawmakers will consider a temporary ban on non-disclosure agreements for data centers and other industrial developments during a September special session. 
Legislative leaders also voted Monday to consider a line of credit for a stalled Military Gallery project, advance a technical correction to a property tax credit and debate two bills related to regulating kratom, the reason the governor called the special session.
An overall moratorium on data center development did not advance. Nor did a proposal to add funding to state childcare assistance, which has nearly 1,900 households on a waitlist.
No members of the committee voiced support for a controversial resolution to urge President Donald Trump to grant clemency for the men convicted of killing two federal officers in the 1983 Medina shootout.
Legislative Management also voted to set aside Sept. 1 to hear public testimony on the proposals, with the special session beginning Sept. 2.
Sen. Tim Mathern, D-Fargo, speaks during a meeting of Legislative Management on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Data center proposals
Sen. Tim Mathern, D-Fargo, proposed that lawmakers consider outlawing non-disclosure agreements between data center developers and public officials.
After feedback from other lawmakers, the proposal was expanded to include all industrial development, and the length of the ban was narrowed to the duration of this biennium ending June 30, 2027. 
“I believe it gets to the heart of concern of citizens around the state,” Mathern said. 
The subject will be studied by the Artificial Intelligence and Data Centers Committee, chaired by Rep. Jonathan Warrey, R-Casselton, in advance of the 2027 legislative session. 
Data centers, vapes, childcare aid emerge for North Dakota special session consideration

Some legislators expressed reservations about the proposal. Sen. Brad Bekkedahl, R-Williston, said he’d like to hear the impact it would have on the Department of Commerce’s economic development efforts during the session, but voted in favor of advancing it for further consideration. 
Mathern also proposed a moratorium on data center development, pausing new construction and expansion of existing facilities, through the end of the biennium. 
“The people are telling us they want a moratorium,” said Rep. LaurieBeth Hager, D-Fargo. “They want more time for things to be figured out before these big facilities go in their area.”
The bill did not advance, with Bekkedahl voicing concern about a moratorium preventing data centers in communities that support them. Sen. Janne Myrdal, R-Edinburg, encouraged the public to bring their concerns to the Artificial Intelligence and Data Centers Committee.
“To move a moratorium out of fear and suspicion, instead of using discernment and wisdom and digging into it openly, doesn’t solve the problem,” Myrdal said. 
The committee is scheduled to meet Sept. 1, but that may be rescheduled.
Sen. David Hogue, R-Minot, speaks during a meeting of Legislative Management on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Military Gallery funding
Lawmakers advanced a proposal for a $35 million line of credit from the state-owned Bank of North Dakota to resume construction of the state’s Military Gallery project on the Capitol grounds. The bill directs the line of credit to be paid back by the State Historical Society with donations.
Senate Majority Leader Sen. David Hogue, chair of Legislative Management, who is the primary sponsor, said the state is in “breach of contract” for the project. 
“The reason for that is that the North Dakota Historical Society, which is a state agency, has run out of money,” Hogue said. “What the bill does is allow construction to continue on as contemplated.”
Construction was paused on the project in early July. The Historical Society confirmed the project has two unpaid invoices for the months of June and July, totaling nearly $4.5 million. A representative for Kraus-Anderson Construction, which is leading the project, declined to comment Monday.
Line of credit, more oversight proposed for stalled North Dakota Military Gallery project

If the project hasn’t raised sufficient donations by March 2029, the proposal directs the Historical Society to request a deficiency appropriation from the Legislature. 
The $78 million project is so far coming in under budget at closer to $74.5 million, Hogue said. But if the Legislature doesn’t act, the project will start incurring additional costs, such as a temporary roof to winterize the uncompleted structure. 
Hogue’s bill would also shift oversight for the construction from an advisory committee to the Capitol Grounds Planning Commission, which includes four state lawmakers.
Myrdal voted to advance the proposal but said she plans to oppose the Military Gallery funding during the special session. She said she’s worried the fundraising will not be fulfilled.
“Going forward, we cannot put our state and our taxpayer monies at risk like this,” Myrdal said.
Legislative leaders did not advance a bill draft by Sen. Sean Cleary, R-Bismarck, that would require state agencies to secure 75% of nonstate funding before starting construction. Myrdal said that proposal could be revisited during the regular legislative session in January.
Sen. Kathy Hogan, D-Fargo, speaks during a meeting of Legislative Management on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Childcare assistance
Legislators in a 6-10 vote rejected a proposal from Senate Minority Leader Kathy Hogan to add $9 million for the Child Care Assistance Program. Hogan, D-Fargo, said her goal was to get low-income families off of a growing waitlist for childcare aid.
“We know we have an emerging childcare crisis that’s bad today, but if we don’t start addressing it now, we could lose, I think, up to 50% of our childcare slots within the next two years,” Hogan said.
Hogue said childcare funding across all of the state’s programs has increased from nearly $28 million during the 2021-23 biennium to about $112 million during the 2025-27 biennium.
Bekkedahl called the increasing amount the state spends on childcare “unsustainable.”
“The childcare crisis is very serious and growing in every community, so I think it’s really important for you to go home and learn about it in your own districts,” Hogan, who is retiring from the Legislature, told the lawmakers. “Because childcare is in trouble.”
Sen. Jeff Magrum, R-Hazelton, speaks during a meeting of Legislative Management on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
No clemency for Medina shootout
Sen. Jeff Magrum, R-Hazelton, asked lawmakers to consider a symbolic resolution urging Trump to grant clemency to Scott Faul and Yorie Kahl for the 1983 Medina shootout. They were convicted of killing U.S. Marshal Kenneth Muir and Deputy Marshal Robert S. Cheshire Jr. and are serving life sentences.
Magrum told lawmakers both men have spent 43 years in federal prison and had “paid their debt” to society.
The proposal will not go to the special session because no committee member made a motion to advance it.
In an interview, Myrdal, who chairs the interim Judiciary Committee, said people should trust the judiciary and parole system in the United States. She added the two men still have avenues to secure clemency through federal procedures.
“It was never going to pass,” she said. “No chance.”
Correction to property tax program
Lawmakers voted to advance a proposal from Sen. Dean Rummel, R-Dickinson, to make a technical correction related to the primary residence property tax credit. During January’s special session, lawmakers approved House Bill 1626, which changes how counties apply a 5% discount to homeowners who pay property taxes early.
The passage of that bill has had unintended consequences and is causing complications for property tax statements that need to be printed by the end of the year, Rummel said. The proposal would undo the action taken during the January special session, said Donnell Preskey, executive director of the North Dakota Auditors Association.
Other proposals
No other proposals advanced, including a bill draft from Rep. SuAnn Olson, R-Baldwin, to require North Dakota driver’s license tests to be conducted in English. 
Hogan pointed out no data was presented to suggest non-English speakers have a higher rate of traffic accidents than English speakers. The lawmaker said the employment rate for immigrants in Cass County is around 90% and that driving is often a necessity for a person to get to work in North Dakota. 
“This will become a huge employment barrier if they can’t get a driver’s license,” Hogan said.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Bills for kratom regulation, synthetic ban advance to North Dakota special session
description: North Dakota lawmakers on Monday advanced two complementary proposals to regulate kratom and ban synthetic substances.  The bill drafts, the result of a Kratom Working Group, will be considered in September during a special session called by Gov. Kelly Armstrong to address the substance’s lack of regulation in North Dakota.  A bill draft proposed by […]
text:
Sen. Michelle Axtman, R-Bismarck, speaks during a meeting of Legislative Management on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota lawmakers on Monday advanced two complementary proposals to regulate kratom and ban synthetic substances. 
The bill drafts, the result of a Kratom Working Group, will be considered in September during a special session called by Gov. Kelly Armstrong to address the substance’s lack of regulation in North Dakota. 
A bill draft proposed by Rep. Pat Heinert, R-Bismarck, would adopt regulations for natural kratom products that mimic existing laws for tobacco products like cigarettes. 
The bill would prohibit the sale of kratom products to anyone under 21 years old, create labeling requirements for kratom products that include a warning it may be addictive, and empower the attorney general to regulate the sale of such products in North Dakota. 
It also bans packaging that imitates candy products or otherwise is marketed in a manner that appeals to children.
“That has become a big thing in the kratom industry. Bright colors, flashy stuff,” Heinert said. “Those things are all marketed towards the underage people.”
Sen. Kathy Hogan, D-Fargo, said she considers Heinert’s proposed legislation to be a good starting point. 
Rep. Pat Heinert, R-Bismarck, speaks during a meeting of Legislative Management on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Sen. Janne Myrdal, R-Edinburg, said she doesn’t see the benefit of leaving kratom legal at all. 
“I would prefer a total ban because I don’t see how good this is for anyone,” Myrdal said. 
The second half of the working group’s legislation, proposed by Sen. Michelle Axtman, R-Bismarck, proposes a ban on synthetic derivatives of kratom such as 7-OH and any other derivatives that hit the market in the future. The bill also includes criminal penalties for use and possession of synthetic derivatives of kratom. 
“It matches the penalty structure of marijuana,” Axtman said. 
Use of synthetic derivatives of mitragynine, a chemical in kratom, would be an infraction for a person’s first offense and a misdemeanor for all future offenses. 
Possession of synthetic kratom derivatives would be considered an infraction for the first offense, misdemeanor on the second occasion, and a felony for all future incidents.
Axtman said the bill was written to add kratom synthetic derivatives as a Schedule I drug to match the expected action from the Drug Enforcement Administration. 
“That is their plan,” Axtman said. “This will match that.”
Both bills, if passed by the Legislature, would take effect as soon as they are filed with the secretary of state. 
Armstrong announced his plans to call for a special session during a press conference earlier this month, and on the same day he issued an executive order banning the sale of kratom products in the state for 30 days due to a public health emergency. 
The governor said his decision was prompted by the DEA’s move to temporarily classify 7-OH and three related compounds as controlled substances.

title: WA state Senate primary separated by 4 votes, set for recount
description: Two Democratic Washington state Senate hopefuls are headed for a recount as just four votes separate them for second place in the primary and a spot on the November ballot.  After examining challenged ballots Monday, Michael Shepard led Eamonn Collins with 13,125 votes to 13,121 in the 42nd Legislative District. Nearly 50,000 votes have been […]
text:
Left, Eamonn Collins and, right, Michael Shepard. (Photos courtesy of campaigns)Two Democratic Washington state Senate hopefuls are headed for a recount as just four votes separate them for second place in the primary and a spot on the November ballot. 
After examining challenged ballots Monday, Michael Shepard led Eamonn Collins with 13,125 votes to 13,121 in the 42nd Legislative District. Nearly 50,000 votes have been counted in total.
The results will be confirmed by a hand recount next week. Recounts don’t often shift electoral outcomes, but the counts are rarely this close. 
“For me, this is uncharted territory,” Shepard said Monday evening. He noted his campaign had been reaching out to voters with challenged ballots to resolve the concerns to ensure their votes could be counted.
Collins didn’t immediately return a request for comment.
The two Democrats are running for an open seat with Sen. Sharon Shewmake, D-Bellingham, forgoing reelection. Shepard or Collins will face Republican Erika Creydt, a psychologist and Blaine school board member, in November.
On Monday, the county canvassing board reviewed challenged ballots, of which there have been a few hundred. Those ballots either were unsigned or the signatures didn’t match those on file. Voters had until 4:30 p.m. Monday to cure ballots challenged for signature issues. An additional 125 votes were tallied Monday.
Going into Monday’s latest tally Shepard had climbed up to 20 votes ahead of Collins. At one point, Collins was just two votes behind Shepard. 
The district covers north Bellingham and rural Whatcom County, including Ferndale, Lynden and Blaine. In recent years, it has become more reliably blue. As recently as 2022, it was represented by a Republican state senator.
Shepard is a Bellingham port commissioner and anthropology instructor at Western Washington University endorsed by Shewmake. Collins, a science teacher at the Lummi Nation School, considers himself a grassroots progressive running to the left of Shepard’s more establishment lane. He’s also a former U.S. Senate policy adviser.
County results are set to be certified Tuesday. The secretary of state’s office will certify them by Friday.
The recount is expected to take about three days and additional time for the canvassing board to certify the final results, said Whatcom County Auditor Stacy Henthorn. The county election’s office will post further details about the recount online Tuesday afternoon, Henthorn said.
The bar for a manual recount like this is that candidates have to be separated by fewer than 150 votes and 0.25% of the total votes. A machine recount is triggered when the difference between two candidates is under 0.5% of the total ballots cast and fewer than 2,000 votes.
The top two candidates in Washington primaries advance to the general election regardless of party.

Creydt picked up 44.6% of the primary vote while the two Democratic candidates combined total was nearly 53%. That bodes well for the party’s chances of retaining the seat. Senate terms last four years.
Creydt, the only Republican in the race, leads the fundraising battle, bringing in $199,000. She’s spent almost all of it. Shepard has raised $105,000 and Collins $75,000.
The two Democrats recently filmed a video together for social media to discuss the close race and to commit to support whoever advances.
“If anyone ever tells you your vote doesn’t matter,” Shepard said, “think differently because we know it does.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Ashley Hinson speaks in support of $1.5 trillion defense funding package
description: U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson said Monday she supports providing the U.S. Department of Defense funding that allows the nation to have a strong military presence during their war with Iran. Earlier Monday, Hinson, who running for U.S. Senate in 2026, appeared alongside U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for a campaign event supporting U.S. Rep. Zach […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is running for Iowa's U.S. Senate seat, gave a speech at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Aug. 17, 2026 at the Iowa State Fair. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson said Monday she supports providing the U.S. Department of Defense funding that allows the nation to have a strong military presence during their war with Iran.
Earlier Monday, Hinson, who running for U.S. Senate in 2026, appeared alongside U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for a campaign event supporting U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn at JR’s Southpork Ranch. Hegseth called for Iowans to support Nunn’s reelection campaign in the 3rd District because President Donald Trump “needs the type of leaders who understand why a $1.5 trillion dollar budget, a one-time generational investment, is what is necessary” for the Defense Department.

Candidates speak at Register Soapbox
Monday was the third day of candidate speeches at The Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the state fair. Here’s the schedule.
Read about previous speakers:
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate: Josh Turek
Republican gubernatorial candidate: Zach Lahn
Democratic gubernatorial candidate: Rob Sand
Republican secretary of agriculture candidate: Mike Naig
Democratic secretary of state candidate: Ryan Peterman
Republican secretary of state candidate: Paul Pate
Democratic state treasurer candidate: John Norwood
Libertarian U.S. Senate candidate: Thomas Laehn
Independent 1st Congressional District candidate: Michael Bridgford
Republican 2nd Congressional District candidate: Joe Mitchell
Independent 2nd District Congressional District candidate:  Dave Bushaw
Libertarian 2nd District Congressional candidate: Rick Stewart
Republican 3rd Congressional District candidate: Zach Nunn
Democratic 3rd Congressional District candidate: Sarah Trone Garriott
Republican 4th Congressional District candidate:  Chris McGowan


Hegseth, who leads the department, made the $1.5 trillion request — the largest request in U.S. history — earlier in 2026, as the U.S. continues its conflict with Iran. But the defense secretary has faced trouble getting this budget across the finish line, with Politico reporting that some Republicans have expressed skepticism about the Trump administration’s large defense budget proposal, especially ahead of a contentious midterm election.
When asked about the funding proposal after speaking at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Monday, Hinson spoke about a bipartisan meeting with one of the vice chairmen of the Joint Chiefs of Staff to “talk about what the Department of War is going to need going forward across all the branches.”
“Let me say, I support our war fighters in this mission,” Hinson said. I want to make sure that our Iowans who are fighting, anyone who’s fighting, is resourced properly and has what they need. The most important thing is deterrence, not just with the situation with Iran, but other conflicts potentially around the world. So I think a strong military, as the secretary talked about, focusing on readiness, not DEI in the military, is going to continue to be my priority.
There are also concerns about the high price tag of the DOD budget request for people concerned about federal spending or an increased national debt. “I would say both parties are blaming for where we are right now in terms of government spending,” Hinson said, adding that she voted against a $6 trillion budget proposal from former President Joe Biden.
Hinson currently represents Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, but joined the Senate race after U.S. Sen. Joni Ernst, who currently holds the seat, announced she would not seek reelection. Hinson is running against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek in the upcoming midterm election.
Political forecasters rate the seat as “leans Republican” — a designation that means while Republicans are predicted to maintain control of the seat, it will be a more competitive race than seen in previous recent election cycles.
Hinson was met with a passionate crowd of  supporters — and some opponents — as she spoke at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Monday. While a majority of people held up signs supporting her campaign before she spoke, some in the crowd held signs saying “Decent Iowans Support Josh Turek,” and others posing questions to the congresswoman.
During her Soapbox speech, Hinson said Turek was an “absentee legislator,” and criticized him for attending a Democratic fundraising event instead of being present at the Iowa State Fair Monday. Turek has been at the fair previous days, and gave his own soapbox speech Friday.
Hinson said Turek “skipped” the Iowa State Fair Veterans’ Parade earlier Monday, “and he also skipped the vote to fund the Department of Veterans Affairs here in Iowa.”
Supporters of U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson’s campaign for U.S. Senate, as well as some opponents who are supporting Iowa Rep. Josh Turek, held up signs before her speech at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Aug. 17, 2026 at the Iowa State Fair. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
On Saturday, Turek was asked by reporters about criticisms that he had missed votes at the Iowa State Capitol this year. The Democrat responded that he was spending time “meeting Iowans all over the state” as he ran for U.S. Senate — then competing in a primary against Iowa Sen. Zach Wahls — and said his record showed he was an effective state legislator.
“Something that I’m very very proud of is my my time in the Iowa Legislature — one of the most effective, one of the most bipartisan,” Turek said. “Ashley Hinson has already also missed 193 votes in her six years up in Congress. … Look, when I joined the Iowa Legislature, I was told, ‘you’ll never get a subcommittee, you’ll never get a committee, you’ll certainly never get anything signed by the governor.’ And I went out there and I worked really, really hard behind the scenes –the kind of work that nobody you will see or hear from — to find strange bedfellows, build relationships across the aisle, and I was able to get a lot of policy to the finish line. That’s what’s missing in D.C., that’s exactly the kind of senator that I will be.”

title: Naig says Secretary of Agriculture race presents ‘distinct’ choice
description: Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig, speaking at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Monday, said he and his opponent have “fundamentally different” views of the office.  Naig is running against water quality researcher and advocate Chris Jones, who has the Democratic nomination for the seat. Jones has been critical of the large-scale farm model […[...]
text:
Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig speaks at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig, speaking at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Monday, said he and his opponent have “fundamentally different” views of the office. 
Naig is running against water quality researcher and advocate Chris Jones, who has the Democratic nomination for the seat. Jones has been critical of the large-scale farm model that is dependent on corn, soybeans and ethanol. 
“He just has a very fundamentally different opinion about how to work on the issues that we need to work on,” Naig said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Jones has suggested policies to improve water quality by taxing or restricting things like fertilizers and animal sales and banning things like new tile drainage lines, fall tillage and chemical applications to ditches. 
Naig said this approach would lead to a “smaller” and “diminished” agriculture. 
“That kind of taxing and regulating drives farmers out of business, which will put our land and our farms in the hands of fewer and fewer farmers, and that is the opposite of what we need to be seeing,” Naig said. “So there is a distinct difference between him and me when it comes to this race.” 
Meet Iowa’s secretary of agriculture candidates

Jones called the attacks “desperate” and said Naig has been “responsible for Iowa’s declining water quality for the past decade.” 
“Under Naig’s policies, the average Iowa farmer is sentenced to an endless and desperate cycle of trying to acquire more and more land, which has led to consolidation and driven the population downward in 70 of our 99 counties while hollowing out many of our small towns,” Jones said in a statement. “I think we need a new approach.”
Naig, who has held the position since 2018, said all Iowans “benefit from a strong agriculture.” 
“A strong agriculture leads to strong families and strong communities, and a stronger Iowa because of it,” Naig said. 
Naig said to continue supporting Iowa agriculture, the state needs to continue expanding international, national and local markets to make sure farmers can get paid for the things they grow and to secure more funding for conservation practices that improve water quality. 
Iowa has continued to adopt conservation practices like cover crops, but Naig said it’s “not good enough.” 
“We need to do more,” Naig said.
Cancer
Iowa’s high cancer incidence rates, which have also been tied to the state’s water quality concerns, has become a top issue in many of Iowa’s political races this year. 
While speaking to reporters about the subject, Naig said, “we’re not in a good place as a state.” 
“I think what we know is that this is more complex than what some want to make it, and I think you’ve got some who have decided that it’s a political issue, and I think that can be very dangerous,” Naig said. 
Farmers he has spoken with, he said, told him they are frustrated at being blamed for Iowa’s cancer crisis as many reports and groups point to nitrate concentrations in the water and pesticide exposure as cancer drivers. 
“It’s okay to to wonder, to ask questions, to want to know the causes, that’s where we need to go,” Naig said. “But let’s actually understand what’s going on, and then let’s address that.” 
Jones is slated to speak at the Soapbox Saturday, the full Soapbox schedule can be found here.
